issues.title: A world of wealth: 12 of the richest people who ever lived
issues.summary: How do you weigh Genghis Khan’s empire against Elon Musk’s shares? Meet 12 people from world history whose fortunes reveal just how many ways there are to be rich
issues.author: Jonny Wilkes
issues.content_html:
When it comes to sifting through history’s uber-wealthy and deciding exactly who was rolling in the biggest pile of cash, a myriad of issues arise. One that stymies historians and economists is how to go about adjusting values across different epochs and different, even defunct, currencies.

Then there’s how to distinguish between personal wealth (essentially, how much money a person has stuffed under their mattress) and the worth of holdings, whether that is in assets, land or glittering treasures. This is especially tricky with sovereign leaders: their domain might bring in spectacular wealth, but that does not necessarily make it their money.

Is it possible to compare Elon Musk – who, in June 2026, made history when a rise in his shares temporarily made him the world’s first trillionaire – with Genghis Khan, who built a colossal empire filled with lucrative resources and industries?

Identifying the richest people in history, therefore, is fraught with difficulty and open to infinite interpretation. Regardless, there's no doubting that these rulers, businessmen and bankers all had the deepest of deep pockets.

Amenhotep III (Unknown–c1353 BC)

Egyptian pharaoh whose wealth is estimated in the trillions of US dollars, though his personal fortune is unknown.

The pharaohs of ancient Egypt were, to put it mildly, not embarrassed about flaunting their wealth. Standing tall above them all as the wealthiest was Amenhotep III of the 18th Dynasty, during the 14th century BC.

His reign witnessed a golden age both for Egyptian culture and political power. Diplomats and leaders from other nations would write to Amenhotep simply to ask him for gifts of gold, such was his reputation. There is no knowing the value of his domain, or personal fortune, but suffice to say that it ran into the trillions, and since he was deified as a god, all of Egypt’s glory was indeed his.

Marcus Licinius Crassus (c115 BC–53 BC)

Roman statesman and general worth approximately 200 million sesterces, according to Pliny the Elder.

While Marcus Licinius Crassus reached the top of Roman politics as one-third of the First Triumvirate, he is better known as “the richest man in Rome”.

As a general, he prospered thanks to proscriptions (the confiscation of property belonging to enemies of the state) and as a businessman, he was a ruthless estate agent and bought up many of the houses in Rome. One of his tricks was to set up his own fire brigade and offer to put out any houses that caught ablaze when the owners promised to sell it to him for slashed prices.

Crassus’s wealth is hard to gauge in modern terms, although Pliny the Elder claimed he had 200 million sesterces, which equated to the entire annual budget of the Roman Republic. Such was his reputation for lucre that a rumour spread after his death in 53 BC that his enemies had poured molten gold down his throat.

Augustus (63 BC–AD 14)

Roman emperor worth approximately US$4.6 trillion, based on his estimated share of the imperial economy.

Calculating the personal wealth of a historical ruler is enough to give historians and economists alike a headache, but the sums attached to Augustus are truly head-spinning.

Not only did he oversee the finances of a mighty empire, but, after defeating Mark Antony and Cleopatra, he took ownership over Egypt. To be clear, the land of the pharaohs did not just become part of the Roman world – it was a personal province of Augustus. Estimates about what this did to his wealth suggest that he owned one-fifth of the imperial economy, which has been translated into a modern-day value of $4.6 trillion (almost £3.5 trillion).

Wu Zetian (AD 624–705)

Empress of China who ruled an economy valued at approximately US$16 trillion.

On top of being the only female emperor in China’s history, Wu Zetian may well hold the title as the richest woman of all time.

Having ruled the Tang Dynasty alongside her husband and in the name of her sons for decades, in AD 690 she proclaimed her own Zhou Dynasty and acted as sole sovereign for 15 years. Under her efficient and brutal leadership, the empire expanded and the economy flourished with the tea and silk trades to western nations. In fact, while she was empress, China accounted for around 23 per cent of the global GDP, which has been estimated to be at the $16 trillion (almost £12 trillion) mark. For context, the richest woman today – Alice Walton, the heiress of Walmart – has a fortune 120 times smaller.

William the Conqueror (c1028–1087)

King of England worth approximately US$230 billion.

After seizing the English throne in 1066, the conquering Duke of Normandy set about confiscating vast swathes of land and bringing the resources of the country under his personal control. For the next 20 years, revenue poured in through rents, taxation and plundered treasures, and William the Conqueror protected his position and his purse with new castles, most famously the White Tower, the central fortification of the Tower of London.

Not content with accumulating wealth for himself alone, he also handed out huge sums to his allies. One relative, Alan Rufus, received such extravagant rewards for his military service in the Norman Conquest that his fortune ballooned to around $194 billion (almost £145 billion), just off the pace of William’s $230 billion (£170 billion).

Mansa Musa (c1280–c1337)

Ruler of the Mali Empire worth approximately US$400 billion, by a speculative estimate.

A name that crops up on every list of the historical rich is Mansa Musa.

In the first half of the 14th century, he presided over the pinnacle of the Mali Empire, a vast realm in West Africa rich in gold and salt, and strategically placed for trade routes. Mansa Musa is often credited as the richest person in history due to his dragon-sitting-on-a-treasure-sized piles of gold, with his mines supplying the Islamic world. Most famously, when he embarked on a hajj to Mecca in 1324, he travelled with 60,000 people and long caravans of slaves, dressed in Persian silk, each carrying gold bars.

According to accounts of his fabulous parades in Cairo, Mansa Musa handed out so much gold that it caused a major devaluation of the precious metal and a currency crisis that lasted years. A conservative estimate of his adjusted wealth is $400 billion (almost £300 billion), although many historians refuse to give a figure at all, instead claiming his wealth was beyond calculation.

Jakob Fugger (1459–1525)

German merchant and banker worth up to US$400 billion.

As the man behind the scenes and pulling the purse strings of medieval politics, Jakob Fugger was far wealthier than emperors, kings and popes.

Born in 1459 into a successful merchant family, he possessed a canny head for business and bookkeeping, shifting from Italian textiles to a more diverse portfolio. Most lucratively, he engaged in silver and copper mining, and tried his hand as a banker. Offering loans to the rich and powerful made him even richer and more powerful, with every deal negotiated bringing in assets and compounding wealth. He funded military campaigns, loaned to the Vatican and acted as chief financier of the Habsburgs, securing the position of Holy Roman Emperors.

On his death in 1525, he left a fortune of 2 million guilders; in today’s money Fugger the Rich may have been worth as much as $400 billion (£300 billion).

Heshen (1750–1799)

Chinese imperial official worth up to US$270 billion.

Heshen has been described as the most corrupt official in Chinese history.

As a favourite of the Qianlong Emperor in the 18th century, he gained control over ministerial posts and imperial revenue, which allowed him to steal funds and take bribes on an almost-industrial scale. At the same time, he built his own commercial empire of banks and pawnshops. During a revolt in 1796, he made sure the military campaign to put it down was prolonged so that he could pocket money being allocated to the army. It all came crashing down with the death of the emperor in 1799, with Heshen arrested and forced to put himself to death. His property was seized, valued at 1.1 billion taels of silver, or possibly as much as $270 billion (£200 billion) in today’s money.

Andrew Carnegie (1835–1919)

Scottish-American steel industrialist worth over US$300 billion before his major charitable gifts.

Andrew Carnegie made his fortune with steel.

Born to a poor family in Scotland and immigrating to the United States as a child, he built a career at the Pennsylvania Railroad Company before setting up the first steel plants in the country in the 1870s. By the time he sold Carnegie Steel in 1901, it was worth around two per cent of the entire US gross domestic product (GDP). While that fortune – adjusted to over $300 billion (£225 billion) – earns his place on this list, Carnegie did not die in 1919 as one of history’s wealthiest people. After retiring, he dedicated his life to philanthropic pursuits and gave way most of his money, espousing the mantra: “The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.”

John D Rockefeller (1839–1937)

American oil industrialist worth well over US$300 billion.

The Rockefeller name is a bulwark of American business: throughout the 20th century, it became synonymous with wealth and success, thanks to its patriarchal figurehead. John D Rockefeller founded Standard Oil Company in 1870, correctly predicting the potential impact of oil on the modern world, and under his leadership, the company grew so powerful that it refined more than 90 per cent of all the oil in the United States. He held the monopoly on what was quickly becoming one of the most precious resources, accruing a fortune worth well over $300 billion (almost £225 billion) today.

In 1916, he was recognised as the first American to hit the magic ten figures to become a billionaire.

Henry Ford (1863–1947)

American automobile industrialist worth up to US$200 billion.

Henry Ford forever changed the world of the 20th century by making the automobile available to the mass market and revolutionising industrial practices through the introduction of assembly line production.

His Ford Motor Company, founded in 1903, unveiled the Model T and sold 15 million of them around the world over the next two decades (no car sold more until the Volkswagen Beetle). Needless to say, this made Ford a fabulous fortune. He joined the billionaire club in the 1920s, only a few years after John D Rockefeller, and by the time of this death in 1947 he had the equivalent of up to $200 billion (£150 billion) today. And, of course, Ford's company is still going strong.

Osman Ali Khan (1886–1967)

Nizam of Hyderabad worth upwards of US$200 billion.

Here’s how rich Osman Ali Khan was: he used the Jacob Diamond – a 184-carat masterpiece and one of the largest diamonds in the world – as a paperweight. During his 37-year reign as nizam (ruler) of the Indian state of Hyderabad (1911-48), he built his monumental wealth by issuing his own currency and controlling the world’s primary diamond mines, including where the Jacob and Koh-i-Noor were unearthed.

His private treasury was reportedly bursting with gold, silver and precious jewels, which would be worth upwards of $200 billion (almost £150 billion) today. No wonder the cover of a 1937 issue of Time magazine described him as “the richest man in the world”.

issues.title: Acceptance and commitment therapy linked to neural shifts in the depressed brain
issues.summary: An eight-week therapeutic program aimed at improving psychological flexibility helped patients with depression reduce obsessive rumination. Brain scans show the therapy strengthened neural connectivity in regions responsible for emotional regulation.
issues.author: Karina Petrova
issues.content_html:
Acceptance and Commitment Therapy reduces depression symptoms and is associated with changes in brain activity in areas responsible for emotional regulation. Brain scans of adults with major depressive disorder showed that this specific therapeutic approach alters neural connectivity related to obsessive, negative thinking. The small study was published in Brain Imaging and Behavior.

Major depressive disorder is a widespread psychiatric condition that causes persistent sadness and a lack of interest in life. While antidepressant medications and traditional talk therapies help many people, a large portion of patients do not experience full recovery. Because of this, mental health professionals continue to explore alternative therapeutic methods.

One such method is Acceptance and Commitment Therapy. Unlike traditional cognitive behavioral therapy, which attempts to change the content of a person’s negative thoughts, this alternative encourages people to change their relationship with those thoughts. The goal is to build psychological flexibility so that patients can live a meaningful life even when experiencing internal distress.

A primary concept in this therapy is cognitive fusion. This happens when individuals treat their internal verbal thoughts as absolute truths or literal reality, rather than just passing mental events. For instance, a person might have the thought “I am a burden” and treat it as a factual reality, leading to psychological distress and avoidance behaviors.

Therapists use this framework to promote cognitive defusion, helping patients distance themselves from rigid thought patterns. While clinical trials show that the therapy works well for depression, the biological changes it produces in the brain remain largely unmapped. Brain imaging research on this specific therapy is scarce compared to traditional cognitive behavioral therapy.

To understand how this intervention physically affects the brain, researchers in South Korea organized a clinical trial. The investigative team included Sang Won Lee, Seungho Kim, Hyunsoo Kim, Yongmin Chang, and Seung Jae Lee from Kyungpook National University. They wanted to track neural activity before and after patients completed a specialized treatment program.

The research team recruited 42 adults diagnosed with major depressive disorder. The researchers note that this relatively small sample size limits the generalizability and statistical power of the findings. Differences in baseline age and education between the participants were not statistically significant.

Half of the participants were randomly assigned to an eight-week, group-based Acceptance and Commitment Therapy program. The other 21 participants were placed on a waitlist. This waitlist group served as a baseline comparison to help the researchers measure the specific effects of the therapeutic intervention.

All participants underwent clinical evaluations and functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI, before the eight-week period began. An fMRI scanner tracks blood flow in the brain to measure neural activity in real-time. During the scanning sessions, the researchers asked participants to complete a specific psychological task.

The task was designed to trigger cognitive fusion by forcing participants to merge their thoughts with real-world consequences. Before entering the scanner, patients provided the names of two people they felt close to, as well as two neutral acquaintances. Inside the machine, participants read negative statements involving these individuals.

For example, they were prompted to imagine one of their close friends or family members experiencing a severe car accident. The patients then rated the intensity of their emotional response using a simple scale and recorded how quickly they reacted. This exercise forces the brain to process distressing, imaginary scenarios as if they were actual events.

After eight weeks, both the therapy group and the waitlist group returned for a second round of psychological assessments and fMRI scans. The researchers then compared the pre-treatment and post-treatment data to look for biological and behavioral shifts.

The behavioral results showed that the therapy group experienced distinct improvements. Patients who completed the eight-week program reported a reduction in the severity of their depressive symptoms. They also displayed lower levels of cognitive fusion and experiential avoidance compared to their baseline scores.

During the imaginary accident task, the therapy group showed reduced emotional intensity. They also reacted faster to the negative prompts. The waitlist control group did not display these behavioral improvements, remaining relatively unchanged from their initial tests.

The brain imaging data provided a biological mirror for these psychological changes. The researchers observed increased activation in two specific brain regions among the therapy group. These regions are the medial prefrontal cortex and the anterior cingulate cortex.

The medial prefrontal cortex is located near the front of the brain and helps manage attention and emotional responses. The anterior cingulate cortex, situated deeper in the brain, plays a major role in emotional control and processing conflicting information. In people with depression, these two regions often show reduced activity during emotional tasks.

The therapy program appeared to boost activity in these regulatory centers. The researchers noted that higher activity in these areas correlated with a drop in depressive symptoms and obsessive thoughts. The faster reaction times during the scanner task also lined up with increased activation in these emotion-regulating zones.

Beyond overall activity levels, the researchers looked at how different parts of the brain communicated with each other. They found enhanced neural connectivity between the medial prefrontal cortex and a region called the posterior cingulate cortex. These linked areas are part of the brain’s default mode network.

The default mode network usually becomes active when a person is resting, daydreaming, or engaging in self-reflection. In depression, the default mode network is often associated with rumination. Rumination is the habit of continuously dwelling on negative feelings and past events.

The brain scans showed that stronger communication between the medial prefrontal cortex and the posterior cingulate cortex correlated with lower scores on a rumination questionnaire. By strengthening this neural pathway, the therapy may help patients break out of repetitive, negative thought loops.

While the results provide biological context for how the therapy works, the experimental design has several limitations. The trial compared the therapy to a waitlist group rather than an active alternative treatment. As a result, the researchers cannot state whether these neural changes are unique to Acceptance and Commitment Therapy or if they would occur with any form of structured psychological support.

Additionally, most participants continued taking their prescribed antidepressant medications throughout the eight-week study. The study could not completely isolate the effects of the talk therapy from the ongoing effects of the medication. The chemical influence of the antidepressants might interact with the behavioral therapy in ways the scans cannot fully separate.

The psychological surveys used to measure concepts like psychological flexibility and experiential avoidance also present measurement challenges. One of the questionnaires, the Acceptance and Action Questionnaire-II, overlaps with general feelings of distress, depression, and anxiety. This overlap makes it difficult to tell if patients truly improved their psychological flexibility or simply felt less distressed overall.

Finally, the researchers only measured outcomes immediately after the eight-week program ended. It remains unknown how long these brain alterations persist after the treatment concludes. Future studies with extended follow-up periods will be necessary to determine the long-term durability of these neural changes.

The study, “Neural correlates of acceptance and commitment therapy in major depressive disorder: a task-based fMRI study,” was authored by Sang Won Lee, Seungho Kim, Hyunsoo Kim, Yongmin Chang, and Seung Jae Lee.

issues.author: Eric W. Dolan
issues.content_html:
Professional artists who painted under the influence of LSD produced markedly more abstract works than they did before taking the drug, according to a new reanalysis of archived mid-century artworks published in Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts. At the same time, blind evaluations by art experts detected no meaningful boost in the paintings’ overall creativity or aesthetic appeal, and no reliable drop in technical skill. The findings indicate that while psychedelic experiences can shift an artist’s visual style toward abstraction, they do not necessarily make the finished work more creative.

Lysergic acid diethylamide, commonly known as LSD, is a potent hallucinogenic substance that alters visual perception, emotion, and thought primarily by stimulating specific serotonin receptors in the brain. Alongside renewed clinical interest in psychedelic substances over the past two decades, anecdotal accounts from technology workplaces and visual arts communities have popularized the claim that taking LSD in either tiny microdoses or full hallucinogenic amounts can unlock artistic breakthroughs. Yet subjective impressions during a drug experience can be misleading, making it difficult to tell whether a substance genuinely improves creative work or merely makes ideas feel deeper in the moment.

In psychological science, creativity is typically defined as the ability to produce something that is both original and fitting or effective for its context. Reaching that balance requires two complementary modes of thinking: divergent thinking, which involves loosening mental filters to generate many unusual ideas, and convergent thinking, which involves focused attention to evaluate, refine, and execute the best options. Neuroimaging research indicates that psychedelics temporarily disrupt communication across brain networks responsible for self-focused thought and executive control, a shift that theoretical models suggest may encourage free-flowing associations while interfering with deliberate evaluation.

Controlled studies have largely echoed that distinction rather than confirming popular claims of an all-purpose creative boost. For instance, a 2023 meta-analysis comparing 12 creativity-enhancement methods in adults found that cognitive-manipulation drugs were the least effective option and essentially ineffective at boosting creativity, whereas non-drug approaches such as structured training courses, meditation, and cultural exposure produced meaningful gains.

Similarly, a 2022 double-blind, placebo-controlled experiment with 24 healthy volunteers found that a low 50-microgram dose of LSD increased novel associations and symbolic thinking on laboratory tasks while reducing convergent thinking and practical usefulness. Even so, a 2022 integrative review of 11 psychedelic creativity studies pointed out that nearly all modern trials tested brief puzzle-like thinking exercises rather than evaluating finished works of art.

To examine how LSD relates to finished visual art, study authors Mathilde Firmin and Baptiste Barbot of the Psychological Sciences Research Institute at UCLouvain in Belgium, with Barbot also affiliated with the Child Study Center at Yale University, conducted a new reanalysis with colleagues using rare mid-century archival materials.

“Research on psychedelics has focused primarily on their therapeutic potential, particularly for alleviating depression and anxiety,” Firmin and Barbot told PsyPost. “Far less attention has been paid to their potential to enhance creativity, and almost none to the creative product itself, such as artworks. Our study set out to address this gap in the literature and offer a more modern perspective on the subject. We also had a unique opportunity to revisit a historical dataset from the 1950s using modern scientific methods and knowledge, reviving Oscar Janiger’s rich collection of artworks from professional artists.”

That historical collection originated with psychiatrist Oscar Janiger, who administered LSD to more than 900 adults in Los Angeles between 1954 and 1962 to document the subjective effects of the drug. As part of that broader project, Janiger invited 60 established professional artists into a naturalistic studio stocked with drawing, painting, and sculpting supplies, asking them to create artworks before taking LSD and again while under its influence. Participants were often encouraged to depict a Hopi kachina doll, a traditional carved figure, though Janiger gave them freedom to choose their own media and subjects so the creative process would feel authentic.

Although Janiger and a colleague published an initial assessment of 250 paintings from 20 of those artists in 1989, reporting that the LSD works looked more abstract, aesthetically pleasing, and creative despite appearing more fragmented, that early report had notable methodological flaws. The paintings had been handpicked by the researchers rather than sampled systematically, and all ratings came from a single college art professor who knew the purpose of the project. Firmin, Barbot, and their team hypothesized that under rigorous modern testing, paintings made during acute LSD intoxication would score higher in creativity, aesthetic appeal, and abstraction, while scoring lower in technical precision.

Working from archival materials made available by Oscar Janiger’s son, study co-author Robert Janiger, the researchers photographed and cross-referenced the collection of 250 artworks against original study records to confirm who created each piece and when it was made relative to dosing. Because 110 pieces lacked verified records of the artist’s identity, production date, or timing relative to LSD administration, those works were excluded from the reanalysis. The final dataset comprised 140 verified artworks created by 20 experienced professional artists, six of whom remained anonymous in the surviving files, including 33 baseline pieces made before taking LSD and 107 pieces produced during the drug’s acute effects.

According to the original study records, every participating artist first passed a medical and psychiatric screening to rule out severe personality disorders as well as heart, liver, or kidney conditions. After completing an average of roughly two baseline artworks (ranging from one to six pieces), each artist received a standardized moderate-to-high dose of LSD calibrated to body weight at 2.5 micrograms per kilogram, and began creating new art roughly an hour later. Working with materials such as oil paint, watercolors, tempera, pastels, pen and ink, and graphite on paper, canvas, or cardboard, artists produced an average of nearly six works during the LSD session (ranging from one to 24 pieces), and later wrote reflections once the drug wore off and again 30 days afterward.

To rescore the 140 digitized, untitled artworks, the researchers recruited six judges from the United States, the United Kingdom, and Belgium: four specialists with more than 10 years of experience in the art field and extensive experience rating art, plus two quasi-experts, consisting of a doctoral student in art history and a formally trained artist with 35 years of professional design and creative experience. The panel used an online adaptation of the Consensual Assessment Technique, an established method in which knowledgeable judges rely on their own subjective understanding of a domain to evaluate creative products.

Each judge independently rated every randomly ordered image on a 7-point scale across four separate criteria: creativity, aesthetic appeal, technical quality, and level of abstraction, with no information about the study’s purpose, the involvement of LSD, or whether a piece was created before or during the drug session. After combining the 3,360 individual ratings into consensus scores using a statistical model that adjusts for how strictly or leniently individual judges use the scale, the researchers capped one extreme creativity score at three standard deviations from the average so a single outlier would not skew the results. All underlying data and analytical code were posted publicly on the Open Science Framework, and the team fitted linear mixed-effects models to account for artists producing multiple pieces within a single session.

Preliminary checks measured interrater consistency on a 0-to-1 scale, where standard guidelines treat values from .50 to .75 as moderate, .75 to .90 as good, and above .90 as excellent. Consistency among the six judges was moderate to good for aesthetic appeal (.71), creativity (.72), and technical quality (.79), and excellent for abstraction (.92). On the resulting standardized consensus scale, where scores are centered around zero and one unit equals a standard deviation, creativity, aesthetic appeal, and technical quality were strongly positively correlated with one another, whereas abstraction varied mostly independently and showed mild negative associations with the other three traits.

When comparing artworks created before and during LSD intoxication, abstraction was the only dimension that changed reliably, climbing by 0.80 points on the standardized consensus scale, a large effect size reflecting a shift away from literal portraits and kachina dolls toward nonrepresentational shapes, colors, and symbols. Differences between pre-LSD and acute-LSD paintings were not statistically significant for creativity, aesthetic appeal, or technical quality, and a secondary check averaging scores by artist across sessions (using a repeated-measures analysis of variance) reached the same conclusion. Although a separate check excluding the two quasi-experts showed a small, marginal uptick in creativity, dropping those two judges also lowered interrater consistency for creativity from .72 to .60, meaning the uptick came from a less reliable rating pool.

“The increase in abstraction was large in size, meaning the shift toward more abstract artworks after LSD was substantial and clearly detectable by raters,” the researchers explained. “For creativity, aesthetic appeal, and technical quality, effects were negligible to very small in size (although going in the expected direction), but with no statistically significant differences between pre-LSD and acute LSD artworks. It is possible that our limited sample size prevented us from detecting effects of smaller magnitude.”

Those null findings stand in direct contrast to Janiger’s 1989 report on the same broader archive, highlighting how blind evaluation by multiple independent judges can alter conclusions drawn from historical experiments.

“Our findings differ from Janiger’s original work, which reported higher creativity in artworks made under LSD,” Firmin and Barbot said. “A key difference is that the original study relied on a single rater based on artistic productions likely selected a priori by the researcher, whereas we used blind ratings from six raters with the Consensual Assessment Technique, a more rigorous method and a selection of artistic productions picked ‘at random.’ This shows how historical data can gain new value when re-examined with modern methods.”

To make sense of why LSD did not translate into higher creativity ratings, the authors point to how the drug pulls different stages of creative thought in opposite directions. Prior research has found that even a low 50-microgram dose can impair focus and practical utility, and the authors note that the 2.5-microgram-per-kilogram dose used in Janiger’s sessions falls in a normal-to-high range that may stimulate loose idea generation while hindering the convergent evaluation needed to develop and finish a cohesive painting.

Psychedelics also tend to heighten feelings of personal meaning; artists in Janiger’s sessions expressed wonder as colors flowed from the brush onto the canvas, and one participant wrote in a follow-up report that LSD had intensified their creative process, suggesting the drug may elevate subjective inspiration without improving objective quality in the eyes of outside judges.

This gap between subjective inspiration and objective quality aligns with a 2021 placebo-controlled neuroimaging study, which found that psilocybin impaired acute performance on cognitive creativity tests even as volunteers felt more insightful. By contrast, a systematic review and meta-analysis of classic psychedelics and MDMA suggested tentative post-acute gains on cognitive creativity tests more than 24 hours after dosing. Both earlier findings, however, rest on laboratory problem-solving tasks rather than expert ratings of professional artists’ paintings created under the direct influence of LSD.

For aesthetic appeal, the researchers suggest that the stylistic shift from representational kachina dolls and self-portraits before LSD to abstract imagery during the trip may have complicated comparisons, since personal preference for an artistic style strongly shapes beauty ratings. Abstract art also tends to provoke wider disagreement among viewers and depends heavily on historical and contextual cues that were stripped from these digitized, untitled images. Together with possible shifts in taste between mid-century California art circles and contemporary judges, wider dispersion in how the six raters scored abstract pieces may have made subtle differences in aesthetic appeal harder to detect.

To account for the pronounced shift toward abstraction, the authors offer two complementary possibilities. One is that the altered state of consciousness induced by LSD pulls an artist’s attention away from precise, literal details toward raw, free-flowing visual elements, consistent with follow-up notes in which participants described losing interest in formal structure and becoming absorbed in color alone. A second possibility is that artists turned to abstract and symbolic forms intentionally as a way to depict the geometric patterns, shifting shapes, heightened colors, and intense emotions of their visual hallucinations.

As for technical execution, anecdotal notes showed that intoxication still posed practical hurdles for some participants, including one artist who labeled a work as a picture of a man trying and failing to draw the kachina doll. Even so, overall technical quality ratings across the sample held steady during the LSD sessions.

“We expected several changes after LSD, but the decline in technical quality was the one we expected most, since skill is widely assumed to suffer under the influence of psychoactive substances,” Firmin and Barbot noted. “Instead, we found no reliable difference in technical quality before and after LSD, which was quite surprising. However, artistic expertise may play a role here, since the participants were established artists. Perhaps their expert technical skills could help ‘compensate’ for the otherwise detrimental effect of LSD on technicality. A study with non-expert artists would be worth doing.”

There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. Because every participant knew they had received LSD and completed their baseline pieces first, the design cannot separate the drug’s pharmacological action from participants’ expectations or the natural progression of warming up during a studio session, and results from established professionals may not extend to everyday creative activities among non-artists.

“There is a general belief that LSD improves creativity (e.g., psychedelic resurgence movement),” the researchers cautioned. “Although our study did not detect a significant effect of LSD on the creativity of professional artwork, we cannot conclude that LSD has no effect on creativity. We found no significant difference in creativity before and after LSD, but our sample was small (20 artists, 140 paintings), which may have limited our ability to detect effects. The study also had no placebo group, so we describe LSD as linked to greater abstraction rather than as its proven cause.”

Working with mid-century archives introduced several additional constraints. Because artists typically completed only one or two works before taking LSD compared with a much larger set during the drug session, those sparse pre-LSD samples may offer less reliable estimates of each artist’s baseline quality. Excluding 110 imperfectly documented artworks further shrank the sample, surviving files lacked exact timestamps and verified individual dosage records (although there was no reason to believe sessions departed from Janiger’s standard protocol), and evaluating digitized photographs may have obscured surface texture, luminosity, and mid-century California art conventions.

“Because this was a re-analysis of historical data with inherent methodological limitations (e.g., no placebo group), more modern, placebo-controlled research is needed,” the researchers emphasized.

“In general, studies of this kind are difficult to conduct today because the risk-benefit ratio of administering LSD to investigate artistic creativity, or creativity more broadly, is often considered unfavorable by ethical review boards,” Firmin and Barbot pointed out. “As a result, undertaking a direct follow-up study would be challenging. The dataset examined here is therefore unique, and we believe that, despite its limitations, archival research of this nature can provide valuable insights into questions that would be difficult, if not impossible, to address through contemporary data collection.”

Looking ahead, the authors suggest that researchers could examine remaining archival works from nonprofessional participants or conduct longitudinal studies tracking whether artists draw lasting inspiration from past psychedelic experiences once the drug has worn off. They also propose using immersive virtual reality to simulate hallucinatory visual environments while participants draw or paint, offering a safe, controlled way to test whether altered perceptual experiences can shift artistic style without administering psychoactive substances.

The study, “Creativity Under LSD: A Reanalysis of Oscar Janiger’s LSD Studies Among Professional Artists,” was authored by Mathilde Firmin, Clément Laloux, Robert Janiger, and Baptiste Barbot.

issues.title: Common classroom accommodations for ADHD fail to improve student behavior or schoolwork in clinical trial
issues.summary: In a clinical trial of elementary students with ADHD, extra time, frequent breaks, standing desks, and low-distraction workspaces failed to improve behavior or schoolwork. Meanwhile, structured behavioral supports and stimulant medication substantially reduced classroom rule-breaking.
issues.author: Eric W. Dolan
issues.content_html:
A clinical trial published in JAMA Pediatrics provides evidence that four widely used classroom accommodations for children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) do not improve student behavior or academic performance. In contrast, structured behavioral classroom supports and a moderate dose of stimulant medication both substantially reduced classroom rule-breaking, while medication also increased assignment completion and quiz scores.

The findings suggest that schools seeking to help students with ADHD succeed may achieve better results from active behavioral strategies than from standard classroom accommodations.

Why classroom accommodations for ADHD needed a test

ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by ongoing difficulties sustaining attention, curbing impulsive actions, and regulating physical restlessness. In elementary school classrooms, those traits frequently surface as trouble staying seated, following classroom rules, completing independent worksheets, and keeping up with group lessons.

In the United States, roughly half of students diagnosed with ADHD receive formal educational services through individualized education programs under federal special education law or Section 504 plans under disability civil rights law. These plans routinely center on academic accommodations, which are adjustments to classroom surroundings, work schedules, or testing conditions meant to help students complete the same assignments as their classmates. Common examples include extra time on assignments and quizzes, frequent short breaks, noise-canceling headphones with desk dividers, and permission to stand while working.

Keeping students with ADHD engaged in schoolwork involves more than simply blocking out hallway noise or visual clutter. For instance, an earlier classroom study of children with ADHD indicated that students with the condition were especially prone to internal mind-wandering, which lowered their classroom work output when they were anticipating a reward, while stimulant medication lengthened reaction times on a sustained attention task without improving productivity in that classroom setting.

Clinical guidelines for elementary school children with ADHD generally recommend stimulant medications, which act on brain chemical signaling involved in focus and self-control, alongside positive behavioral interventions, which use structured expectations, frequent specific praise, daily behavior goals, and earned privileges.

Ordinary teacher reminders alone rarely match the impact of systematic reinforcement; a 2026 single-student classroom study observed that a first-grader with ADHD stayed focused on assignments for only about a minute and a half when teachers relied on routine verbal prompts, whereas introducing structured positive reinforcement extended the student’s on-task time.

Even though accommodations are common in school plans, researchers had not systematically tested how they perform on their own or alongside behavioral therapy and stimulant medication. To test all three approaches separately and together, Gregory A. Fabiano, a professor of psychology at Florida International University and co-author of the book “Daily Behavior Report Cards,” led a clinical trial at the university’s Center for Children and Families, one of its preeminent programs, and its Center for Children and Families of Western New York.

“Children with ADHD experience considerable difficulties in school settings, and this is coupled with concerning long-term academic outcomes,” Fabiano told PsyPost. “Given this, it is critical that we are adequately supporting and treating these children, to give them the best opportunity to proceed. One of the most common approaches includes provision of academic accommodations such as extra time to complete tasks or a low distraction workspace, but these approaches have typically not been rigorously evaluated to see if they work.”

Inside the summer classroom crossover trial

The researchers conducted a crossover randomized clinical trial registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, with the study protocol and statistical analysis plan published alongside the paper. Rather than dividing participants into separate permanent groups, a crossover design rotates every child through every treatment condition in a randomized, counterbalanced order so that each student serves as their own comparison.

Across four summers from 2022 to 2025 at sites in the southeastern and northeastern United States, the team screened 306 children in kindergarten through sixth grade and enrolled 280 who met diagnostic criteria for ADHD based on parent and teacher symptom ratings and caregiver diagnostic interviews. Children with an IQ below 70, prior adverse reactions to methylphenidate, a school suspension or expulsion in the past year, psychosis, or higher-support-needs autism were excluded.

Of the 280 enrolled children, 25 did not start the summer program, including six whose families had concerns about medication or side effects. Among the 255 children (79 percent male and 21 percent female) who began the intervention, 235 completed the trial; of the 20 who left early, 11 departed to pursue alternative treatments, four left over medication or side-effect concerns, three had scheduling conflicts, and two no longer wished to participate.

The study took place inside a structured eight-week summer treatment program, which was adjusted to seven weeks with modified block lengths and added class periods for the fourth cohort due to local school calendars. Grouped by age into classes of 12 to 15 peers, students attended two one-hour classroom sessions each day before spending the remaining hours in recreational activities such as sports, board games, and arts and crafts. Each classroom was staffed by a teacher and an aide who completed a week of intensive training and received daily supervisor feedback, following prescribed procedures 97 percent of the time during seatwork and 94 percent of the time during lessons.

During the first daily class hour, students worked independently at desks on reading, math, and language arts assignments. During the second class hour, teachers led a whole-group science or social studies lesson followed by small-group cooperative tasks and a 10-question multiple-choice quiz scored from 0 to 100 percent.

Testing behavior therapy, medication, and four accommodations

Three treatment factors were systematically varied for every student across the summer. Classroom behavior management alternated in two-week blocks between a general classroom modeled on typical school practices and an enhanced behavioral intervention classroom. In the general classroom, staff reviewed rules at the start of class, quietly logged rule violations on a private clipboard, gave praise sparingly at a ratio of one praise statement for every three commands, awarded recess regardless of behavior, and sent students out to speak with a supervisor after three aggressive, defiant, or disrespectful acts.

In the enhanced behavioral classroom, staff recorded rule violations on a public point board and delivered three specific praise statements for every command or correction. Students also received individualized daily report cards tracking personalized classroom behavior targets, earning free time at the end of each period for meeting their goals alongside public recognition and points they could trade weekly for small toys and games.

Stimulant medication alternated in one-week blocks under double-blind conditions, meaning neither the children nor the classroom staff knew which capsule was given each week. Every morning between 7:30 and 8:00 a.m., participants swallowed an opaque capsule containing either an inactive placebo or extended-release methylphenidate at a moderate weight-based dose of 0.3 milligrams per kilogram, rounded to the nearest 10 milligrams and averaging about 19 milligrams.

Academic accommodations rotated randomly each day of the week, cycling every child through a standard classroom day with no special adjustments and four common school accommodations. On extended-time days, students received 50 percent more time than usual, expanding the independent worksheet period from 30 to 45 minutes and the daily quiz from 10 to 15 minutes. On frequent-break days, staff paused work for a one-minute quiet break to rest, draw, or read after every five minutes of seatwork and every 2.5 minutes of quiz time, working out to roughly six breaks per hour.

The other two accommodations altered the student’s physical workspace rather than the schedule. On adapted-seating days, children were permitted to stand at their desks instead of remaining in their chairs, while low-distraction days provided noise-canceling headphones to muffle classroom sounds and three-sided desk dividers to block visual clutter.

Daily outcomes included observed classroom rule violations in both class periods, quiz scores, and academic productivity. Observers recorded rule violations with moderate-to-good consistency across raters, reflected in an intraclass correlation of 0.71 on a 0-to-1 agreement scale.

The researchers initially planned to analyze the outcomes using analysis of variance, a standard method for comparing group averages. Because counts of rule violations and completed problems varied widely from student to student, they shifted to statistical mixed models built for count data. To account for the extra minutes given on extended-time days, they measured seatwork productivity as the rate of problems completed correctly per minute.

Accommodations failed to improve behavior or schoolwork

When the researchers first tested whether any treatments modified one another’s effectiveness, none of the two-way or three-way interactions were statistically significant. Academic accommodations did not become helpful when paired with stimulant medication or behavioral therapy, and medication and behavioral therapy worked independently rather than amplifying or blunting each other.

Across all four accommodations, none produced a statistically significant drop in rule-breaking during either class period, and none produced a statistically significant increase in quiz scores compared with the standard classroom without accommodations. On seatwork productivity, every accommodation leaned in the opposite direction, with none increasing the rate of problems completed correctly per minute.

Extended time and low-distraction workspaces lowered per-minute problem completion by 11 percent and 4 percent, respectively, with both reductions holding up after the researchers adjusted for multiple statistical tests; in the unmedicated general classroom, for example, students averaged 1.25 correct problems per minute with extended time compared with 1.41 without accommodations.

Frequent breaks showed a 3 percent dip that was not statistically significant at any threshold, while a 3 percent dip with standing desks was no longer statistically significant once adjusted for multiple tests. In the paper’s discussion, the authors write that accommodations produced no benefit and, if anything, a general worsening, and argue that school effort spent evaluating students for and providing them may be useless at best and counterproductive at worst.

“We were surprised that accommodations did not work alone, or in combination with any of the other treatments,” Fabiano explained. “The results we obtained suggested that these approaches really don’t move the needle with regard to improving classroom functioning in children with ADHD.”

Behavior supports and medication drove the gains

In contrast, both the enhanced behavioral classroom and stimulant medication substantially curbed disruptive behavior. During independent seatwork, students averaged 5.74 rule violations per hour in the unmedicated general classroom without accommodations, dropping to 3.96 violations per hour with behavioral support alone, 2.75 with medication alone, and 1.27 when receiving both. Across conditions in the statistical model, the behavioral intervention reduced expected seatwork rule violations by 37 percent compared with the general classroom, and stimulant medication reduced them by 61 percent compared with placebo, with comparable reductions during the group lesson hour.

Stimulant medication also boosted the rate of seatwork problems completed correctly per minute by 22 percent compared with placebo, lifting the unaccommodated general classroom average from 1.41 to 1.62 correct problems per minute. The behavioral classroom intervention produced a much smaller 3 percent uptick in per-minute work rate that still reached statistical significance. On the daily 10-question science and social studies quizzes, stimulant medication raised scores by an average of 3.9 percentage points relative to placebo, from roughly 66 percent to about 70 percent, while the effect of behavioral therapy on quiz scores was not statistically significant.

Asked how large the effects were in practical terms, Fabiano said, “Practically, the accommodations had no effect, or at times a slightly negative effect, on performance in the classroom. Positive behavior supports and medications improved behavior, and medication improved completion of independent work. Medication improved quiz scores as well, but only by an average of 3-4 points.”

The authors point out that these classroom gains occurred on a moderate stimulant dose, noting very few instances where side effects led to stopping the medication, although four children left during the trial and six withdrew before the start date over medication or side-effect concerns. Because clinical guidelines often favor raising stimulant prescriptions to the highest tolerated dose despite long-term high-dose risks such as slowed growth, the authors suggest that a moderate dose may be sufficient to support daily classroom functioning for many children with ADHD. Notably, the behavioral classroom tools tested in the trial required no additional staff time or extra financial expense to run.

“Even though academic accommodations such as extra time are among the most commonly recommended approaches for a child with ADHD, there was no evidence in our study that they worked,” Fabiano noted. “Stimulant medication improved academic productivity and quiz scores, consistent with many other studies. Both medication and positive behavior supports promoted rule-following. Because schools do not prescribe medication, our results suggest they should direct much more effort toward providing positive behavior supports.”

Caveats and next steps for schools

There are a few things to keep in mind when weighing these findings, starting with a financial disclosure: Fabiano reported receiving book royalties during the study from Guilford Press, which publishes his manual on daily behavior report cards, a core component of the behavioral classroom intervention tested in the trial.

Beyond that, the study took place during a seven- to eight-week summer program staffed by intensively trained teachers and aides who received daily supervision, rather than across a full school year in everyday classrooms, and medication was tested in one-week blocks rather than over months.

Academic accommodations also rotated every day instead of remaining consistent over weeks, individual students varied in how actively they used options like standing desks or headphones, and the authors note that separate ongoing analyses are examining whether specific accommodations still help certain children depending on their individual cognitive profiles.

“It is important to note the study was conducted in a rigorously implemented summer treatment program setting, so results will need to be replicated in typical school settings,” Fabiano cautioned. “Though it is unlikely that accommodations will work better in a less structured setting.”

Looking ahead, the research team plans to test how schools can weave effective behavioral tools into multi-tiered systems of support. Widely used in public education, these school-wide frameworks organize student help in graduated layers, starting with universal classroom routines for all students and adding progressively more targeted interventions for learners who need extra assistance.

“We urgently need to better support students with ADHD,” Fabiano added. “Next steps include working to partner with schools using Multi-Tiered Systems of Support to embed effective positive behavioral supports within these frameworks. We also think the findings suggest reduced efforts to conduct lengthy assessments if the only outcome would be to establish academic accommodations, as these did not appear to appreciably improve behavior.”

The study, “Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Accommodations, Behavior Therapy, and Stimulant Medication: A Randomized Clinical Trial,” was authored by Gregory A. Fabiano, Brittany M. Merrill, Rosalia F. Gallo, Marcela Ramos, Morgan Jusko, Devon Tower, Elizabeth M. Gnagy, Amy Boeckel, Jennifer Piscitello, Maya Renaud, Alyssa Dawson, Jennifer Sikov, Carolina Ramirez, Grant C. Edmondson, Michael S. Adragna, Carlos A. Salgado, and Timothy B. Hayes.
