issues.title: New Guidelines Recommend Routine Prostate Cancer Screening for Men Over 50
issues.summary: New ACS guidelines encourage men over 50 to get regular PSA tests to screen for prostate cancer. miodrag ignjatovic · E+/Getty The American Cancer Society (ACS) now recommends prostate-specific antigen (PSA) screening every 2 years starting at age 50 for men at average risk, and annually starting at age 45 for those at higher risk, including Black men and men with a family history of prostate canc
issues.content_html:
• The American Cancer Society (ACS) now recommends prostate-specific antigen (PSA) screening every 2 years starting at age 50 for men at average risk, and annually starting at age 45 for those at higher risk, including Black men and men with a family history of prostate cancer.
  • The updated guidance reflects new evidence that regular PSA screening can reduce the risk of dying from prostate cancer by 13% and help detect potentially aggressive cancers before they spread.
  • If PSA levels are elevated, additional testing, including prostate MRIs and biomarker tests, can help determine whether a biopsy is necessary, potentially reducing unnecessary procedures.

As rates of advanced prostate cancer continue to rise, the American Cancer Society (ACS) has issued new guidelines recommending routine prostate cancer screening for many men starting at age 50.

The updated recommendations, published November 12 in CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians, mark a shift from the organization’s previous emphasis on shared decision making about whether to undergo screening.

Under the new guidelines, the ACS recommends regular prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing beginning at age 50 for men at average risk of prostate cancer and age 45 for those at higher risk.

Advances in MRI technology and biomarker testing may also help doctors determine which men need further testing, potentially reducing unnecessary biopsies and overtreatment.

How Often Should Men Get Screened for Prostate Cancer?

The ACS last updated its prostate cancer screening guidelines in 2010, when conflicting research findings raised questions about whether the benefits of PSA screening outweighed the potential harms.

At the time, the organization emphasized informed, shared decision making between patients and healthcare professionals.

However, longer-term follow-up studies have since provided stronger evidence of the benefits of early detection, prompting the ACS to conduct a systematic review and update its recommendations.

The authors of the report noted, “In making these recommendations, we recognize that PSA testing is only the first step in a screening cascade that includes secondary testing of men with an elevated PSA level and treatment decisions for men diagnosed with prostate cancer.”

The new guidelines recommend a PSA test every 2 years for men ages 50–69 with an average risk of prostate cancer.

The recommendation for those at high risk is a PSA test every year starting at age 45.

For men ages 70–74, the ACS recommends individualized decision making. If an individual chooses to be screened, the ACS recommends a PSA test every 2 years until the age of 74.

Ramkishen Narayanan, MD, Director of the Center for Urologic Health at The Roy and Patricia Disney Family Cancer Center at Providence Saint Joseph Medical Center in Burbank, CA, who wasn’t involved in the report, told Healthline that screening shouldn’t automatically be ruled out for men over 75.

“[A] point worth noting is that for men over 75, their PSA history as well as their individual clinical scenarios should be evaluated, and that PSA should not be discouraged in this group of men if their life expectancy and clinical history warrant a PSA check.”

Who is at a higher risk for prostate cancer?

According to the ACS, approximately 1 in 8 men will be diagnosed with prostate cancer during their lifetime.

Individual risk depends on age, race/ethnicity, and other factors:

  • Prostate cancer is more likely to develop in older men, with an average diagnosis age of 68.
  • Black men are also at a higher risk than those of other races.
  • Men with a family history of prostate cancer, particularly a father or brother who has been diagnosed, may be at higher risk.

Why the ACS Updated Its Prostate Cancer Screening Guidelines

Prostate cancer diagnoses in the United States increased by around 3% per year between 2014 and 2022, according to the ACS.

The rise in diagnoses, particularly advanced-stage prostate cancer, has renewed attention on the importance of regular screening.

“[The] current state of prostate cancer screening guidelines is vague and generalized. This has led to ambiguity, disagreement, and variation of opinion among healthcare providers and institutions in their approach to men’s health,” said S. Adam Ramin, MD, board certified urologist, urologic oncologist, and medical director of Urology Cancer Specialists in Los Angeles, CA, who wasn’t involved in the report.

The updated ACS guidelines drew partly on findings from a 2025 follow-up of the European Randomized Study of Screening for Prostate Cancer (ERSPC), which found that regular PSA screening was associated with a 13% reduction in prostate cancer deaths over 23 years.

A 12-year ERSPC follow-up in 2012 also suggested that regular screening was associated with a decrease in metastatic prostate cancer diagnosis, which is another finding that influenced the updated guidance.

“Prostate cancer can take many years, even decades, to become clinically significant, so it takes a long time for us to see the consequences of changes in screening practices,” Taylor Goodstein, MD, assistant professor of urology in the College of Medicine at the University of Cincinnati, who wasn’t involved in the report, told Healthline.

“With longer follow-up from randomized trials, we now have more convincing evidence that PSA screening reduces the risk of dying from prostate cancer,” she said.

“The ACS guidelines are important now because they drive home the most important point that prostate cancer screening saves lives,” said Narayanan.

What PSA Levels May Require Further Testing?

Healthcare professionals use PSA levels to help determine whether additional testing for prostate cancer may be necessary.

The ACS recommends further testing for men under 70 with PSA levels of 3 ng/mL or higher.

For those ages 70 and older, the ACS recommends further testing if their PSA is 6.5 ng/mL or higher. This is because PSA levels tend to be naturally higher in older men.

You can speak with your healthcare professional to find out more about PSA cutoff levels.

How New Screening Guidelines Could Improve Prostate Cancer Outcomes

Goodstein told Healthline that the ways this new guidance can change the outlook for prostate cancer are simple.

“If we screen men, we can catch troublesome cancers early, before they have a chance to spread,” she said.

Goodstein also emphasized how much the evaluation process has changed. In the past, an elevated PSA level often led directly to a biopsy.

Today, doctors generally repeat the PSA test within two weeks to three months to confirm the result. If PSA levels remain elevated, additional testing, including a prostate MRI or validated biomarker test, can help determine whether a biopsy is necessary.

Narayanan told Healthline, “The new guidelines will hopefully remove any confusion about the value of PSA screening and encourage prostate cancer screening as an integral part of a man’s ‘checkup’.”

He added that it is worth noting that the DRE (digital rectal exam) adds little value to the initial prostate cancer screening and is no longer something that men should fear.

“Adoption of this set of specific guidelines standardizes the approach to screening for prostate cancer. It provides a unified effort among all levels of healthcare. It most likely will increase the chances of finding prostate cancer in earlier stages and lead to improved cancer treatment outcomes,” said Ramin.

issues.title: Mind Games: My ‘Secret’ to Enjoying Coffee Without Anxiety
issues.summary: Adding L-theanine to your morning coffee could help relieve caffeine-induced side effects like anxiety and jitters. Oleg Breslavtsev/Moment/Getty Images This article is part of a mental health content series called “Mind Games,” in which Healthline editor Morgan Mandriota draws on personal experience and research to challenge misconceptions, reduce stigma, review trends, and share hot takes and le
issues.content_html:
This article is part of a mental health content series called “Mind Games,” in which Healthline editor Morgan Mandriota draws on personal experience and research to challenge misconceptions, reduce stigma, review trends, and share hot takes and lessons learned about what it means to be mentally well.

Coffee and I don’t exactly have the best relationship.

My morning cup tends to give me jitters, worsen my anxiety, and keep me up until 2 a.m. if I drink it past noon. As an already anxious human, the last thing I need is to exacerbate my symptoms, even if it’s coming from a delicious source.

Over a year ago, I noticed that my anxiety was higher than usual. I was also tossing and turning and waking up at all hours of the night for weeks on end.

One night in particular, I woke up every hour for 8 hours. Naturally, I wanted to blame it on the full moon or anything other than my beloved coffee, but alas, I realized that my caffeine consumption was the most likely culprit.

Could I have aimed to set a strict drinking schedule to see if that fixed things? Sure. But instead, I decided to quit cold turkey and undergo an experiment to see how I’d feel going coffee-free for the first time in years.

Over the next 8 months, I’d swap my coffee station for a matcha setup, dabble in exotic herbal blends from my local teahouse, and become a self-proclaimed tea connoisseur. Lo and behold, my anxiety eased up, and my sleep quality improved, too.

Fast forward to 4 months ago, when I hopped back on the coffee train. But this time, I’m relying on a handy amino acid to help avoid anxiety and other unwanted side effects: L-theanine.

Health and wellness touch everyone’s life differently. This is one person’s story. The views and opinions expressed are those of the speaker and do not necessarily reflect the views or positions of Healthline Media and should not serve as a substitute for medical advice from a healthcare professional.

How L-theanine can help offset coffee side effects

L-theanine is mainly found in green and black tea and one type of wild mushroom. The mental health benefits of L-theanine consumption are an emerging area of research, but one 2024 review found that consuming around 200 to 400 milligrams (mg) may help relieve symptoms in people with anxiety disorders.

Still, anecdotal reports suggest there may be benefits of adding L-theanine to coffee. Over the last 5 years, the combo has been gaining traction on Reddit and TikTok for managing caffeine-related side effects.

Despite an overwhelming amount of rave reviews online, I couldn’t find much research to support these claims, so I spoke with a neurologist to see if they had any thoughts.

“This trend has real science behind it,” said Fawad Mian, MD, who is board certified in neurology, clinical neurophysiology, and sleep medicine and the founder of Ascend Regenerative.

“Controlled studies show caffeine plus L-theanine improves focus and attention more than caffeine alone, and some suggest it softens caffeine’s side effects, like tiredness, headaches, and blood pressure spikes,” Mian said. “It smooths caffeine’s effects but doesn’t erase them, so it’s not a license to drink more coffee,” he added.

With all of this in mind, especially after realizing just how calm I was while drinking black and green teas during my coffee break, I decided to give it a try.

So, does it help? Here’s my personal experience

After about 4 months of “testing,” I’ve found that adding L-theanine to my coffee works extremely well for me.

No more anxiety, scatterbrain, shakiness, or staying up until 3 a.m. And no lifestyle overhaul needed. The supplement, which I prefer in liquid form, has become a seamless addition to my daily routine.

Every morning, I make a fresh batch of French press coffee with (strong) local beans, then I squeeze some L-theanine into my cup.

I’ve noticed that I get the usual coffee benefits like improved focus and concentration, plus a nice, calm, stable energy throughout the day.

Even if I drink it until 2 p.m., I’m fighting to keep my eyes open at night before I finally fall asleep around 10. Perhaps this is because L-theanine may also support quality sleep.

The L-theanine product I use and love

Mindful L-Theanine Drops is the liquid supplement that I use every day.

I add a one-second squeeze (which contains 200 mg of L-theanine) into my morning coffee, then I’m good to go. I even started carrying a bottle in my bag just in case I get a latte from a coffee shop on a whim.

You can also add it to a glass of water, a cup of tea, or another drink of your choosing. It’s unflavored, so it doesn’t alter the taste of your drinks. Real secret stuff.

Out of curiosity, and because I’m a natural skeptic and overthinker, I asked Mian if my positive experience could be a placebo effect, or if I’m seeing real results.

“Expectation may play a small role, but the effect is biologically plausible,” he said. “L-theanine boosts calming brain activity that offsets caffeine’s stimulation, and 200 mg matches the doses used in studies.” However, he noted that it doesn’t speed caffeine clearance, so drinking coffee only in the morning still matters for sleep quality.

While L-theanine is generally safe to consume, it’s best to speak with a healthcare professional first, especially if you’re pregnant, nursing, receiving cancer treatment, or taking blood pressure medication or sedatives.

“Choose a third-party tested brand, and if caffeine makes you anxious, cutting back is still the simplest fix,” Mian added.

So, if you’re anything like me and drinking coffee also leads to anxiety and jitters for you, I highly recommend trying this supplement once you get the green light from your doctor. It’s been working for me. It may work well for you, too.

💌 Over to you: I’d love to hear your thoughts on this. Does coffee also give you unwanted side effects? Have you tried L-theanine to remedy them? Let me know, or ask any questions about my experience by emailing me here.

issues.title: How to Plan Your Holiday Meals in a Year of Unprecedented Recalls
issues.summary: While many people are concerned about foodborne illness and food recalls, experts say with the right preparation, foods are safe to eat. LumiNola · E+/Getty About 60% of U.S. adults say they’re more concerned about foodborne illness this year than in previous years. However, experts say past recalls don’t mean entire food categories need to be avoided. Experts recommend checking FDA and USDA recal
issues.content_html:
• About 60% of U.S. adults say they’re more concerned about foodborne illness this year than in previous years. However, experts say past recalls don’t mean entire food categories need to be avoided.
  • Experts recommend checking FDA and USDA recall lists before shopping or preparing holiday meals to ensure ingredients aren’t affected by active recalls.
  • Safe holiday food preparation involves four basic practices: clean, separate, cook, and chill to reduce the risk of foodborne illness.
  • Holiday leftovers should be refrigerated within 2 hours and can typically be stored safely for 3 to 4 days.

Following a series of high-profile food recalls and outbreaks this year, many Americans may be concerned about keeping their families safe from foodborne illness during the holidays.

In fact, according to a recent national survey by Orlando Health, around 60% of U.S. adults say they’re more concerned about foodborne illness this year than in previous years.

Although several major foodborne illness outbreaks have ended and their associated recalls are no longer active, food safety remains an important concern. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that 48 million people in the United States experience foodborne illness each year.

However, there are simple steps you can take to reduce the risk of foodborne illness when preparing holiday meals and storing leftovers.

Are foods safe to eat after a recall has ended?

While there were several food recalls in the United States over the summer, two of the largest involved Salmonella linked to jalapeños and Cyclospora linked to lettuce.

These outbreaks prompted widespread recalls and raised concerns about the safety of certain foods, particularly fresh produce.

Although health officials have since declared the major outbreaks over, some consumers may still be hesitant to purchase foods associated with previous recalls.

Even with this declaration, you may still feel nervous about purchasing certain foods, but experts say you don’t need to worry.

“Here in the United States, we have the safest food supply in the world. The recent recalls show that our food safety system is working,” said William Schaffner, MD, Professor, Division of Infectious Diseases at Vanderbilt University.

Michelle Routhenstein, preventive cardiology dietitian at Entirely Nourished, told Healthline that past recalls do not mean entire food categories need to be avoided. The important thing is whether the specific product you have matches a current recall, based on details such as brand, lot number, package size, and expiration date.

“You should enjoy familiar foods, including properly cooked poultry, washed fruits and vegetables, and pasteurized dairy products,” she said. “The key is checking relevant recalls and practicing safe food handling.”

Check for recalls

“Before shopping or cooking, review FDA and USDA (U.S. Department of Agriculture) recall information and compare any relevant notices with the labels on your ingredients,” said Routhenstein.

Check the pantry and freezer, too: something purchased months ago may still be affected.

“Stay alert to any news reports about food recalls and use good food preparation practices. Those simple actions should keep your holidays happy and safe,” said Schaffner.

Consumers can sign up for food recall alerts through the FDA or visit FoodSafety.gov for recall information from both the FDA and USDA.

How to safely prepare and store holiday foods

Schaffner emphasized the importance of following safe food-handling practices when preparing everyday meals and holiday gatherings.

“Remember the longstanding advice: keep food hot or cold. Avoid long times at room temperature,” he said.

Routhenstein advised focusing on four basics: clean, separate, cook, and chill.

  • Clean: Wash hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds and rinse produce under running water. Avoid washing raw poultry, which can spread bacteria through splashing.
  • Separate: Keep raw meat and poultry away from ready-to-eat foods to prevent cross-contamination.
  • Cook: Use a food thermometer. Turkey and stuffing should reach 165°F (74ºC). Cooking stuffing separately is generally the safer option.
  • Chill: Refrigerate perishable foods within 2 hours of serving, or within 1 hour if the temperature exceeds 90°F (32°C).

How long can holiday leftovers sit out?

Schaffner noted the importance of refrigerating leftovers promptly rather than leaving them at room temperature for extended periods. He recommends clearing the table and refrigerating leftovers soon after the meal ends.

Routhenstein reiterated that you should refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours rather than leaving them out to cool.

Divide turkey into smaller portions and transfer sides and gravy into shallow containers to help them cool quickly, she advised.

Leftovers can typically be stored in the refrigerator for 3–4 days. If you don’t plan to eat them within that time, consider freezing them.

The important thing is to keep an eye out for any new recalls, practice food safety, and enjoy your holiday meals!

issues.title: Planning to Stop Taking a GLP-1? Here’s How to Maintain Weight Loss
issues.summary: Research shows that having an “exit strategy” after stopping at GLP-1 can help maintain your weight loss. coldsnowstorm · E+/Getty A Cleveland Clinic study found that bariatric surgery and switching GLP-1 medications were associated with greater weight loss than discontinuing treatment entirely. After two years, participants who underwent bariatric surgery lost an average of 28.2% of their body we
issues.content_html:
• A Cleveland Clinic study found that bariatric surgery and switching GLP-1 medications were associated with greater weight loss than discontinuing treatment entirely.
  • After two years, participants who underwent bariatric surgery lost an average of 28.2% of their body weight, compared with 16% among those who switched between semaglutide and tirzepatide and 4% among those who stopped GLP-1 treatment.
  • Stopping a GLP-1 medication can lead to increased hunger and weight regain. Experts recommend working with a healthcare professional to develop a long-term weight management plan before discontinuing treatment.

Switching GLP-1 medications or undergoing bariatric surgery may help people maintain greater weight loss than stopping treatment entirely, according to a new study presented at ObesityWeek and published in eClinicalMedicine on November 14.

The Cleveland Clinic study compared five strategies for managing weight after treatment with GLP-1 medications, analyzing data from 20,486 adults with obesity or type 2 diabetes.

People who stop taking GLP-1 medications often regain weight. Researchers examined whether continuing treatment, switching medications, or undergoing bariatric surgery could help limit weight regain or support further weight loss.

The findings showed that people who underwent bariatric surgery or switched between semaglutide (Ozempic) and tirzepatide (Zepbound) experienced the greatest overall weight loss.

Bariatric surgery and switching GLP-1s led to greater weight loss

The study participants had an average age of 56.7 years, an average weight of 109 kg (240.3 lbs), and an average body mass index (BMI) of 38. All had been taking either semaglutide or tirzepatide for at least 90 days.

The researchers categorized the participants into five groups:

  • continuation
  • switching between semaglutide and tirzepatide
  • switching to another weight-loss medication
  • undergoing bariatric surgery
  • discontinuation

After 2 years, those who underwent bariatric surgery saw an average loss of 28.2% of their body weight or about 31.5 kg (69.4 lbs).

“We increasingly view medications and surgery as complementary tools rather than competing ones,” said Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“For patients with severe obesity (typically a BMI of 35 or higher, or 30+ with metabolic conditions like type 2 diabetes), bariatric surgery remains the most durable, cost-effective intervention available,” he added. “Using a GLP-1 beforehand can safely reduce liver volume and lower surgical risk, while surgery provides the permanent anatomical and hormonal reset needed to maintain that weight loss long-term without relying indefinitely on weekly injections.”

During the same period, those who switched between semaglutide and tirzepatide lost 16% of their body weight, or about 18 kg (39.6 lbs).

Participants who switched from semaglutide to tirzepatide lost 3 kg (6.6 lbs) more than those who continued taking semaglutide. However, participants already taking tirzepatide lost 4.5 kg (9.9 lbs) more by continuing treatment rather than switching to semaglutide.

The other groups experienced lower amounts of weight loss:

  • Continuation of initial GLP-1 medication: average of 10.9% of their body weight or 12.3 kg (27.1 lbs)
  • Switching to another weight loss medication: average of 8.2% of their body weight or 9.2 kg (20.2 lbs)
  • Total discontinuation of a GLP-1 medication: average of 4% of their body weight or 4.5 kg (9.9 lbs)

After one year, participants with type 2 diabetes experienced HbA1c reductions of 1.76% following bariatric surgery, 1.43% after switching GLP-1 medications, and 1.32% after continuing their original medication, compared with 0.48% among those who discontinued treatment entirely.

After one year, participants with hypertension (high blood pressure) also experienced greater reductions in blood pressure following surgery or switching GLP-1 medications than those who discontinued treatment entirely.

“[This study] reinforces the need for a long term, multi-modal continuum of care rather than treating GLP-1s as a temporary fix,” said Ali.

Other options for continued weight loss after GLP-1s

Ali also recommended the following strategies to help maintain weight loss after stopping a GLP-1 medication:

  • Prioritize protein and resistance training: People who stop taking GLP-1 medications may regain body fat after losing muscle mass during treatment. Eating enough protein and regularly doing strength-training exercises can help preserve muscle mass and support metabolism.
  • Seek nutritional and behavioral support: Working with a registered dietitian can help people develop sustainable eating habits as the medication’s appetite-suppressing effects wear off. This may include focusing on fiber-rich foods, balanced meals, and consistent meal timing.

What to consider when thinking about stopping a GLP-1

The findings highlight the importance of having a long-term weight management plan in place before stopping a GLP-1 medication.

Before stopping a GLP-1 medication, talk with a healthcare professional. They can help you explore your options and determine which strategies may be most appropriate for your health needs.

Ali told Healthline that identifying the reason for stopping treatment is an important first step. He noted that people often discontinue GLP-1 medications because of gastrointestinal side effects, supply issues, or loss of insurance coverage rather than because they no longer need treatment.

He said that if side effects are the issue, adjusting the dose or switching to a different agent often solves the problem.

Ali also emphasized that stopping a GLP-1 medication shouldn’t be viewed as a test of willpower. Increased hunger after discontinuing treatment is a biological response, not a personal failure.

“Have a concrete ‘off-ramp’ plan in place with your doctor before taking your last dose, so you have medical, nutritional, or surgical support ready to protect the health gains you worked hard to achieve,” advised Ali.

issues.title: Dancing with the trophy shortage
issues.summary: It’s easy to get distracted by (and hooked on) the quest for a trophy. It’s easy to measure and a bright light to focus on. But this skips the key question: What’s it for? The Savannah Bananas never won their league. But they made more money (and their fans had more fun) than any other […]
issues.author: Seth Godin
issues.content_html:
It’s easy to get distracted by (and hooked on) the quest for a trophy. It’s easy to measure and a bright light to focus on.

But this skips the key question: What’s it for?

The Savannah Bananas never won their league. But they made more money (and their fans had more fun) than any other team.

Your favorite episode of the Mel Robbins show might not be the one that got the most views. And of course, the best video on YouTube is unlikely to be the one that went the most viral. That’s simply the easiest to measure.

High school sports seems to be about solving the trophy shortage, but is that what it should be for? Are all the other teams and all their athletes failures? Or is it simply a shortcut that lets the coach off the hook when they hesitate to do the hard work of developing their students?

If it’s easy to measure, it might not be the thing you ought to be measuring. In fact, it probably isn’t.

issues.title: One swell foop
issues.summary: It’s definitely tempting. All at once. Once and done. Over with. Pay the money, grit your teeth, launch with verve and then move on. Except… it almost never works. Foops aren’t swell. Foops fail. The successful path is a process, an iterative, evolving, persistent path toward better.
issues.author: Seth Godin
issues.content_html:
It’s definitely tempting. All at once. Once and done. Over with.

Pay the money, grit your teeth, launch with verve and then move on.

Except…

it almost never works.

Foops aren’t swell. Foops fail.

The successful path is a process, an iterative, evolving, persistent path toward better.

issues.title: Selling to friends
issues.summary: There are two versions, very different: FAVOR: This is what multi-level marketing preys on. You ask a family member or a friend to buy something, not because they need it, but because you do. This doesn’t always end well. Someone might want to further their relationship with you by doing you this favor, but if […]
issues.author: Seth Godin
issues.content_html:
There are two versions, very different:

FAVOR: This is what multi-level marketing preys on. You ask a family member or a friend to buy something, not because they need it, but because you do.

This doesn’t always end well. Someone might want to further their relationship with you by doing you this favor, but if the unspoken promise is that the item or service is worthwhile, the disappointment that ensues hurts everyone. Real estate brokers or middlemen in a bind often seek to build friendly relationships at the club or community meetings, but then try to leverage this friendship into a significant sale without doing the hard work of actually being the best choice.

TRUST: This is the sort of sale that happens when you begin with the benefit of the doubt but actually deliver a great outcome. You’ll know this is the case when the person who trusted you ends up testifying on your behalf to others.

“No pressure” is something that’s showing up more and more in the pitches I’m seeing. Of course, there’s no pressure! Just saying it implies that you wish there were.

If you’re asking for a favor, you’re not serving and you’re not selling. You’re trading.

And if you’re asking for trust, be prepared to honor the obligation it creates.

issues.title: Practical empathy
issues.summary: I don’t know what you know. I don’t want what you want, see what you see, believe what you believe. And that’s okay. In fact, it’s the only way to be of service, to make a sale or to cause a change to happen. Of course, we’re more intimate with our ideas, our products and […]
issues.author: Seth Godin
issues.content_html:
I don’t know what you know. I don’t want what you want, see what you see, believe what you believe.

And that’s okay.

In fact, it’s the only way to be of service, to make a sale or to cause a change to happen.

Of course, we’re more intimate with our ideas, our products and our approach than anyone else. We have a noise in our head, a narrative and a point of view we’ve spent our whole lives creating. It’s naive to believe that anyone else is completely in sync with us.

And so, our only opportunity is to go where they are, not to demand that they come to us.

Practical empathy isn’t primarily an act of kindness (though it’s an essential component of kindness.) Instead, it’s a direct and straightforward path from here to there. It’s how we create action, learning and change.

Marketing is the simple and brave act of going to where someone else might be, and helping them get to where they hope to go.

issues.title: Claude Cowork skills: How they work and what to build
issues.summary: If you’ve yet to understand Claude Cowork skills, let me help you out: Claude Cowork is a mode that can access your desktop files and complete tasks for you. A skill is a set of instructions that tell Claude exactly how to perform a specific workflow. When combined, the two can boost your productivity in a way that Claude Chat alone cannot.
issues.author: arigby@hubspot.com (Amy Rigby)
issues.content_html:
If you’ve yet to understand Claude Cowork skills, let me help you out: Claude Cowork is a mode that can access your desktop files and complete tasks for you. A skill is a set of instructions that tell Claude exactly how to perform a specific workflow. When combined, the two can boost your productivity in a way that Claude Chat alone cannot.

Claude skills aren’t limited to one Claude surface or tool. Skills work in Claude Chat, Claude Code, and Claude Cowork. So “Claude Cowork skills” are actually a feature across the AI, not just a single mode.

This is even truer since Anthropic announced that Claude Cowork, Chat, Artifacts, and Design are merging into a single unified experience, starting in October 2026. Skills, projects, connectors, and tasks all carry over, but users no longer have to dance between tabs. Claude simply decides which tools to use based on what you ask.

These changes are meant to reduce confusion, but it’s natural to still have questions. We’ll clear things up as they stand now, share what Claude Cowork skills are, and what you should build to get the most out of them.

Note: These changes are rolling out to Claude’s Pro and Max plans first, on the web, desktop, and mobile over the coming weeks, with plans to extend them to the free and team tiers later.

Table of Contents

  • What are Claude Cowork skills?
  • Claude Skills vs. Projects vs. Instructions vs. Memory
  • How Claude Cowork Skills Work
  • How to Create Your First Claude Cowork Skill
  • Claude Cowork Skills: Best Uses for Revenue Teams
  • Claude Cowork Best Practices for Safety and Reliability
  • Connect Claude to HubSpot
  • Frequently Asked Questions About Claude Cowork Skills
  • All it takes is one skill to start.

What are Claude Cowork skills?

A Claude Cowork Skill is a reusable instruction folder (with optional supporting templates, scripts, or reference documents attached) that Claude loads when a task needs it, and ignores when it doesn’t. You can use Claude Cowork skills across every other Claude surface, so truly, any Claude skill is a Claude Cowork skill and vice versa.

If you want to get into the nuts and bolts of it, a Claude skill is technically a folder that can contain the following:

  • Instructions: the step-by-step procedure and the rules Claude should follow.
  • Templates and reference files: brand guidelines, sample outputs, or layouts that show the standard to match.
  • Scripts: code for the deterministic parts, such as reformatting data or generating a file.

What makes a skill different from a detailed prompt you paste every time is:

  • It’s portable. One skill works in Chat, Cowork, and Claude Code; you don’t rewrite it for each surface. You can also use Claude skills in different AI or LLM tools like ChatGPT.
  • It’s consistent. Claude follows the same steps, in the same order, every time. No drift, no improvising.
  • It’s smart about context. Claude only loads what it needs, which keeps the conversation focused and efficient.

Thanks to Cowork and the recent merger, a skill can now also access internal documentation and do things like reading and writing to folders on your computer, running multi-step tasks autonomously, coordinating sub-agents, and producing finished files like spreadsheets and presentations, not just responding in text like it would with Chat alone.

When you need Claude to repeat a multi-step process the same way every time (i.e., formatting a weekly report, triaging leads, summarizing support tickets), that’s where a skill comes in handy.

For example, when I’m using Claude for fact-checking assistance, I often prompt it with detailed instructions on what to verify in the article, how to verify it, and what to include in its citations so that I can double-check its work. Instead of repeating that prompt every single time I’m done with an article, I have a “blog-fact-checker” skill that contains my detailed instructions. Now, instead of 500 words, I simply type two words, “Fact check,” and attach my draft via Google Docs. Easy.

Note: Record a Skill is a Cowork feature still exclusive to Claude Cowork on Mac desktops with Pro, Max, and Team plans, but we’ll get into that later.

Where to Access Claude Skills

Claude automatically selects and uses skills depending on the context. You don’t have to tell it when to use a skill or which one to invoke, though you can do so in a few ways:

1. When creating a skill, you can include explicit wording in the skill description on how Claude can know when to invoke the skill (Anthropic recommends writing in third person). Example: “Use this skill whenever the user says ‘generate an image,’ ‘make an infographic,’ or ‘create an image.’”

2. Add the instructions to your prompt. Example: “Use your infographic skill to create a bar chart showing the monthly sales comparison.”

3. Click the + icon to the lower left of the chat, hover over Skills, and select the skill you want from the menu.
4. Type a forward slash ( /) in the chat, and all of your skills will pop up in a dropdown menu, allowing you to select the one(s) you’d like to use.

Claude Skills vs. Projects vs. Instructions vs. Memory

As a marketer, I’m often overwhelmed by the sheer number of features that Claude offers (and new ones get released seemingly every week!). So, here’s a quick demystifier on the difference between Claude skills, projects, instructions, and memory.

      • Memory is what Claude learns from your chats (either automatically or because you told it to remember). There is also project-specific memory, where Claude will remember info relevant only to that specific project.
      • Skills are repeatable instructions that can be invoked explicitly (you tell Claude to use it) or implicitly (Claude automatically figures out which skills are needed for that task). Skills are usable across your projects and tasks.
      • Projects are folders that organize related tasks and chats by topic, each holding its own files and context.
      • Instructions are broad directives that shape how Claude works, either account-wide by default or project-specific.

Which one you use depends on what problem you’re running into:

      • If you keep retyping the same prompt, create a skill.
      • If you want your files and campaign context in one place, create a project.
      • If you need Claude to remember an important detail across chats, add it to memory.
      • If you need Claude to behave a certain way every time, write instructions.

As Alex Banks puts it: “Skills are the tools in the workshop. Projects are the workshop itself.”

These four can also be combined: A single project can carry its own instructions and project-specific memory while you invoke skills inside it.

Claude plugins bundle skills, MCP connectors, commands, and agents into one package.

How Claude Cowork Skills Work

Adding a skill doesn’t “retrain” or “fine-tune” Claude, and it doesn’t change how the model thinks. A skill is simply a set of task-specific instructions Claude reads at the moment you need them, like handing a colleague an SOP and asking them to follow it.

Claude reads the skill using progressive disclosure: It brings a skill into the session piece by piece as needed, rather than all at once. Progressive disclosure works in three stages:

      • Metadata (always on): At startup, Claude loads only each skill’s name and description. That’s how it knows which skills exist and when to reach for one, and it’s why you can keep dozens installed without slowing anything down.
      • Instructions (loaded when triggered): Once your request lines up with a skill’s description, Claude pulls in the full instruction set, including the steps, rules, and formatting it should follow.
      • Resources and scripts (loaded on demand): The templates, reference files, and code inside the skill folder stay put until a task calls for them, so they cost nothing until used. When Claude runs a script, only the result enters the chat, not the code itself.

The benefit of this is that a skill can bundle large brand guidelines, datasets, or utilities without slowing down every conversation, because none of it loads until Claude needs it.

How to Create Your First Claude Cowork Skill

This article covers two ways to create a Claude Cowork skill:

      1. Prompt Claude in conversation to build a skill based on your specifications.
      2. Use “Record a skill” in Claude for Mac desktop app and let Claude build a skill based on the video recording.

If you already have a skill file, you can also upload it as a ZIP from Customize > Skills.

When I first learned about Claude Cowork skills, I had a hard time deciding what exactly I should turn into a skill. If you’re in the same boat, I recommend starting with any saved prompts or those you repeatedly type. Comb through your old chats and Claude projects and see what prompts or instructions you frequently use. Or if you have a prompt library in a spreadsheet or doc, mine that for ideas of what you can turn into a skill.

You can also spend one day observing what tasks you repeatedly carry out but have never documented. Capture these workflows by using Claude’s “Record a skill.”

When to Use “Record a Skill”

Claude for Mac’s “Record a skill” feature is perfect for multi-step workflows you do all the time but have never formally documented. Anything where you can record a screenshare video while verbally walking through each step in under ten minutes is an ideal candidate. Some examples:

      • Webinar lead routing: Sort an attendee export into sales, customer success, and marketing follow-up (the skill I’ll record below).
      • Security questionnaire first pass: Match a prospect’s questions to your approved answers and flag any without one.
      • Refund request review: Compare each request against your refund policy and mark it Approve or Escalate.

How to Use “Record a Skill”

Below, I’ll walk you through the steps to use the “Record a skill” feature to make your first Claude Cowork skill. To demonstrate, I created a test skill for routing webinar leads for a fictional company using fake contacts.

Important steps before you get started:

      • Check that you have the Pro, Max, or Team plan and are using Cowork in the Claude for Mac or Windows desktop app. “Record a skill” is not available on Free or Enterprise plans, and it can’t be accessed via Claude Chat (if you don’t yet have the unified Cowork/Chat experience).
      • Check that Code execution and file creationis turned on under Settings > Capabilities. If you’re on an Enterprise account, an Owner must enable Code execution and file creation as well as Skills in Organization settings > Plugins & skills.
      • Hide any passwords, secrets, private conversations, or other sensitive information before you hit record. During the session, “Record a skill” captures everything on your screen and what you say aloud, so Anthropic warns against displaying sensitive information.
      • Make sure the process you’re about to record does not take more than 10 minutes — the recording will cut off at around 10 minutes.

1. In a Claude desktop app session, click + and select Record a skill from the dropdown menu.

2. You’ll get a pop-up. Click the Start recording button.

3. Start showing the workflow you want to turn into a skill, and be sure to narrate each step that you’re taking. Think of it like filming a Loom for a coworker — you need to give all the context so Claude knows why you did each thing. You’ll know Claude is recording when a coral-colored halo surrounds your screen, and an overlay appears at the bottom showing “Capturing” and a timer.

4. When you’re done showing the workflow, click the Done button.

5. Once you click Done, Claude will automatically open a new session with a prompt that says “I recorded a demonstration of a desktop workflow for you to learn from” and start building the skill. You do not have to do anything but wait for it to finish.

6. When Claude is finished and delivers the skill, click Content to expand the instructions and read the skill to ensure it’s what you want.

7. After reviewing the contents, if you’re happy with it, click the Save button. If you want to make changes, ask Claude to make updates to the skill within the chat. It will then deliver an updated skill, and you must click the Update button to save the changes.

8. After you save your new skill, check to make sure it appears in Customize > Skills. Now, it’s ready to use! Click + and Add folder to give Cowork access to the folder with the files it needs to read and modify for this task. I recommend testing the Claude Cowork skill on dummy data first to ensure it works properly before trying it on a real task.

I tested my new webinar-lead-routing skill on fake contacts, and it worked exactly as I’d described it in the recording.

Claude Cowork Skills: Best Uses for Revenue Teams

Marketing Team Use Cases

Proving month-end marketing wins to leadership can be a challenge when you’ve got so many reports and dashboards to pull from. A performance-memo skill turns a folder of channel exports into a one-page summary in your preferred reporting format.

What goes in the skill:

      • Instructions: Compare each metric to the previous month and to the plan, flag any swing over 10%, and write “Cause unknown” rather than guess
      • Reference file: Your metric definitions and quarterly targets
      • Template: Headline, wins, risks, and next month’s focus

Example input: “September exports: Google Ads, LinkedIn Ads, GA4, webinar platform. Plan: 1,200 registrations, $85 cost per lead.”

Example output:

      • Win: Google Ads cost per lead came in at $71, about 16% under plan.
      • Risk: Registrations reached 930, about 23% under plan. Cause unknown, though the LinkedIn export shows the promo campaign paused Sept. 14.

Two more marketing use cases:

      • Competitor launch teardown: Save a competitor’s announcement and pricing page, and get a battlecard-format brief on what changed and which of your claims it affects.
      • Win/loss interview synthesis: Upload a quarter’s anonymized win/loss interview transcripts and get the top reasons deals were won or lost, with supporting quotes and the messaging changes each insight suggests.

Sales Team Use Cases

When a prospect sends contracts back with redlines, it can take days for legal to review, which can stall the deal. A redline-triage skill sorts a prospect’s changes against your approved fallback positions before the file reaches legal — so the team doesn’t waste time reviewing cases already outlined by your playbook.

What goes in the skill:

      • Instructions: Label each changed clause Accept, Counter, or Legal review; route anything the playbook doesn’t cover to Legal review; never draft final contract language
      • Reference file: Your playbook, with fallback positions by clause
      • Template: A clause-by-clause list, then a two-line rep summary

Example input: “Copperline Foods returned our MSA. Payment terms changed from Net 30 to Net 60, liability cap raised to 2x annual fees, new termination-for-convenience clause.”

Example output:

      • Payment terms: Counter. Playbook allows up to Net 45 without approval.
      • Liability cap: Accept. Within approved range.
      • Termination for convenience: Legal review. No playbook position exists.
      • Rep summary: “Two of three changes can be resolved today. Hold the termination clause for legal.”

Two more sales use cases:

      • Business case one-pager: Enter the numbers a buyer shared in discovery and get a business case built on your approved ROI model, ready for a champion to forward to finance.
      • Mutual action plan: Give the buyer’s go-live date and get a backward-planned timeline with an owner from each side on every step.

Service Team Use Cases

Support teams sometimes first hear about a product change from a confused customer. A release-briefing skill converts engineering’s release notes into an internal briefing so agents are ready before launch.

What goes in the skill:

      • Instructions: Restate each change in customer-facing language, anticipate likely questions, and find every help article or saved reply that mentions the affected feature.
      • Reference files: Your terminology list and an exported index of help articles and saved replies
      • Template: What changed, potential customer questions, suggested replies, and content to update

Example input: “Release 4.12: CSV export moves from Settings to Reports. Exports over 50,000 rows now arrive by email.”

Example output:

      • Likely question: “Where did the export button go?”
      • Suggested reply: “Export has moved to the Reports menu. For files over 50,000 rows, we’ll email you a download link.”
      • Content to update: Three help articles and two saved replies still point to Settings.
      • Status: Draft, needs support lead review

Two more service use cases:

      • Bug report for engineering: Paste a customer’s problem description and get a ticket in engineering’s template, with reproduction steps and a severity level from your rubric. Clean handoffs prevent team collaboration from stalling on follow-up questions.
      • Quarterly business review deck: Add a customer’s usage export and support summary to get a draft QBR deck in your slide template, with talking points on adoption and risks.

Claude Cowork Best Practices for Safety and Reliability

Use caution with Claude Cowork because it can read, write, and delete files from the folders you point it to (with your permission, of course). I think this Claude Academy lesson paints the picture best with this analogy:

“Pointing Claude at Documents, Downloads, or Desktop is the equivalent of letting a new colleague rummage through every file you have. Make a folder for the work. Move (or copy) in what’s needed. Point Claude there.”

On top of the access you grant Claude through Cowork, skills downloaded from the internet can contain malicious code, so it’s important to know where the skill came from and review its content before installing.

This section covers the basics of how to keep your data safe while using Claude Cowork skills. For a deeper dive, I recommend reading Claude Support’s article on using Cowork safely.

Screen and Data Hygiene Before Recording

Everything visible during a recording is evidence for the model. Claude’s safety regulations recommend:

      • Close notification banners; sign out of unrelated accounts.
      • Hide API keys, tokens, and passwords.
      • Swap real customer data for a sanitized sample file before you start recording.
      • Close any files, apps, or conversations you don’t want recorded.

A skill built on a real spreadsheet can carry names, account numbers, or internal URLs into a document you later share with others. So, build the skill on filler data. Test it on real data only after you review it.

QA Checklist and Escalation Rules

Before you use, share, or deploy a skill to your team, check these items:

      • Triggers: Test several prompts that should invoke the skill, then review Claude’s thinking to confirm it loaded. You can also directly ask Claude in the chat, “Did you use the [skill name] skill?”
      • Source: Anthropic recommends sticking to skills you built yourself or got from Anthropic. For skills from elsewhere, read the files before installing the skill. Red flags include code that contacts outside servers, reaches into files it shouldn’t need, or does something not mentioned in its description.
      • Security scan: On Enterprise plans with scanning enabled, skill and plugin scanning checks third-party skills and plugins for malicious content whenever they’re uploaded or edited. Skills already installed before scanning was enabled aren’t checked. Here’s what a security scan looks like on a recent skill I uploaded:
        • Approval mode: Cowork can be set to automatically approve or manually approve. Use “Manually approve” for sensitive accounts, a tool or plugin you haven’t tried before, or actions you can’t easily reverse.
        • Stop rules: If Claude opens files or sites you never mentioned, or the job outgrows your request, stop the task. When you build a skill, write stop conditions into its instructions as well. “If X is unclear, stop and ask before continuing” is a valid instruction.
        • Ownership: On Team and Enterprise plans, owners can require review before a skill is published. Assign one person to maintain each skill, since skills drift if nobody owns them. That person should verify it after product updates and version it before changes.

Connect Claude to HubSpot

Skills are useful for detailing how to do a task, but they can’t on their own get up-to-date information about your business and customers. So if a workflow depends on a deal stage or sales call notes, you would have to manually enter that yourself — unless you have a connector.

This is what the HubSpot connector for Claude does. It’s an official MCP (Model Context Protocol) connector built by HubSpot that gives Claude read and write access to your CRM — directly from the Claude chat window.

What the HubSpot Connector Does

The connector is a permission-based integration. You connect it once via OAuth; a Super Admin or user with HubSpot Marketplace permissions must authorize it in your HubSpot account first.

Once connected, Claude can:

        • Search contacts, companies, deals, and tickets in plain language
        • Create and update CRM records, including contacts and deals (currently capped at 10 records per bulk operation in beta)
        • Log activities, tasks, and notes directly from Claude
        • Surface insights from your engagement history — calls, emails, meetings

It also does not support delete operations. It also does not access HubSpot Sensitive Data properties. If your account has Sensitive Data enabled, it affects engagement data access as well — verify with your admin before building workflows on top of it.

Pro tip: Set the connector’s write tools to “Needs Approval” in Claude, as HubSpot recommends, so nothing changes until you confirm it.

Also worth knowing: according to HubSpot’s connector page, Anthropic does not use information shared through HubSpot to train its models, except when you choose to provide feedback or opt in.

Example CRM-Grounded Skills to Try First

1. Pre-call brief skill: Before a meeting, ask: “Pull everything we know about [Company] and give me a one-page brief.” The connector fetches the contact record, recent notes, open deals, and engagement history. The skill structures the output: background, open items, suggested talking points.

2. Post-call note and update skill: After a call, describe what happened in plain language. The skill formats a note in your standard structure. The connector logs it to the right deal or contact in HubSpot. No tab-switching required.

3. Pipeline review skill: “Which deals in Negotiation haven’t been touched in 10+ days?” The connector pulls the data; the skill formats it as a prioritized list with suggested next actions per deal.

4. Lead enrichment skill: When a new contact comes in, trigger a brief: company overview, LinkedIn context (if you’ve added a web search tool), recent news. Attach a suggested outreach opener. Log the research as a note.

These workflows live in the HubSpot connector for Claude — explore it here.

Frequently Asked Questions About Claude Cowork Skills

Do skills work in Cowork, Claude Chat, and Claude Code?

Yes, skills enabled in Cowork also work in Claude Code because they sync whenever you sign in with the same Claude account (as long as you have v2.1.273 or later). However, it’s a one-way sync — so skills you install in Claude Code do not sync with Claude Cowork or chat. Skills also work in Claude Chat. They’re a Claude-level feature, and the only Cowork-exclusive feature was Record a Skill, which still has some limitations since the September 2026 merger of Cowork and Chat.

Can I safely use Record a skill with customer data?

Use fake test data instead of real customer data when recording your skill. Anthropic warns against displaying sensitive information while recording, because anything visible on your screen or spoken aloud during the session is captured. Test with real data only after you’ve reviewed the generated skill carefully, since it can carry visible information into a reusable document.

How do I share skills with my team and control updates?

On Team and Enterprise plans, once an owner turns on sharing, open Customize > Skills, click the three-dot menu beside a skill you built, and choose Share. You can then add people by name or email. Recipients get a view-only copy that picks up your edits the next time they use it. Admins can control what’s published to the org directory, and recorded skills default to private until the creator shares them. Cowork keeps internal version history per skill, so you can roll back if an update breaks something. On Team plans, there’s a soft cap of 50 custom skills per workspace; Enterprise caps at 200.

How are skills different from projects and instructions?

Skills are invoked only as needed when the context calls for them in a conversation, whereas profile instructions apply globally across all chats at all times. Skills are a narrow set of instructions for a particular task, whereas projects are broader containers that can hold documents, project-specific instructions, project-specific memory, and conversations opened within that project. Memory stores facts about you that persist across conversations. These features complement each other: a project can house the context that a skill then acts on.

How do I connect Claude to my HubSpot data?

Install the HubSpot connector for Claude, which is available on any HubSpot plan (even free) alongside a paid Claude subscription. Open Claude’s Settings > Connectors, browse for HubSpot, click Connect, and pick permissions. Unless you’re a Super Admin or have App Marketplace Access, a Super Admin must approve the connector. Claude sees only what your HubSpot permissions allow, and it can create and update records, but it cannot delete them. Once connected, you can ask Claude about your CRM from any conversation.

All it takes is one skill to start.

The biggest mistake people make with Claude skills is trying to automate everything at once. They build ten skills before they’ve tested one, and end up with a junk drawer nobody uses.

A better approach: pick the one task your team does every week that follows the same steps every time. A report. A brief. A follow-up sequence. Build a skill for that, test it on messy inputs, and get it working reliably before you add another.

Once that first skill is running, connecting it to live data is what takes it from a time-saver to an actual workflow. That’s where the HubSpot connector for Claude comes in.

Skills handle the how. The connector supplies the what. Together, they’re the closest thing to a reliable AI teammate that doesn’t need to be briefed from scratch every Monday.

Ready to try it? Explore the HubSpot connector for Claude and connect your CRM context to the workflows you’re already building.
