issues.author: HubSpot Staff
issues.content_html:
I’ve been experimenting with Claude AI for marketing workflows over the past year, and it’s now my go-to assistant. In this field, AI use is close to universal: 98% of marketing teams use it in some way, according to HubSpot’s State of AI in Marketing report. For campaign marketers, that might look like turning a product announcement into a week of social posts, tightening ad copy to fit character limits, or pressure-testing campaign messaging before a stakeholder review.

But Claude only knows what you tell it. It can’t automatically see which contacts converted, which campaigns generated pipeline, or what customers keep asking your support team, so even sharp output can miss what’s actually happening in your business.

The HubSpot connector for Claude brings your HubSpot CRM data into the conversation and lets Claude act on it, like drafting a marketing email or creating a follow-up task directly in your account. This guide covers how to set up the connector, the marketing workflows and prompts it supports, how to govern its use, and when a dashboard is the better choice.

Table of Contents

  • What is Claude AI for marketing?
  • Why Connect Claude to HubSpot?
  • How to Connect Claude to HubSpot Using the HubSpot Connector for Claude
  • Claude AI for Marketing Workflows Inside HubSpot
  • Claude Prompts for Marketers Using HubSpot Context
  • How to Govern Claude AI for Marketing and Measure Impact
  • When to Use Dashboards Instead of Claude AI for Marketing
  • Frequently Asked Questions About Claude AI for Marketing

What is Claude AI for marketing?

Claude AI for marketing means using Claude, Anthropic’s AI assistant, to handle the writing, research, and analysis work that campaigns depend on. Claude helps marketers draft, analyze, and summarize work, such as writing and editing first drafts, turning meeting notes into briefs, and assembling campaign readouts from numbers in separate analytics tools. It can also pull current information from the web, which makes it handy for early-stage market research.

As with all large language models (LLMs), the quality of Claude’s output depends heavily on the context it receives. Anthropic’s prompting guidance compares Claude to a sharp new employee with no background on how your team operates, and it recommends telling Claude who the output is for and how it will be used.

Claude works well on its own for one-off drafting and research. It becomes far more powerful once it can read your real customer records, campaign results, and engagement history.

Why connect Claude to HubSpot?

Picture a marketer asking Claude why last quarter’s webinar series underperformed. Without a link to HubSpot, Claude can only work with what gets pasted into the chat: an exported spreadsheet, a few copied metrics, a paragraph describing the audience. Each fresh analysis means exporting and explaining that background again, and the answer stops wherever the export does.

Connected workflows move that context gathering out of the marketer’s hands. The HubSpot connector for Claude links HubSpot context to Claude, giving it read access to contacts, deals, campaigns, marketing emails, and other records, scoped to each person’s current HubSpot access rights. Logged calls, meetings, emails, tasks, and notes are readable too, unless the account has Sensitive Data turned on. The webinar question can now pull event records, follow-up activity, and campaign attribution data into a single answer.

The connection also runs in reverse. Claude can create and update HubSpot records, such as changing a deal stage or adding a task, from the chat window, though it can’t delete data.

HubSpot Smart CRM unifies customer context and campaign records. It sits beneath Marketing Hub, Sales Hub, and HubSpot’s other core products as their shared database, showing where each contact stands at every point in the relationship. Claude then works from one consistent record rather than fragments stitched together from separate tools. Connected AI workflows improve personalization and execution for that reason.

Getting there takes a one-time setup in Claude’s connector settings.

How to Connect Claude to HubSpot Using the HubSpot Connector for Claude

The HubSpot connector for Claude is free, but it requires a paid Claude plan (Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise) and an active HubSpot user account on any plan, including free. Super Admins and users with App Marketplace Access permissions can connect immediately; everyone else needs Super Admin approval first.

Then, in Claude:

  1. Log in to the HubSpot account you want to use.
  2. Select the permissions to grant, then click Connect app.

What the Connector Does

Toggling HubSpot on under + > Connectors in any chat lets Claude reference your HubSpot records in its answers. Set the connector’s Write tools option to Needs Approval, as HubSpot recommends, so Claude confirms each proposed edit with you before making it. Every create or update action is recorded in HubSpot’s Audit Log and attributed to both the user and the connector, and bulk edits run in batches of 10 records or fewer.

What Marketers Can Do Once Connected

HubSpot’s marketing examples include ranking last month’s campaigns by revenue, finding the subject lines that drew the most clicks, measuring how long contacts stayed in each lifecycle stage, and queuing follow-up tasks for recent email openers. Claude can also publish a blog post once the prompt supplies a title, author, featured image, meta description, and slug. Workflows are the exception: Claude drafts the content, and you build the workflow in HubSpot, where marketing automation runs.

Claude AI for Marketing Workflows Inside HubSpot

With the HubSpot connector in place, Claude supports four everyday marketing jobs: analyzing campaigns, drafting content and email, tailoring outreach, and even serving as a virtual assistant for routine marketing tasks. It follows the access rules already set in HubSpot, so results depend on what the signed-in user is allowed to view and change.

Campaign and Performance Analysis

Campaign records, attribution data, and marketing email performance are all readable, so one prompt can compare a campaign’s engagement with its attributed results. Prompts about individual page or post performance must name a campaign and a date range, and drafts return only metadata. Results can come back as charts, such as a pie chart isolating contacts who opened an email but never clicked. For AI analytics use cases beyond the connector, see AI marketing analytics.

Content and Email Drafting

HubSpot Content Hub supports content creation and publishing workflows. Through the connector, Claude can create and update landing pages, website pages, and marketing emails, and page designs built in Claude Design can be sent into HubSpot. Campaigns are writable too: Claude can create one and attach new assets, so a launch email and its landing page start out grouped together. Ask Claude to study your recent top-performing emails before it drafts the next one.

Personalization and Segmentation Support

Claude can read segments (lists) but can’t create them, so building segments stays in HubSpot. Use Claude instead to trace a contact’s conversations across chat, email, and SMS before tailoring outreach. Inbox and help desk conversations add another source of buyer language: Claude can summarize the month’s most common questions, surfacing recurring concerns in customers’ own words. For events, Claude can take an imported registrant list and produce follow-up emails. From there, Claude can match registrants to existing contacts and update lifecycle stages, subject to any conditional property rules configured in HubSpot.

Follow-Up, Task, and Reporting Assistance

After a sales call or campaign debrief, a single plain-language request can log the notes, create follow-up tasks, and update a contact’s lead status. Our guide on using Claude as a virtual assistant shows a comparable follow-up routine that stays inside Claude: Project instructions define how to track action items, and uploaded meeting transcripts supply the notes.

Recurring report prep suits Claude marketing automation in Claude Cowork: A skill stores your prep steps, and a scheduled task runs them remotely, even while your computer sleeps. Tasks that need local files or apps run only on your machine. Claude can then turn that prep into a team doc or a one-slide leadership summary.

Claude Prompts for Marketers Using HubSpot Context

Each prompt below opens by assigning Claude a role. Anthropic’s prompting guide lists role-setting among its core techniques and says even a one-line role steers what Claude focuses on and how it sounds. The rest names the records to pull, the work to produce, any HubSpot action, and the answer format. Swap in your own bracketed details, then save the versions that work as a team library of Claude prompts for marketers.

Pro tip: Once a prompt proves useful week after week, turn it into one of your team’s Claude skills. A skill stores the parts of a prompt that never change, like the role, the HubSpot records to check, and the output format. Claude recognizes when a request calls for that skill and applies it without being asked, so teammates only need to supply details like the campaign name and date range.

Reporting and Analytics

“You’re a marketing analyst reporting to a CMO. Pull the HubSpot campaign record and marketing email results for [Campaign Name] from [date range]. Compare open rates with click rates, break down engaged contacts by lifecycle stage, and show the campaign’s attributed revenue. Return a three-bullet summary, then a comparison table. Cite the HubSpot records behind each figure.”

Campaign Planning

This prompt grounds a Claude AI marketing strategy in deals you’ve already won:

“You’re a campaign strategist for a [industry] company. Review our closed-won deals from last quarter and identify the buying triggers that appear most often. Use them to draft a four-week launch plan for [Product] with audience criteria from our existing segments, a three-email nurture outline, and a landing page structure. Then create a campaign in HubSpot called [Campaign Name].”

The connector can’t edit a campaign once it exists, so confirm the name and details before you approve Claude’s proposal.

Content Ideation

“You’re a content marketer. Read last month’s inbox and help desk conversations in HubSpot. List the five most common questions or objections, each with a short example of how customers phrased it. Then suggest 10 blog headlines and five email subject lines that answer them in the same vocabulary.”

Email Drafting

“You’re an email copywriter focused on re-engagement. Find contacts who opened [Email Name] but didn’t click, and group them by lifecycle stage. For the largest group, draft one follow-up email that offers a 15-minute demo. For any customer example, use only these details: [case study summary]. Create it in HubSpot as a marketing email so I can review it before it goes out.”

Account and Touchpoint Summaries

“You’re a GTM strategist preparing a sales handoff. Pull the full engagement history for [Company Name] in HubSpot, including emails, meetings, calls, and notes. Summarize it in three short paragraphs: background and key stakeholders, open challenges and recent interactions, and recommended next marketing touchpoints.”

Review before you act on the output.

HubSpot acknowledges that Claude’s answers can be wrong and advises having a person check them. Adding “cite the HubSpot records behind each figure” to any analysis prompt lets you open each record and confirm the number. Before running a write prompt across many records, test it on one, and read each proposed change before typing Yes. Drafted emails and pages still need a brand voice and a link check in HubSpot before they are published.

Turning those individual checks into a repeatable team process is the job of governance.

How to Govern Claude AI for Marketing and Measure Impact

Governing Claude AI for marketing comes down to four controls: skill review, shared standards, connector access, and measurement. Together, these controls also build the readiness that HubSpot’s guide to AI agents for marketing links to success with agentic AI: clear processes and steady testing.

Set review rules for shared skills.

  • Test first: Anthropic recommends running a skill on your own account before rolling it out organization-wide.
  • Require sign-off: Set Publishing to Requires review, so nothing a teammate builds, including later edits, reaches the organization library until an owner approves it. Reviewers can’t approve their own work.
  • Scan uploads: Enterprise plans can also check each submitted version for malicious content.

Standardize terminology and claims.

  • Build a style skill: Store voice guidelines, approved product names, and banned phrases in one skill. Team and Enterprise owners can push it to everyone, and Enterprise plans can limit marketing skills to one group via a plugin.
  • Update in one place: Once an owner approves a new version of a published skill, everyone using it receives the change automatically, so a product rename gets fixed once.
  • Write verification into it: Require a source record link for every figure and a direct customer quote before any feedback summary.

Control connector access.

  • Scope access: Super Admins who approve the HubSpot connector for Claude also set its data permissions and install list.
  • Audit connections: HubSpot’s audit logs show who has connected it and when.
  • Restrict accounts: Claude Enterprise admins can block HubSpot connections from Claude accounts outside their Enterprise organization.

Measure efficiency and pipeline contribution.

  • Time savings: Time one recurring task, like the weekly campaign readout, for a few cycles before and after rollout.
  • Adoption: Team and Enterprise owners can see who uses Claude and which features stick in its usage analytics. On Enterprise, the dashboard also splits usage and cost by group and lists the skills and connectors each group used beside its spend.
  • Follow-up speed: Track the days between event registration and first personalized outreach, plus how quickly stalled deals get a next step.
  • Revenue: HubSpot Marketing Hub supports automation and reporting, including campaign Revenue reports (Professional) and model-based Revenue Attribution (Enterprise). Treat gaps between Claude-assisted and manual campaigns as leads to investigate, since timing, budget, and audience also move revenue.

When to Use Dashboards Instead of Claude AI for Marketing

Dashboards support recurring KPI monitoring better than ad hoc AI analysis. Questions that repeat on a fixed cadence, like weekly lead volume against goal or monthly pipeline created, deserve a saved report that answers them without anyone typing a prompt.

HubSpot dashboards group related reports on one screen for a specific audience or goal. Owners control access by keeping a dashboard private, opening it to the whole account, or limiting it to chosen users and teams. Report emails can run on a daily, weekly, or monthly schedule, and dashboard emails can recur as well, though only HubSpot users can receive the recurring versions. Each recipient gets the same report configuration every cycle, with no prompt involved.

Claude covers the questions nobody has built a report for. Saved reports and dashboards don’t appear among the objects the HubSpot connector for Claude can read, so Claude works from records such as contacts, deals, campaigns, and marketing emails instead. That suits one-off, multi-condition questions, like which contacts opened a launch email in the past two weeks, have an open deal, and haven’t heard from sales since. Claude also handles the conversation and help desk summaries mentioned earlier, where the answer is a pattern in written text.

The Claude Cowork scheduling from the follow-up section still fits here: It can draft commentary on recurring numbers while the numbers themselves stay on a dashboard.

Teams get the most from running the two in sequence:

  1. Spot the change: A dashboard shows landing page conversions dropped last week.
  2. Diagnose it: Claude reviews that page’s campaign results alongside recent customer conversations and email clicks to suggest likely causes.
  3. Act on it: Claude drafts revised copy and, once you approve the edit, updates the landing page in HubSpot.

Frequently Asked Questions About Claude AI for Marketing

How can I connect Claude to HubSpot without developer support?

The HubSpot connector for Claude installs without code. You need a paid Claude subscription plus an active HubSpot user account at any edition, even free. Open Claude’s Settings > Connectors, click Browse, find HubSpot, click Connect, and sign in to grant permissions. Unless you’re a Super Admin or have App Marketplace Access, a Super Admin approves it first.

What are the best Claude prompts for email and ads in HubSpot?

Strong prompts give Claude a job title, the HubSpot records to check, and an output shape. For email, have Claude write a follow-up for contacts who opened a send without clicking, saved as a HubSpot marketing email. Ads differ: Since the connector can’t create them, Claude drafts headline variants from help desk objections for your ad platform.

How do I keep Claude on-brand and compliant?

For brand voice, convert your style guide into a skill that Team and Enterprise owners can provision org-wide. For compliance, set Write tools to Needs Approval so every edit waits for your Yes.

When should I rely on dashboards instead of Claude?

Rely on dashboards for metrics your team revisits every week or month, since HubSpot can email those reports automatically. Turn to Claude for unplanned questions that combine several filters and for themes hidden in support conversations. Dashboards aren’t on the connector’s readable object list, so Claude pulls numbers straight from deals, campaigns, and other records.

How should I measure ROI from Claude inside HubSpot?

Measure time and money separately. Clock a repeat task, like a campaign recap, now and again once Claude handles it. Team and Enterprise owners can see connector users, read and write action counts, and estimated time saved in Claude’s analytics. For money, Marketing Hub Professional and Enterprise include a campaign ROI report weighing revenue against spend.

issues.title: AI influencers: What consumer sentiment data tells brands
issues.summary: As you scroll through your TikTok or Instagram feed, you’ll no doubt come across at least a handful of influencers trying to sell you something by wearing the latest viral lip gloss, hopping into luxury cars, and taste-testing popular treats. But what if I told you that while these content creators may look like real people, they’re actually AI influencers?
issues.author: esantiago@hubspot.com (Erica Santiago)
issues.content_html:
As you scroll through your TikTok or Instagram feed, you’ll no doubt come across at least a handful of influencers trying to sell you something by wearing the latest viral lip gloss, hopping into luxury cars, and taste-testing popular treats. But what if I told you that while these content creators may look like real people, they’re actually AI influencers?

If you’re a marketer or business owner who is already fully using AI in your digital marketing strategy, then you’re likely already familiar with the concept. You may even be curious about leveraging AI influencers in your influencer marketing strategy.

But how will your target consumers feel about the use of AI influencers? Will they be receptive, or can AI influencers erode the trust you’ve built with your audience? Can AI influencers really save you money compared to working with human influencers? And are all virtual influencers AI? Keep reading for answers to these questions and more.

Table of Contents

  • What are AI influencers, and why are brands considering them?
  • What do consumers think about AI influencers and AI models?
  • Do AI influencers build or erode brand trust?
  • Notable Virtual Influencers + Brand Examples to Learn From
  • Do AI influencers save brands money?
  • How to Use AI-Assisted Content Workflows Without Losing Authenticity
  • Common Pitfalls With AI Influencers and How to Avoid Backlash
  • What’s Next for AI Influencers
  • Frequently Asked Questions About AI Influencers

What are AI influencers, and why are brands considering them?

AI influencers are virtual personas whose appearance, voice, behaviors, or content are created or assisted by generative AI. An example of an AI influencer is Aitana Lopez, who has over 400,000 followers on Instagram. She’s marketed as a virtual fitness and lifestyle influencer and has promoted brands such as Amazon, Victoria’s Secret, Olaplex, and Razer.

Her work as an influencer has reportedly earned her and The Clueless, the Barcelona-based tech company that created her, over $11,000 per month.

          View this post on Instagram                      

A post shared by Aitana Lopez (@fit_aitana)

AI influencers fall under the umbrella of “virtual influencers,” but make no mistake — while every AI influencer is a virtual influencer, not all virtual influencers are AI-generated. For example, the virtual influencer, singer, and model Miquela Sousa (formerly known as Lil Miquela) was created in 2016 using artist-driven CGI, and her music is created by a collective of singers, songwriters, and instrumentalists—not generative AI.

Over the last decade, Miquela Sousa has worked with brands like Gucci, Prada, and Calvin Klein. She’s also the first virtual avatar to sign with a model agency, having signed to CAA in 2020 and previously being represented by WME.

          View this post on Instagram                      

A post shared by Miquela (@lilmiquela)

Why are brands interested in AI Influencers?

Brands are dabbling with using AI influencers and virtual models like Aitana Lopez and Miquela Sousa for three reasons — creative control, reduced costs, and scalable content.

Creative Control

Ruben Cruz, founder of The Clueless, says Aitana Lopez was created so the company could make a “better living and not be dependent on other people who have egos” or “who just want to make a lot of money by posing.”

In other words, Cruz wanted to avoid working with influencers whose personalities, creative processes, and work styles clash with his company’s creative vision—a sentiment brands wanting to leverage AI influencers can relate to.

AI and virtual creators will recite a script, deliver a video, or conform to a brand’s aesthetic exactly as agreed upon. Companies never have to worry about unwanted input or script changes that could slow production.

Reduced Costs

The initial creation of an AI influencer or virtual internet personality can cost anywhere from a few hundred dollars to a few hundred thousand. However, once out of the initial setup phase, AI influencers can save companies money on lighting, production, and paid partnerships.

Scalable Content

Human influencers need to sleep, eat, take breaks, pick up their kids from school, or walk the dog — they can’t make content 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. But AI influencers can. Though AI influencers like Aitana Lopez may look super busy doing their makeup, traveling, and hopping into luxury cars, it’s all fake— so they always have time to make content.

What do consumers think about AI influencers and AI models?

Many consumers feel that AI influencers corrode trust, with one Reddit user saying, “If I see something that is AI but tries to appear real, it’s an instant turn-off and trust killer. It’s enough for me to see it once for a brand, and the trust is gone forever.”

The skepticism toward AI influencers shows up in surveys, too. According to a study published via ResearchGate, 45.3% of consumers would view an ad with an AI influencer without taking action, 28.3% would ignore the ad completely, and only 26.4% would actively engage with the ad, such as by clicking or searching.

Do AI influencers build or erode brand trust?

AI influencers pose a high risk of eroding trust between brands and consumers because using a fake person to promote a brand’s goods or services doesn’t read as authentic. The appeal of human influencers and content creators is that they’re real people who cultivated a consistent following by being their genuine selves.

Influencers and content creators bond with their followers over shared interests, hobbies, and beliefs, and they often get their audience interested in a product or service by using it themselves.

In fact, a survey by Clutch shows that if a human influencer is found to use AI-generated content, 71% of consumers say they would question the recommendation, and 53% are less likely to buy from a brand known for using AI in social content.

An AI or virtual influencer can’t use a product or service, can’t have a genuine interest, nor a human experience to connect with human followers.

That said, the trust risk is not equal in every situation. It concentrates where audiences are skeptical, where safeguards are missing, where disclosure is weak, and where nobody is measuring the effect. Score each area below before you decide to leverage AI influencers.

How to score it:

  • Any No-go: Don’t launch. Fix the issue or choose a different approach.
  • All Go: Proceed to a limited pilot.
  • Mix of Go and Conditional: Launch only if each Conditional item has an owner and a fix date before the first post.

Why these four areas matter: Consumers aren’t rejecting AI across the board. That same Clutch survey also found that 42% view AI positively when it’s used for educational content, but 64% would trust a brand or creator less if AI were used to misrepresent products. Nearly 90% say it’s important to disclose AI-generated content.

Disclosure is also becoming a legal matter. For example, as of June 9, 2026, New York requires certain ads featuring AI-generated human performers to include a disclosure, and the EU’s Article 50 transparency obligations have applied since August 2, 2026. Always double-check to confirm what applies to your markets.

Notable Virtual Influencers + Brand Examples to Learn From

Virtual influencers have been working with brands for years, so their campaigns show what works and what doesn’t. Each example below is broken down by what it teaches about creativity, community, transparency, representation, and governance.

1. Miquela x PAC SUN Back-To-School Campaign

PacSun teamed up with Miquela for its back-to-school and holiday 2022 campaigns, and said the deal marked the start of a broader push into virtual influencers. The two collaborated on social content to amplify those seasonal campaigns after both had taken part in the ComplexLand digital event.

Source

Creative

The partnership was built around a persona who already lived online, with roughly 3 million Instagram followers at the time. Choosing a virtual star with an existing audience meant the brand didn’t have to build one from scratch.

Community

The fit rested on shared audience territory. PacSun framed the move as a way to strengthen its connection with a core demographic exploring the digital space. Takeaway: pick a persona whose community already overlaps with yours.

Transparency

Miquela is open about being a virtual influencer, describing herself as a “Robot living in LA,” so there was no deception to manage. The audience was in on it from the start.

Representation

PacSun’s president pointed to Miquela’s involvement in the Black Lives Matter movement and the Rally the Vote campaign as aligned with the brand’s values. That raises a fair question for any brand: a persona’s advocacy is authored by its creators, so scrutinize whose voice is really speaking.

Governance

A virtual star never ages, clothes always fit perfectly, and she does what you ask, but that control is also a responsibility. Set clear approval processes for any social or political messaging attached to a persona, since you are effectively the speaker.

2. Samsung and Sam

Sam is Samsung’s own virtual influencer, created in collaboration with Cheil and the Brazilian design firm Lightfarm. She is used mainly in Latin America, and in July 2023, she connected to the regional launch events from Seoul, where she covered the global Galaxy Unpacked event.

In January 2024, she was named Samsung’s AI ambassador ahead of Galaxy Unpacked 2024, where she was set to present products and interview five live influencers from Latin America.

Source

Creative

Sam works because she’s integrated into real brand moments rather than confined to social posts. She has blogged, made tutorials, released a music video promoting the Galaxy Z Flip 5, and helped sell devices at Unpacked events.

Giving a persona several jobs, from host to educator to performer, builds her into the brand’s story rather than treating her as a one-off stunt.

Community

Samsung paired Sam with real people. At Unpacked 2024, she interviewed Latin American creators live, bridging the virtual and human sides of the community. Her role was also regionally focused, which suggests a persona can work better as a local community figure than as a global one.

Transparency

Sam is openly presented as a virtual influencer, and Samsung’s own newsroom calls her one. Her role is also clear (host, guide, ambassador), so audiences aren’t asked to believe she personally uses Samsung products.

Representation

As a brand-owned character, Sam’s look, voice, and personality are entirely Samsung’s choices. Treat that as a casting decision: involve regional teams and creators in shaping a persona who will speak to their audience, rather than designing her centrally and exporting her.

Governance

Samsung reported that Sam helped boost early sales of its new devices in Latin America, including a 30% increase in sales on its Mexico live-shopping portal.

Set measurable goals and a content plan before launch, attribute any performance claims to their sources, and decide in advance who will maintain the persona, since a neglected virtual influencer can quickly feel stale.

3. Amazon Prime, boAt & Kyra

Kyra was launched by FUTR Studios in January 2022 as a virtual influencer that is both CGI and AI-powered. Her first brand partner was boAt for the #FutureOfAudio campaign, which launched its Rockerz 330 and 333 ANC neckbands.

Amazon Prime Video followed, integrating Kyra into the promotion for its sci-fi series “The Peripheral,” with her creator noting that the team recreated the show’s VR headset and transported her to its setting.

Source

Creative

Both campaigns leaned into science fiction, which is where a virtual persona excels. boAt said the collaboration enabled a sci-fi-like audio-visual experience that wouldn’t be possible with any other influencer. Choose briefs a human can’t easily deliver.

Community

The boAt launch reached beyond social posts. Kyra appeared at an in-person boAt party through a 3D projection installation, alongside human creators. Bridging virtual and live moments helps a persona feel part of a scene rather than an ad.

Transparency

The pairing with Prime Video worked partly because it was an obvious fiction-meets-fiction match. When the story is openly synthetic, disclosure becomes part of the creative rather than a caveat.

Representation

Kyra was positioned as India’s first virtual influencer, and her creators said they planned a new model with a South Indian focus. That’s a useful prompt for brands: local relevance matters, and a single persona rarely represents an entire market.

Governance

Early results were strong, but they come from launch-novelty periods. Judge a persona on sustained performance, not a debut.

4. Dior & Noonoouri

In 2018, Dior’s beauty team had Noonoouri recreate its Rouge Dior Ultra Rouge launch film. The original starred Natalie Portman; the tribute was nearly a shot-for-shot reenactment, down to the Dior ring. Noonoouri also took over the Maison’s Instagram during the Dior Cruise show.

Source

Creative

Rebuilding a famous campaign with a stylized animated character created instant buzz. The contrast between the original and the tribute did most of the work.

Community

Dior used the persona to reach younger Instagram audiences interested in high-end beauty. The takeaway is to match a persona to an audience you’re trying to grow, not just one you already have.

Transparency

Noonoouri’s doll-like proportions make her unmistakably an animation, so nobody is misled about what they’re seeing. A clearly stylized persona carries less deception risk than a photorealistic one.

Representation

Her exaggerated features reflect a stylized ideal, not a real body. Brands should consider what beauty standard a digital character promotes, especially in cosmetics.

Governance

Stepping into a role originally played by a real actress raises questions about likeness, permission, and optics. Clear agreements around any reference to a real person’s work are essential.

Do AI influencers save brands money?

AI can save brands money, but it depends on what you count. AI influencers can cut the most visible line item, production, while adding costs elsewhere: oversight, disclosure, rework, reputation, and measurement. A fair comparison looks at the total cost of the program, rather than the cost of a single post.

You can look up costs online but be aware that cost claims are mostly published by vendors and agencies that sell AI content, and they vary widely. Some guides puts AI influencer creation at $15,000 to $100,000+ upfront, with monthly costs of $500 to $15,000+. But other sources claim 80-95% savings on large volumes of video. Treat all of these numbers as starting points for your own testing, not benchmarks.

Taking a Total-Cost View

1. Production. This is where savings are most credible. Once a persona exists, the marginal cost of producing one more piece of content approaches zero, and there are no talent fees, travel, or scheduling.

The catch is the upfront build and the ongoing work of generating, editing, and approving content. A persona that looks effortless usually still has a team behind it.

2. Risk management. Brands often cite reduced risk of scandal as a draw. In a World Federation of Advertisers finding reported by Favikon, 58% of brands interested in AI influencers named reduced risk of influencer scandals as a top draw. But the risk doesn’t disappear completely; it only changes shape.

You swap the risk of a creator’s behavior for the risk of your own content errors, off-brand outputs, or a backlash against the concept itself. Budget for review and an escalation plan.

3. Disclosure compliance. This cost is growing. Platforms like Instagram and TikTok have their own AI labeling rules and protocols. And other countries and regions have legal requirements regarding AI disclosure. In the EU, for example, transparency obligations for AI-generated content began to apply in August 2026.

The direct cost is modest, covering labels, templates, and legal review. The hidden cost is audience trust: consumer distrust is a recognized downside when disclosure is unclear.

4. Rework. Generated content needs corrections: anatomical glitches, inconsistent facial expressions, misreading cultural cues, tone issues. Rework hours rarely appear in a vendor’s cost comparison, so track them in your own use case.

5. PR and reputation. As I said earlier, public perception of AI influencers or synthetic personas ranges from curiosity to hostility, and it varies by category and audience. Set aside time and budget for a communications plan, including how you’ll respond if people accuse you of replacing real creators.

6. Community impact. Human creators bring a ready audience and a relationship with it. A new AI persona has to build both. The savings can also be offset on the other side: some AI adopters found that when creators use AI to cut their own costs, those savings haven’t led to lower fees, because brands pay for influence and credibility.

And partnerships with AI accounts aren’t a sure thing; Data shows that brand deals with AI social accounts fell by about 30% in the first eight months of 2025 compared with the same period in 2024.

7. Measurement. Fairly comparing AI and human influencers takes planning. You need matched campaigns, consistent metrics, and enough time to see past the novelty effect. Some of this has a real cost in analyst hours and tooling, and without it, you’re making decisions based on anecdotes.

As one analysis puts it, the honest comparison isn’t a cost debate but a question of what a campaign asks the influencer to do.

Where AI Influencers Tend to Save Money (and Where They Don’t)

They tend to help when you need high volumes of content, many variations to test, a tightly controlled brand look, or multilingual output. They tend to be a poor fit when the sale depends on lived experience or personal credibility, such as skincare results, health claims, parenting, or financial advice.

There, the cheaper post can cost you in conversion and trust.

A Qualitative Worksheet to Complete Before You Model Any Finances

Before you build a spreadsheet, answer these in plain language. If your team can’t answer them, then you’ll already know you need to reevaluate your strategy.

Then add two summary questions: What is the strongest reason this would save us money, and what is the strongest reason it wouldn’t? Count the “High” ratings. A cluster of them in risk, disclosure, or community impact is a signal to slow down, no matter how good the production savings look.

Then, build the model.

Once you’ve done the worksheet, a simple model has four parts: one-time setup costs, recurring monthly costs, the hidden costs from your worksheet (rework hours, legal review, monitoring, crisis reserve), and the performance side (conversions, engagement, or sales per dollar spent). Run it against a human-creator pilot of similar scope, and revisit it after a quarter, not a week.

The Bottom Line

AI influencers can lower the cost of making content. Whether they lower the cost of the program depends on your category, your audience, your compliance exposure, and how honestly you count what’s outside the production line. The brands most likely to come out ahead are the ones that measure the whole picture and start small.

How to Use AI-Assisted Content Workflows Without Losing Authenticity

Audiences forgive AI-assisted content that’s honest and consistent. They don’t forgive content that feels off-brand, evasive, or unreviewed. Build the workflow around human judgment, and aim for consistency over perfection.

Codify your brand voice.

Write the voice down in a form both people and AI tools can use.

  • Voice guide: Tone, vocabulary, phrases to use and avoid, and a few on-brand and off-brand examples.
  • Persona sheet (if you use a virtual influencer): Backstory, values, topics they will and won’t discuss, and visual style.
  • Standing prompts: Turn the guide into reusable instructions so every draft starts from the same baseline.

Set clear approvals.

Not every asset needs the same scrutiny. Tier them by risk:

  • Low risk (routine posts, repurposed content): Social lead approves.
  • Medium risk (sponsored content, product claims): Brand and social approve.
  • High risk (health, finance, political or social topics, anything involving a real person’s likeness): Brand, legal, and social all approve.

Name one person who can pull a post immediately.

Standardize disclosure.

Create templates in advance so disclosure is never improvised. Cover three cases: AI-generated persona, AI-assisted content from a human creator, and paid partnerships. Each should state who made it and whether it’s an ad, in plain language. Have legal review the templates once, then reuse them.

Check requirements for each platform and market, since they differ and are changing.

Govern your assets.

Keep one source of truth for approved content.

  • Store approved images, prompts, character references, and disclosure templates in a single library with version history.
  • Log which tool and prompt produced each asset.
  • Record usage rights, especially for any real person’s likeness or voice.
  • Retire outdated assets so they can’t be reused by accident.

A content management system, such as HubSpot Content Hub, can serve as a shared home for assets and approval steps, but the process matters more than the tool.

Run review loops.

  • Before publishing: Check voice, accuracy, cultural fit, and disclosure. Reject anything that looks polished but feels hollow.
  • After publishing: Review comments and sentiment weekly in the early weeks.
  • Monthly: Compare a sample of recent posts against the voice guide to catch drift, and update the guide with what you learn.

Establish who owns what.

Escalate questions on tone to brand, questions on claims or rights to legal, and questions on audience reaction to social. One person should own the overall workflow so nothing falls between teams.

Favor consistency over realism.

Hyper-realistic output isn’t the goal. A persona that stays recognizable, sounds like your brand, and is clearly labeled will earn more trust than one that’s flawlessly lifelike but inconsistent. When in doubt, a human decides.

Common Pitfalls With AI Influencers and How to Avoid Backlash

Most backlash comes from a few repeatable mistakes, but each one is avoidable.

Weak Disclosure

The problem: Audiences feel tricked when they discover a persona is AI after the fact, and regulators and platforms increasingly expect clear labeling.

How to avoid it: Say it upfront. Put the AI label in the bio and on sponsored posts, and use plain language rather than burying it in hashtags.

Uncanny Visuals

The problem: Almost-human faces, odd hands, and inconsistent features break trust fast and invite mockery.

How to avoid it: Choose a stylization you can execute well and keep it consistent. A clearly stylized character often lands better than a flawed attempt at photorealism. Have a human review every image before it goes live.

Values Misalignment

The problem: A persona that comments on social issues or endorses products it can’t plausibly use will seem opportunistic, because a company is writing every word.

How to avoid it: Define what the persona will and won’t talk about. Skip causes you aren’t prepared to support with real action, and avoid testimonials that depend on personal experience.

Poor Representation

The problem: Using AI to depict diverse identities without involving those communities can read as tokenism, and generative models can reproduce stereotypes.

How to avoid it: Involve people from the communities being portrayed in development and review. Use AI personas alongside human creators rather than as a replacement for them.

Over-Automation

The problem: Fully automated posting and replies produce tone-deaf responses, repeated phrasing, and errors nobody catches in time.

How to avoid it: Keep a human in the approval loop for anything public, especially replies, sensitive topics, and sponsored content. Automate drafting and scheduling, not judgment.

Unclear Ownership

The problem: If it’s unclear who owns the persona, the underlying model outputs, or any real person’s likeness or voice involved, disputes can surface at the worst moment.

How to avoid it: Document ownership and usage rights in contracts from the start, including agency and vendor agreements. Record which tools and training materials were used.

Mitigation Checklist

Disclosure

  • AI label appears in the bio and on every relevant post
  • Sponsored content is marked as an ad
  • Disclosure wording is approved by legal and checked for each platform and market.

Visual Authenticity

  • Style is consistent and deliberate, not a half-realistic compromise
  • A human has checked every asset for glitches and artifacts
  • A reference sheet defines the persona’s look

Voice Consistency

  • A written voice guide and persona sheet exist
  • Off-limits topics are defined
  • Posts are sampled monthly against the guide

Cultural Review

  • Content is reviewed by people familiar with the target market
  • Imagery and language are checked for stereotypes
  • Community members are consulted where the persona represents them

Consent

  • Written consent covers any real person’s likeness or voice
  • Contracts specify permitted uses, duration, and compensation
  • Rights to the persona and its assets are documented

Privacy

  • Follower data and DMs are handled under your privacy policy
  • No personal data is entered into AI tools without approval
  • Data practices comply with the rules in each market you serve

Crisis Response

  • One person has authority to pause or remove content immediately
  • A holding statement is drafted in advance
  • Roles for brand, legal, and social are assigned
  • A plan exists for retiring or pausing the persona if trust breaks down

What’s Next for AI Influencers

I can absolutely see both virtual and AI influencers becoming more common as businesses further integrate AI into their digital marketing strategy, but three shifts are worth planning around: more interactivity, more personalization, and tighter regulation. The regulatory evidence is much stronger than the evidence on the other two, so plan accordingly.

Near-term Shifts

Interactivity: expect more, with thin evidence so far. Industry commentary points to AI influencers paired with chatbots to offer 24/7 personalized engagement. Marketers also describe tracking conversation depth and return engagement as AI-driven interactions grow. Most of this is vendor and agency commentary rather than measured results, so treat it as direction, rather than proof. One practical point is firm, though: if a persona chats with people, EU rules now require that they be told they’re interacting with AI (see below).

Personalization: promised, not yet proven. Brands can use AI personas to give customers more personalized attention without expanding costly support teams. I found no independent data showing this works better than human-led engagement, so test it before building a strategy on it.

Regulation: the clearest shift. Governments are starting to set rules for AI-generated content in advertising, particularly around disclosure. For example, the EU’s AI Act includes transparency requirements for AI-generated content and for AI systems that interact with people.

In the US, New York has passed a law requiring disclosure of AI-generated “synthetic performers” in ads, and the FTC has indicated that its endorsement guidance applies to virtual endorsers as well as human ones. Other jurisdictions are considering similar measures.

Now, I’m not a lawyer and this isn’t legal advice, but I can tell you these rules differ by region and platform, and they change frequently. So, before running a campaign with an AI persona, check the current requirements for each market you’re targeting with qualified counsel.

Review quarterly.

Rules, platforms, and tools are changing quickly enough that annual reviews will lag. Each quarter, review four things:

  • Policies: Check disclosure language and templates against current EU, US federal, and state requirements. Update anything that changed.
  • Voice standards: Compare a sample of recent posts against your voice guide and persona sheet. Fix drift and add new examples of on-brand and off-brand content.
  • Vendors: Reconfirm contracts, usage rights, data handling, and AI-labeling features. Ask what changed in their tools and terms.
  • Pilot results: Review performance against your human-creator benchmark, plus sentiment, rework time, and incidents. Decide to continue, adjust, or stop.

Assign one owner to run the review, with brand, legal, and social each contributing.

Start with a phased pilot.

The timeframes below are suggestions, so adjust them to your campaign cycle.

Phase 1: Limit channels (weeks 1-4). Launch on one or two channels and in a limited set of markets. Start with the markets where disclosure rules are clearest. Write starter creative guardrails before the first post, covering topics to avoid, tone, and approval steps.

Phase 2: Test messages (weeks 4-8). Run small A/B tests comparing AI-persona content with a human-creator benchmark on the same message. Change one variable at a time and measure conversion, not only engagement.

Phase 3: Monitor sentiment (ongoing from launch). Review comments, mentions, and shares weekly. Track whether audience reaction is curious, neutral, or hostile, and flag any confusion about whether the persona is AI. Set a threshold in advance for when you pause.

Phase 4: Codify guardrails and decide (weeks 8-12). Turn what you learned into written rules for visuals, voice, topics, disclosure, and escalation. Then make an explicit scale, hold, or stop decision based on results and sentiment, not momentum.

Expand only after a pilot passes your own criteria. Keeping it small is what lets you change course cheaply.

Frequently Asked Questions About AI Influencers

Do AI influencers need to disclose that they are AI?

In practice, yes, and the rules are tightening. Platforms like Meta, TikTok, and YouTube have their own AI labeling requirements. On the legal side, the EU’s AI Act transparency obligations (Article 50) began to apply from 2 August 2026, and they cover content generated or modified with AI.

In the US, the FTC still expects a clear “this is paid” disclosure on sponsored posts. Some sources also report that the FTC treats presenting an AI-generated persona as a real human without disclosure as potentially deceptive, and that several states are moving toward requiring a synthetic-performer disclosure.

Treat the legal details as a moving target and have counsel review any paid campaign, especially if it reaches EU audiences. Beyond compliance, disclosure is also good brand hygiene: audiences tend to react worse to a reveal than to an upfront label.

How should brands measure AI influencer success?

Use the same core metrics you’d apply to any creator: reach, engagement rate, click-through, conversions, and cost per acquisition. Then add a few that are specific to synthetic personas.

Track audience sentiment (are comments curious, indifferent, or hostile?), brand-lift or recall in the persona’s target segment, and content production efficiency, since one of the main advantages is speed and cost.

Be cautious with headline numbers. Some analyses suggest AI personas can be cheaper than human creators. In contrast, others find human influencers drive higher engagement, so run your own test against a human-creator benchmark rather than trusting industry averages.

When should brands avoid AI influencers?

Avoid them wherever personal credibility is the product. That includes skincare or supplement claims that rely on real results, health and wellness advice, parenting, financial guidance, and any category where followers expect lived experience.

An AI persona can’t truthfully say “I tried this and it worked for me.” They tend to fit better into visual, aspirational, or entertainment-led categories such as fashion, gaming, and lifestyle.

Also steer clear if your audience is hostile to synthetic content, if you can’t commit to clear disclosure, or if your team lacks the capacity to manage the persona consistently over time. Public backlash against AI-generated models in fashion advertising shows the reputational risk is real.

Can AI influencers fit DEI and representation priorities?

They can broaden the range of faces and identities a brand shows, but they come with real trade-offs. A brand can create personas across ages, body types, ethnicities, and abilities without a casting budget.

The risk is that this substitutes for hiring and paying real people from those communities, and it can read as tokenism or “representation without the representatives.” Generative models also carry biases from their training data, so outputs often skew toward narrow beauty standards unless you actively guide them.

A sensible approach is to use AI personas alongside human creators rather than instead of them, involve people from the communities being depicted in the creative process, and review outputs for stereotypes before publishing.

How do we keep brand voice consistent with AI-assisted content?

Start with a documented voice guide: tone, vocabulary, words to avoid, and example posts that are on-brand and off-brand.

Feed that guide into your prompts or tooling as a standing reference, and keep a fixed character sheet for the persona (backstory, values, visual style) so the look and personality don’t drift between posts. Keep a human editor in the approval loop, especially for anything customer-facing or sponsored.

Finally, audit regularly by comparing a sample of recent posts against your guide, since drift tends to creep in gradually.

issues.title: Send the Firefighters to the Fires
issues.summary: Send the firefighters to the fires Enterprise software keeps forgetting a century of good advice about what deserves our attention. House fire in New Zealand neighborhood If a user’s job is to fix what’s broken, the screen should show what’s broken first. Sounds pretty obvious. It’s also not new. issues.author: Francis Wu
issues.content_html:
Send the firefighters to the fires

Enterprise software keeps forgetting a century of good advice about what deserves our attention.

If a user’s job is to fix what’s broken, the screen should show what’s broken first. Sounds pretty obvious. It’s also not new. Frederick Taylor argued for it in 1903. Xerox PARC designed for it in the ’90s. Industrial control rooms wrote it into a standard. Yet enterprise software keeps forgetting this.

Imagine a fire department that dispatches trucks in the order houses were built. Or by date last renovated. Every house gets a visit eventually, and some of them happen to be on fire. That’s pretty absurd, right? Yet I’ve seen the equivalent more times than I care to remember.

A lot of enterprise work boils down to one job: here’s a collection of things, some of them have problems, go fix the problems. Devices out of compliance. Certificates about to expire. Invoices that failed to reconcile. Tickets breaching SLA. The KPI is simply “issues resolved.”

The UI has one job: get the user to the fires and hand them the hose.

So how did we forget? Not because the ideas are hard. Enterprise software just has a habit of designing for everyone except the person actually using it. It’s designing for the buyer in the demo, for the team racing to ship, for the data model that sorts things for free. None of them pay for it. But the user does, every shift, one scroll at a time.

Start with the job

Clayton Christensen had a simple idea: people don’t buy products for their features. They hire them to get a job done. It’s now known as Jobs to Be Done, or JTBD (Christensen et al., 2016; open-access overview). In enterprise triage, the job is about as plain as it gets: fix what’s broken. Finding it should be the product’s job.

So why do so many screens ignore this? Here’s the pattern I see over and over again. A screen lists 400 objects, and twelve need attention. They’re scattered somewhere between page 3 and page 17. It’s Where’s Waldo, except Waldo is a production outage.

Sometimes there’s a status column. Maybe a small red pill, sitting politely in column six of a list sorted by anything but what matters. A human can work out which items are broken. But the interface is acting obtuse and unhelpful.

Consider the following twenty services. I’ll keep coming back to them.

Before: 20 rows, sorted by last updated, every column visible

After: focus on the fires

In the first table, the two critical services sit in rows sixteen and nineteen, and nothing calls them critical. You have to cross-reference Health and Tier yourself: search-index is only Degraded, but it’s Tier 1; mail-relay is Failing, but it’s Tier 3. Meanwhile, Uptime reads 99.92% for payments-gw, which is failing right now. The fires-first view does that math for you. Same data, different job.

Now imagine hearing that table instead. If the headers are marked up properly, a screen reader announces which column you’re in as you move through it (W3C, F91). So a screen reader user can walk down the Health column one cell at a time. That’s still twenty announcements to find six problems, plus a hop to the Tier column for each one. And that’s the best case: many enterprise data grids are built from divs, virtualized, or paginated, and those shortcuts break. Many enterprises don’t hire people who can build accessible tables (Brad Frost calls them front-of-the-front-end developers), but that’s another story. For every column of noise we leave in, someone has to sit through it.

None of this is malicious. Nobody in the review said “hey, let’s bury the critical issues!” The order happened by default, because nobody dug into the JTBD.

The table as a design cop-out

Bad sort order is an outcome of enterprise’s unfortunate love affair with the table as a magic bullet.

The reasoning goes: we don’t know exactly what users want, so let’s give them all the data and let them search, filter, and sort. It sounds like giving users control. In reality, it’s an abdication.

Those are tools for exploring and hunting: browsing to see what’s there, or tracking down something you know exists. But when they become the main interface for task work, the product team has handed its job to the user. Every session, someone sorts by health, scrolls past the Passing rows, cross-checks the tier, and finds payments-gw. Again. Multiply that by every user, every day. That’s triage the product could have done once.

At some point, some smarty-pants will suggest saved filters: let users build and save their own “To-dos” view (health is failing, sorted by tier). Problem solved, right? Not quite! That’s a workaround stacked on the cop-out. Users end up designing the default screen for you because you shipped the wrong one.

Why smart teams keep doing this

To be fair, the people shipping these screens aren’t careless. The forces pushing them toward the table are real, and a lot of them trace back to one thing: in sales-led enterprise software, the buyer isn’t the user.

Jason Lemkin said it bluntly back in 2012: “you, the end user, aren’t the customer for most true enterprise software” (Lemkin, SaaStr). A year later, Martin Eriksson made the same distinction for product managers: “the user and the purchaser are different people with different needs” (Eriksson, Mind the Product).

The buyer’s worst case is a boring demo. The user’s worst case is an outage with their name on it. Guess who the screen gets designed for. Not every lazy sort comes from sales, but a sales-led motion makes lazy sorts easier to ship and harder to undo.

Defaults feel safe. Every record has a created_at and an updated_at, so sorting by them is free. “Severity” doesn’t exist until someone designs it. Meanwhile, stakeholders worry that if healthy items aren’t visible, users will assume they’re missing, and on an RFP checklist, a hidden column might as well not exist. So everything stays on screen.

Nobody talks to each other. Taiichi Ohno’s 5 Whys only works if you can reach the person with the answer. In enterprise, there are too many layers between the people willing to ask and the people able to answer. The only two people reliably talking are the salesperson and the buyer. The salesperson is paid for the close, and asking why five times only gets in the way. Conway’s law predicts the result: systems mirror how their makers communicate. A neutral sort is what that silence looks like on screen.

“Ask ‘why’ five times about every matter.”
— Taiichi Ohno, Toyota

Dashboards are built for the demo. People love dashboards that look like command centers in movies. Walls of screens! Scrolling numbers! Blinking maps! Stephen Few was criticizing exactly this two decades ago, arguing that dashboards should support real-time situation awareness for decision making, not impress the room (Few, 2007; Information Dashboard Design, 2006). Density still wins sales calls, which is the sales motion showing up in the UI. Developers and PMs love it too: every widget and column is a feature someone built.

Tables are cheap and familiar. Every component library ships one, and every IC has built a dozen, so it’s what everyone reaches for first. Inline editing is one prop away, so someone will eventually float turning every cell into a form field. Cheap to build, expensive to use.

Notice what these have in common? Each one optimizes for the team’s comfort or the buyer’s first impression, not the user’s job. The table can never be wrong, because it never commits to anything.

Tables aren’t the enemy

To be clear, I’m not anti-table. Reporting, analysis, and bulk admin are table work. User questions can change week to week, and pinning them down takes the kind of conversations we’ve already seen are rare. Designing for that is tough, so a flexible table is an honest answer.

The line I draw is this: open-ended questions need flexible tables. Known jobs need opinionated ones.

Yet sometimes the best table is the one you don’t build! Think about what people actually do with a big table, and where that work belongs:

  • Slice and pivot? Let them export to (or integrate with) the BI tools they already know.
  • Report up to leadership? Send a scheduled summary, not a screenshot of 400 rows.
  • Reconcile against another system? That’s an integration or an API. Please don’t subject a human being to comparing two systems row by row.
  • Hand evidence to auditors? Send an export instead of buying them a seat, which only gets them a login they’ll barely use, to a worse BI tool.

Excel, Tableau, and Power BI are established, they’re good at analysis, and your users already know them. Your product doesn’t need to compete. Just keep the fires list live and in-app.

So the question isn’t table or no table. It’s what goes in it, and in what order. If you can write the user’s job in one sentence, and “resolve the issues” is that sentence, you know enough to decide: fires first, ranked by severity, healthy rows summarized. A table sorted by last updated with every row at equal weight is just an inventory. It tells users what exists, not what needs their attention.

Management by exception, a century later

One of my core design principles fits in four words: no news is good news. I didn’t invent it. In 1903, Frederick Taylor called it the exception principle: a manager shouldn’t be swamped with every report, only with what deviates from the standard (Taylor, Shop Management).

“The manager should receive only condensed, summarized, and invariably comparative reports.”
— Frederick Winslow Taylor, Shop Management (1903)

Swap “manager” for “user” and it’s a design brief. There’s no reason to emphasize what’s working. Working is the expected state; it’s what the customer pays for. But there’s every reason to emphasize what isn’t, because that’s the only part that needs a human.

Every pixel that gives a healthy object the same weight as a broken one is friction against the KPI. If the metric is issues resolved, a screen that hides issues isn’t neutral. It’s working against the business. And noise isn’t just visual. For a screen reader user, it’s time.

So design as if the user’s job performance depends on your decisions. Because it does! When issues slip through the cracks, nobody blames the designer who picked the default sort. They blame the user who didn’t spot payments-gw in time. They inherit our defaults, our clutter, and our shallow thinking, and they’re the ones who get penalized for it.

That’s the bar. It’s not “does it follow the design system” or “did stakeholders sign off.” It’s “does this make the person using it better at their job?”

What control rooms already know

Ironically, real control rooms don’t look like the movies. In refineries and power plants, operator screens are guided by the ISA-101 standard for industrial interfaces (ISA, 2015), which builds on the high-performance HMI work of Bill Hollifield and colleagues (The High Performance HMI Handbook). Normal operation stays gray and calm. Color is saved for when something’s wrong.

The unsexy truth is that sometimes, that’s all a dashboard needs to be: a prioritized list of what’s on fire and the means to put it out, not a bunch of widgets fighting for the user’s attention. Many may not like it, but that’s what peak performance looks like. Operators knew it long before enterprise SaaS did.

Silence has to be earned

Here’s a fair objection: users need reassurance. If I only show problems, how does anybody know the rest is fine?

Sure, Jakob Nielsen’s first usability heuristic covers it. Systems should keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback within reasonable time (Harley, NN/g). No news is only good news if the silence is trustworthy. An empty screen could mean everything is healthy, or that the sync broke an hour ago. If users can’t tell the difference, they’ll go back to scanning the full table.

So design the quiet state as deliberately as the loud one. Don’t list the healthy items. Summarize them with confidence.

Just a count, a timestamp, and a way to dig deeper. You’re still reporting the good news. You’re just not giving it top billing.

Mark Weiser and John Seely Brown described this balance in 1995 as calm technology: information that sits in the periphery of our attention and moves to the center only when it matters (Weiser and Brown, 1995). In their words, the periphery is “informing without overburdening.” That’s the quiet state. It gives users permission to stop looking. Giving users their time back might be the most underrated thing an enterprise tool can offer.

What fires-first actually looks like

A fires-first approach isn’t just the same table with a different sort. Here’s what separates it, with credit where it’s due.

  • Severity, not just status. A small fire next to a gas station beats a big one in an empty lot. An expired certificate on payments-gw outranks one on a test server, even if both say “Failing.” Health tells you what broke. Tier tells you how much it matters. Severity needs both. Remember that severity doesn’t exist until someone designs it? This is what designing it looks like.
  • Urgency and importance are separate axes. The idea is usually traced to a 1954 Eisenhower speech, and Stephen Covey, A. Roger Merrill, and Rebecca Merrill turned it into four quadrants in First Things First (Hoang, Rework). Plot issues on that matrix, and users can make meaningful choices about what to fix now, schedule, delegate, or snooze.
  • Lead straight into investigation. Fires seldom have a one-click fix. The real job is usually figuring out what went wrong, so each item should invite investigation.
  • Notify, so nobody has to watch. People have better things to do than babysit your app. When payments-gw catches fire, tell the person who can fix it, wherever they already work: email, Slack, Teams. The fires list is where they go to act, not where they sit and wait.
  • Restraint on alerts. Healthcare has studied the opposite failure for years. When clinicians are flooded with warnings, they become desensitized and start overriding the critical ones along with the trivial ones (AHRQ PSNet, “Alert Fatigue”). If 300 of 400 items say “Warning,” your users will do the same. A severity model that can’t say “this doesn’t matter now” isn’t a severity model.
  • Let users snooze. Some fires can’t be fought today: a vendor hasn’t replied, or the fix needs a maintenance window. Snoozing dials down the noise without pretending the issue is solved, and it comes back on schedule.
  • Resolution is visible. When a fire goes out, it leaves the list and the count drops. That feedback loop makes the KPI real to the person doing the work.
  • Everything is still one click away. The full table, healthy rows included, for the audit, the export, and the curious.
“I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important.”
— Dwight D. Eisenhower, quoting J. Roscoe Miller, 1954

The top-right quadrant leads the fires list. Everything else still has a home.

Not sure where to start? Watch how users triage today: what they sort by, what they scroll past, what they export. Your users have already mentally drafted the spec.

Dispatch, not census

A census counts everyone equally. That’s its job. A dispatch center decides who needs help first and sends people there.

Most enterprise dashboards are built like a census: complete, neutral, accurate. And no help to someone whose job is putting out the fires.

Taylor got there in 1903. Weiser and Brown in 1995. Few in 2006. The ISA-101 committee in 2015. Same direction, a century apart. The knowledge isn’t missing. What’s missing is defining what “on fire” means, ranking it, designing the quiet state, and wiring up the notifications.

Do the extra work so your users don’t have to. That’s the job.

Further reading

In order of appearance:

  • Clayton M. Christensen, Taddy Hall, Karen Dillon, and David S. Duncan, “Know Your Customers’ ‘Jobs to Be Done,’” Harvard Business Review, September 2016. Open-access overview: Kelsey Miller, “The Jobs to Be Done Framework Explained & Real-World Examples,” Harvard Business School Online, 2020 (updated 2026)
  • W3C, “F91: Failure of Success Criterion 1.3.1 for not correctly marking up table headers,” WCAG 2.2 Techniques
  • Brad Frost, “Front-of-the-front-end and back-of-the-front-end web development,” bradfrost.com, 2021
  • Jason Lemkin, “Real Ent Software Don’t Need No Stinkin’ UI/UX,” SaaStr, 2012
  • Martin Eriksson, “Consumer vs Enterprise Product Management,” Mind the Product, 2013
  • Melvin E. Conway, “How Do Committees Invent?” Datamation, April 1968. Overview: “Conway’s law,” Wikipedia
  • Taiichi Ohno, Toyota Production System: Beyond Large-Scale Production, Productivity Press, 1988. Overview: “Five whys,” Wikipedia
  • Stephen Few, “Dashboard Design for Real-Time Situation Awareness,” Perceptual Edge, 2007; and Information Dashboard Design, O’Reilly, 2006
  • Frederick Winslow Taylor, Shop Management (1903). Context: Management by exception, Rework
  • International Society of Automation, ANSI/ISA-101.01-2015, Human Machine Interfaces for Process Automation Systems, 2015
  • Bill Hollifield, Dana Oliver, Ian Nimmo, and Eddie Habibi, The High Performance HMI Handbook, PAS, 2008
  • Aurora Harley, “Visibility of System Status (Usability Heuristic #1),” Nielsen Norman Group, 2018
  • Mark Weiser and John Seely Brown, “Designing Calm Technology,” Xerox PARC, 1995
  • Victor Hoang, “The History of the Eisenhower Matrix: From a 1954 Remark to Covey’s Four Quadrants,” Rework, 2026
  • Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, “Alert Fatigue,” PSNet, 2019 (reviewed 2024)

issues.title: If AI works from anywhere, why are we commuting to watch it?
