"Performance belongs on the design system team's priority list, next to accessibilit
issues.content_html:
#​495 — October 30, 2026

Read on the Web

React Status

Putting MUI, Mantine, Ant Design
and React Spectrum Under Load

Den Odell wanted to see how popular design systems cope when you give them real work, so he timed ten of them, including MUI, Mantine, Ant Design and React Spectrum, and profiled the slowest cases. "Performance belongs on the design system team's priority list, next to accessibility," he says. Some highlights:

  • 📊 With the CPU slowed 4x, opening a 249-country dropdown took 84ms in Mantine and 134ms in Ant Design, but over 200ms in MUI and React Spectrum, both of which froze the UI past his 100ms budget.

  • 🔍 React Spectrum's problem was React Aria measuring options one at a time and forcing layout for each. Den filed an issue and a fix is in review.

  • ⚖️ Framework alone didn't decide the results as non-React Ionic was by far the slowest to open (1,266ms) yet was quick at checking 100 checkboxes, while MUI handled them in 70ms compared to Ant Design's 421ms.

  • 🧪 Want to try this on your own components? Den's Playwright tests are available on GitHub.

Agentic Mobile Development Needs Mobile AI Infrastructure — Your agent writes mobile screens fast. Getting them built and into the App Store is where it stalls. Expo is mobile AI infrastructure: native builds, store submits, over-the-air updates and workflows your agent can run. Start free.

Expo sponsor

TanStack Redact: A Smaller React for the Browser — A drop-in replacement for React/React DOM in the browser. Add it to your build config (Start, Vite, Vinext and Next.js are supported) and ship less JavaScript. But it renders synchronously, with no time slicing, so the compatibility guide is handy.

Tanner Linsley

💬 Does Redact pay off? On r/reactjs, commenters pondered who needs it and how it differs from Preact, while one tester found re-renders cost about twice the CPU across two production sites.

IN BRIEF:

  • ⚠️ Next.js has a security release scheduled for November 3, fixing seven medium-severity vulnerabilities. Advisories will be published with the patches.

  • Dan Abramov is fuzzing React's Flight protocol, the format behind Server Components, by streaming random value graphs through the real server and client. It's turned up six stream bugs and three writer bugs so far.

  • TanStack AI 1.0 is stable: a vendor-neutral AI toolkit with React hooks like useChat(), 23 provider adapters and MCP support.

  • 📱 React Native Windows 0.85 completes its move to the New Architecture, and there's more React Native on the desktop with Expo Desktop (an independent project – not by Expo) and Legend Spark for macOS.

React.lazy, Suspense and the Hidden 300ms Startup Delay — A lazy component can suspend on its first render even when its code is already loaded, and React can throttle reveals of suspended content to once every 300ms. Here's how one team traced the delay, and what fixed it.

Matthew Wong (Tab Widgets)

TanStack DB 1.0 RC1, and How 'Oracles' Found Its Bugs — The reactive client data layer is now API stable, but check the migration guide, as mutation handlers, hooks and errors have changed. Kyle explains how agents, checked against simple reference models, found many of the bugs fixed.

Kyle Mathews (TanStack)

🤖 Ship Less JavaScript in Next.js with Your AI Agent – A new skill hunts bundle bloat using Turbopack's module graph. Will Binns-Smith (Vercel)

📄 Porting 287,000 Lines of React to Foldkit in 3 Days – Focuses on how they built a harness to ensure visual and behavioral parity. David Granzin (Maple)

📄 Async React and Progressive Server Actions – How to keep server action forms working before hydration, even with optimistic UI. Jacob Ebey

📊 React Compiler in Next.js 16.4: Babel vs Rust, Benchmarked Waseem Anjum

🛠 Code, Tools & Libraries

Puck 0.24: The Visual Page Editor for React — A drag-and-drop page editor you embed in your own app, using your own components. 0.24 lets you lay out a component's settings panel as you wish, improves drag and drop, and more. GitHub repo.

Fede Bonel Tozzi

react-window 2.5: Virtualized Lists That Scroll with the Page — Brian's long-standing virtualization library adds a scrollElement prop, so lists/grids can scroll along with the page or an ancestor, plus a headless useVirtualizer() for building your own virtualized layouts. Docs and demos.

Brian Vaughn

Vinext 1.4: The Vite-Powered Next.js Reimplementation Gets Faster — A Vite plugin that reimplements the Next.js API so you can deploy anywhere. 1.4 focuses on performance, with a Hacker News clone example now using 43% less server CPU per request vs 1.3, putting it slightly ahead of Next.js in that test.

James Anderson

  • OpenTUI 0.8 – Terminal UI library with React bindings that powers OpenCode. Now repaints only what changed each frame.

  • React Hook Form 7.91 – Lots of useFieldArray and async validation fixes, plus fewer re-renders. v8 is also now at beta 5.

  • React-Toastify 11.2 – Popular toast notification library. Now with theme="auto" to follow the OS color scheme.

  • emoji-picker-react 5.1 – Full-featured customizable emoji picker. Live demo.

🎃 And finally…

Halloween is almost upon us, so how about a round of Graveyard Pinball? It's built with React Three Fiber, with skulls, cauldrons and a skeleton mage. Its creator explains more about how it works here, including how the 3D table actually uses 2D physics.

issues.content_html:
#​494 — October 23, 2026

Read on the Web

React Status

TanStack Start Reaches 1.0

After a year as a release candidate, TanStack Start 1.0 is officially stable. Tanner Linsley explains how it grew out of TanStack Router, and is candid about RSC, which felt like "this box we had to check to be taken seriously as a React framework", and which tanstack.com itself no longer uses. Plus:

  • 📊 The same app in Start and Next.js 16.4, benchmarked – Start handled 2.9x-8.6x more dynamic requests and built ~1.7x faster with type-checking included.

  • 🚚 Moving over? There are official guides for migrating from Next.js and from the RC. Sarthak Mishra moved his site over from Astro (and explains why) and Lovable offers older projects a migration option (here's how one went).

  • 💬 Ryan Carniato called it "a React metaframework with an architecture I can get behind", while in the r/reactjs thread Tanner explained why '1.0' is listed as 1.169 on npm.

TypeScript in the Age of AI — Knowing TypeScript deeply is how you get better code out of AI. Adam Rackis of Spotify shows you how to steer AI toward simpler, correct types and catch the mistakes it slips in.

Master.dev sponsor

IN BRIEF:

  • ⚠️ Last week, Next.js patched two critical RCEs, one rooted in React Server Components, and a public PoC is now out. Update Next.js to 16.4.1 or 15.5.28; for other RSC setups, update the react-server-dom-* packages to 19.3.1 (or 19.2.9/19.1.10/19.0.9).

  • React DevTools for agents now has official docs, covering how it exposes profiling and component data to coding agents through Chrome DevTools MCP.

  • 📱 Expo SDK 58 is out, using the new React Native 0.88, targeting iOS 27 and ready for the iPhone Duo on day one.

  • React Native for Web has active maintainers again and is moving to the React Foundation's GitHub org.

  • TypeScript 7.1 is now in beta, adding a programmatic API and more speed. Type-checking MUI's docs is 1.9x faster and uses half the memory.

Improving Navigation Experience in v0 with Next.js 16.4 — How the Next.js team used Partial Prefetching, intent-based prefetching and the new navigation() API to cut loading skeletons across its v0 AI app builder.

Aurora Scharff (Vercel)

React Only Where Needed: Owner's Next.js to Astro Move — Owner's 10,000+ restaurant sites now run on Astro and Cloudflare Workers, keeping React for interactive islands. Menu-page p75 LCP went from 5.4s to 0.7s.

Selden and Hanford (Owner)

Dead Code Shouldn't Exist — The slides and transcript from a popular talk Dominik has given at several conferences this year on how Sentry removed 28K lines of unused code with Knip.

Dominik Dorfmeister

🤖 Testing AI-Generated Code: Lint the Pattern, Test the Decision – Structural lint rules and shared harnesses beat a test beside every component. Robin Wieruch

📱 Apple Didn't Invent the Foldable. It Might Make You Support One. – Getting a React Native app ready for the iPhone Duo's three compatibility tiers. Sean Barker (Infinite Red)

📄 Loading a 9MB WebAssembly Module Earlier Made Recraft's Editor 17% Faster – Suspending components left the module's download waiting its turn in the React tree. Sergey Patrakeev (Recraft)

🛠 Code, Tools & Libraries

Pixel: Build Graphical Applications in the Terminal — Like Ink, but with "pixel perfect" graphics. It's a React renderer that draws rounded corners, gradients and proper fonts in terminals that support the Kitty graphics protocol, and that can even embed Chromium WebViews to run web apps in a pane(!)

Rob Pruzan (Zenbu Labs)

TanStack Hotkeys Beta: A Type-Safe Library for Keyboard Shortcuts — Hotkeys takes care of the fiddly, cross-platform edge cases of keyboard shortcuts, sequences, and user-recorded hotkeys. The beta adds scopes, so that, say, a dialog's Escape doesn't close the panel behind it. Try the demo on the homepage.

TanStack

React Router 8.5 Hands View Transitions Over to React — Its own view transition APIs are deprecated in favor of React 19.3's <ViewTransition>. Migrating starts with wrapping an <Outlet> and removing the old props and state styling. There's also an unstable 'API-only' mode that serves static HTML but keeps a server for loaders and actions.

Remix Team

env.style: Style Every Environment with Colors or Custom Icons — A utility that wraps your Next.js config or Vite setup to tint the favicon per environment at build time, so you can see at a glance where you are.

Ryan George

Tamagui 3: One React UI Codebase for Web and Native — A styling system and UI kit for sharing one codebase between React web apps and React Native. v3 adds an opt-in (beta) C++ native runtime that applies theme changes without re-rendering, plus React Strict DOM and Tailwind-style syntax.

Nate Wienert

  • Hydrogen 2026.10 – Shopify's commerce toolkit is now a library you can drop into existing Next.js or React Router apps.

  • Morphicons 2.0 – Spring-physics morphing between SVG icons. Now filled icons morph too, not just stroked ones. See it in action on its homepage.

  • Unistyles 3.6 – High-performance React Native styling library. Now with an experimental zero-config Metro integration instead of the Babel plugin.

  • Motion 14.6 – Adds keyboard grab-and-move to Reorder lists, plus stepFrames for deterministic animation testing.

📰 Classifieds

Build and deploy durable AI agents in TypeScript, without managing your own infrastructure. Ship your first agent with Trigger.dev.

Expo is mobile AI infrastructure: Your agents build, test and ship iOS and Android apps, and you approve what goes out. Try it.

🎶 And finally… make a little noise

Fancy making a little music with React? Strudel Flow 2 is an open source React app built with React Flow and shadcn/ui. Connect instruments and effects to generate Strudel code, or load a community patch and start turning knobs.

The source code offers a neat extension point: define an instrument or effect in a small .node.ts file, then supply a React component for a custom interface. As the team says, "coding is a fun thing to do for its own sake." 🤘

issues.content_html:
Claude Code + Obsidian: My family’s AI brain | Scott Farrar

Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts

Brought to you by:

  • WorkOS—Make your app enterprise-ready, with SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and more

  • Jira Product Discovery—Prioritize with insights, build with confidence

Scott Farrar is a math educator and parent who built a shared household brain using Claude Code and Obsidian. In this episode, he shows how the system tracks appliances and warranties, compares insurance quotes, organizes family projects, and keeps household tasks moving through a shared to-do list and wall display. He also explains why persistent files work better for him than long AI chats, and how the same philosophy shapes his approach to using AI without taking the thinking away from students.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. The problem with chat is not intelligence, but memory drift. Scott moved to Claude Code because it stores context in Markdown files he can inspect, correct, and reuse across sessions. His memory is no longer trapped inside an opaque conversation.

  2. Let the AI tell you what context it needs. When Scott asked Claude how to document his home, it suggested photographing every appliance. Those photos became a searchable inventory of model numbers, serial numbers, and warranty details.

  3. Unstructured input is fine when the system handles the organization. Scott gives Claude raw information and lets it maintain the underlying files. A custom linter prevents verbose agents from bloating documents such as his household to-do list.

  4. Better context helps people ask better questions. Claude compares insurance quotes with detailed information about Scott’s home, identifies potential coverage gaps, and prepares specific follow-ups. He no longer has to rely entirely on the agent selling him the policy.

  5. One master list can eliminate a house full of mental clutter. Scott and his wife captured every household task they could think of, then Claude organized them by priority, cost, and supporting information. The system now surfaces overdue work before it becomes another fire.

  6. Multiplayer household systems require practical compromises. Claude recommended GitHub to avoid file conflicts, but that added more complexity than Scott’s wife wanted. They settled on GitHub for shared scripts and Dropbox for everyday files, matching the tools to how they actually work.

  7. A household system becomes more useful when it leaves the laptop. Scott’s wall display shows upcoming trips, open tasks, recent wins, and small daily suggestions. It turns a private collection of files into something the whole family can see and use.

  8. Scott rebuilt his father’s file cabinet as an AI system. His dad saved every receipt and warranty and could explain repairs from decades ago. Claude now gives Scott that same dependable household memory, only searchable through conversation.

  9. AI should help children think, not think for them. Scott prefers tutors that ask students to explain their reasoning and work through productive struggle. He also believes some children may share unfinished ideas more comfortably with AI than with another person.

  10. Infinite patience is not always good teaching. Scott wants AI to act as a “warm demander” that encourages students without doing the work for them. When his own agent goes off track, he starts fresh or investigates its reasoning before incorrect information reaches his memory files.

How I fight token fraud as a solo founder

Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts

Brought to you by:

  • WorkOS—Make your app enterprise-ready, with SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and more

  • Auros—The human network behind AI

In this solo episode, Claire explains how token fraud cost ChatPRD tens of thousands of dollars and consumed much of her engineering time. She walks through six forms of abuse, including farmed free trials, resold promo codes, card testing, product relays, and a custom MCP running as a 24/7 compute worker. She also shares the business and technical defenses she built, how Jev classifies suspicious activity in real time, and why she ultimately eliminated free trials.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. Token fraud is a business risk most AI founders underestimate until the bill arrives. Unlike traditional SaaS abuse, every fraudulent model call costs real money. It cost Claire tens of thousands of dollars despite ChatPRD being SOC 2 compliant, regularly penetration-tested, and run by an experienced technical founder.

  2. Free trials may no longer work for AI products. Fraudsters automated account creation and used ChatPRD’s most expensive models for unrelated work. Claire ultimately removed free trials, sacrificing a valuable source of product-led growth and enterprise leads after credit-card gates and paid trials also failed.

  3. Promo codes have become a serious attack vector. Codes intended for partners were stolen, resold, and used to power other AI businesses. After discovering that roughly half of her promo codes had reached resellers, Claire stopped issuing them entirely.

  4. MCP access creates a new category of abuse. One fraudster turned ChatPRD’s custom MCP support into a compute worker that ran around the clock. Claire responded by restricting approved hosts and blocking free tunnels and infrastructure that did not appear connected to legitimate companies.

  5. Cheap decision models can classify fraud in real time. When a session crosses ChatPRD’s abuse threshold, a zero-data-retention Jev loop categorizes the activity. Confirmed fraud results in either a ban or a silent downgrade to a less expensive model.

  6. AI support agents need firm boundaries around fraud. After mass bans, ChatPRD received both clumsy appeals and polished messages written by AI. Claire equipped her support agent with fraud tools and explicit rules preventing it from restoring accounts or distributing promo codes.

  7. Blunt defenses are sometimes the most effective. Blocking traffic from certain countries using Vercel Firewall significantly reduced abuse and forced Claire to reconsider ChatPRD’s international strategy. Her new default is simple: trust must be earned rather than assumed.

  8. Token fraud is affecting companies of every size. Claire found the same people abusing ChatPRD through rotating proxies across several major AI products. She has started discussing the problem publicly and filed FBI cybercrime reports with help from Codex.

  9. If a company sells AI, it is ultimately selling compute. Founders should track dollars instead of requests, monitor model spending continuously, close every free entry point, and verify the client rather than only the account. Claire also learned that fraud disappears quickly when expensive models are no longer available to steal.

↳ Detect Automated Abuse on AI Routes with Vercel BotID: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/detect-automated-abuse-ai-routes-botid

I was a Claude hater. Fable 5.2 changed my mind.

Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts

In this solo episode, Claire tests Claude Fable 5.2 to see whether Anthropic has finally built a model she enjoys using. She turns a tweet into an animated marketing video, creates assembly instructions from photos of unboxed furniture, reworks a complex ChatPRD pipeline, and builds a fully functional 3D typewriter. She also explains where Fable fits alongside Opus 5.5, why its creative work impressed her, and why she still would not trust it to design a website on its own.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. Fable 5.2 turned Claire from a Claude skeptic back into a fan. She found the original Fable difficult to understand and unpleasant to use, with Opus 5 offering little improvement. Fable 5.2 feels fast, capable, creative, and dramatically easier to work with.

  2. Fable 5.2 complements Opus 5.5 rather than replacing it. Opus remains the better default for most coding and knowledge work. Fable is the model Claire would choose for greater complexity, broader scope, or tasks that demand more creativity.

  3. Its speed changes how the model feels to use. Many benchmark tasks finished in under a minute, and even a complex animation took only 16 minutes. Fable also communicates sparingly during autonomous work, surfacing only the moments that require input.

  4. Fable 5.2 made AI video feel animated instead of assembled. From one tweet and the CXO.dev brand guidelines, it created a narrated story featuring custom invader-bot sprites that walk, jump, and cheer. No other model Claire tested produced anything comparable, so the task is becoming a permanent benchmark.

  5. Its spatial reasoning solved a real-world problem every other model failed to. Claire gave Fable low-resolution photos of an unassembled piece of furniture with no instructions. It identified the parts, created a diagram, and produced the correct assembly sequence, which her household successfully followed.

  6. Fable 5.2 is unexpectedly funny. It designed a bug-fighting game around real engineering tradeoffs, then made a trailer in which finance sees the token bill and downgrades the team to a cheaper model. The humor felt intentional enough to make Claire genuinely laugh.

  7. It also holds up on serious engineering work. Fable created a sensible migration plan for ChatPRD’s messy product-intelligence pipeline and aligned closely with Claire’s own roadmap. It worked autonomously and paused at appropriate moments, though the migration is still underway.

  8. Fable needs strong direction for visual design. It follows an existing brand system well, but its unguided web and storybook designs were unattractive. Claire expects to pair it with Opus 5.5 for frontend work and use a separate image model when original visuals are needed.

  9. The 3D typewriter was Claire’s “AGI moment.” Fable built a working keyboard in one shot, then added white-out, music, weather, timers, writing prompts, and multiple immersive settings. It turned an idea Claire never imagined building into a tool she wants to use every day.

  10. Fable 5.2 is available now, with an even faster mode coming. It is launching across the Claude API, cloud platforms, Claude apps, and Claude Code. Claire plans to compare it with the other new models in a full How I AI benchmark.

issues.title: Obituaries
issues.summary: The demise of Jensen Huang was the end of a great many things, including Nvidia's long-term prospects, the AI bubble, and the exceptional way in which the U.S. viewed itself in the world.
issues.author: Ben Thompson
issues.content_html:
Listen to this post:

Dearly beloved, we are gathered here today to get through this thing called life.
― Prince

Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, 1993–2026

Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday, November 12, 2026. He had been CEO of the company ever since he founded it on April 5, 1993. Nvidia started out as a graphics card company; Huang’s exit — nominally because of affairs with a buyer who may or may not have been a Chinese spy, as well as at least two company employees — was ultimately because Nvidia was, by the powers that be, considered a defense contractor, and Huang never adjusted.

In this, Huang was the ultimate victim of his own success. Nvidia’s first graphics cards simply translated triangles into pixels. The 2001 GeForce 3 introduced a programmable pixel shader, which meant a video card’s functionality was no longer pre-defined. The killer move, however — which almost killed the company — was the 2006 introduction of CUDA, which was an API for programming those shaders. For much of the next 16 years Huang sold the gospel of CUDA, convinced it was the platform for a future of accelerated computing; then, in 2022, came ChatGPT.

ChatGPT made clear what GPUs were most useful for: large language models, and Nvidia made the best GPUs. More than that, Huang had realized that the future of accelerated computing was not just chips, but rather systems; that drove the purchase of Mellanox in 2019, which provided the technology for Nvidia to scale out from chips, setting it down the road to being the best option for the sort of large scale training that made large language models possible. For this Nvidia charged very high prices, with margins exceeding 70%, because they could: they had the platform, the technology, and, over the past few years as others sought to make their own chips, the supply chain.

Huang’s impact on the Asian supply chain in particular cannot be overstated. Byrne Hobart, in his book Boom: Bubbles and the End of Stagnation, notes that one of the benefits of bubbles is that they provide a coordination function, as the fear of missing out incentivizes multiple entities with interlocking dependencies to all commit to building at the same time; Huang was, in many respects, a one-person coordination function. Huang gave multiple keynotes a year, which he explained as how he communicated with the ecosystem broadly, and was famous for eating and drinking his way across Asia in particular, convincing reluctant suppliers that the AI boom was real, and locking up the lion’s share of their output for Nvidia and its stunning commitment to a yearly release cycle.

Huang, who had toiled for decades in relative obscurity, known primarily to gamers, and only barely to the tech industry, became a rock star, swarmed wherever he went, always in his black leather jacket. He also, to his ultimate detriment, became a political figure. Nvidia had long had no presence in either Washington D.C. or Beijing, and was blindsided by the Biden administration’s imposition of chip controls in 2022. Nvidia’s immediate reaction to those initial controls, which restricted exports based on interconnect speed, was to immediately release the A800 in China, which was an A100 with a third of its interconnects disabled. That set the tone for the conflict that I believe was the true cause of Huang’s downfall: Huang strenuously disagreed with the various iterations of the chip ban, and Nvidia only bothered to do the bare minimum to abide by the letter of the law, never the spirit.

That approach, in all likelihood, extended to Nvidia’s oversight (or lack thereof) of Singaporean entities that were alleged to be fronts for chips for China. Some of these were legal: Chinese companies are allowed to access cloud computing facilities outside of China that house leading edge Nvidia chips, although chip control advocates are seeking to close that loophole; some were not legal, in that the chips were ultimately ferried to China. Megaspeed, whose executive, Alice Huang, was the first person Huang was alleged to have an affair with, was officially in the former business, and alleged to actually be in the latter. There are whispers that Megaspeed’s ultimate customer was not, or not just, Alibaba, but also the Chinese military. These are whispers, to be clear; it was the affairs that were enough, at least publicly, to lead to Huang’s resignation.

Nvidia, Most Valuable Company in the World, 2024–2026

Nvidia’s durability — at least that of their margins — was already an open question. Start with CUDA: when the market was software written for GPUs, a platform — including not just an API but a huge set of libraries targeting every conceivable market for accelerated computing — was a nearly impenetrable moat. That is why LLMs like GPT were written using CUDA.

LLMs, though, both brought Nvidia its incredible success, and also seeded its greatest risks. The first is that the vast majority of developer energy moved up the stack, using the LLM’s API as a platform; for most companies, CUDA didn’t matter. The second is that Anthropic, which found funding from Amazon and Google, originally also-rans to the Microsoft-OpenAI partnership, had to learn how to use Trainium chips from Amazon and TPUs from Google; this was difficult, but ultimately meant that the leading LLM did not have any Nvidia dependency at all (Anthropic runs on Nvidia chips, because they learned how to run on anything). The third is the most devastating: LLMs are so effective at writing software that any software-based moat will inevitably dry up.

Nvidia’s second moat, its networking and systems approach, is more durable, although challenged by Google (and by extension, Anthropic) in particular. Nvidia’s systems approach is also the easy answer for enterprises and governments seeking to own their own hardware, and neoclouds seeking to build data centers that are independent of the hyperscalers. The latter market rents chips to both hyperscalers and frontier labs, as well as individual companies, but is challenged as obvious sources of power and political permission disappear. They also need money to afford Nvidia’s systems, which has increasingly come from Nvidia itself.

Nvidia’s third moat is its mastery of the supply chain, and this is the moat that suddenly looks much more tenuous. Huang has bragged about the fact that he has never signed a contract with TSMC over their three decades of partnership; it’s a relationship built on a handshake and mutual trust with Huang specifically. This is, per the point above, a very Asian way of doing business, and Huang was the master of that. It’s questionable whether or not that trust and willingness to commit will persist when the handshake is no longer there.

Nvidia’s most important moat, however, was the degree to which it was not a normal company. Huang organized Nvidia as an exoskeleton around one man: himself. There is very little management at Nvidia — Huang famously has 60 direct reports — for the same reason that there was no succession plan: Nvidia could move so quickly and so aggressively because the company still behaved as if it were a startup. Indeed, lots of established companies — including those still led by founders — claim to still be a startup, but only one, Nvidia, really was organized that way. That paid off with all of those successful bets; it also created an environment where there were no checks on Huang. And, now that he is gone, the exoskeleton is much more poised to collapse than you might expect.

The AI Bubble, 2025–2027?

The first part of the AI buildout was funded by free cash flow, particularly from the hyperscalers. Then, during the second half of last year, nearly everyone started turning to debt. Now — starting with Google this past summer — the primary funding mechanism is equity. In the long run, this should come full circle, and future build-outs will once again be funded by free cash flow, generated from the infrastructure that is being built now.

The problem for Nvidia is that the companies most able to navigate this progression are the hyperscalers, which have the resources to challenge Nvidia’s hold on the chip market. To that end, Nvidia has been very eager to ensure that it is selling not only to the hyperscalers, but to other would-be competitors, like the neoclouds; there will likely, at some point, be serious questions raised about exactly how Nvidia went about allocating compute in pursuit of this goal.

The neoclouds, however, are at a meaningful disadvantage when it comes to funding. First, their debt is significantly more expensive, given that their only business is renting GPUs (as opposed to, say, running the most valuable advertising businesses in the world, or the world’s largest e-commerce platform, or dominating enterprise software). Second, their equity is increasingly worthless, given the significant risks attached to that credit. If a neocloud can’t pay, it’s the equity holders that get wiped out first.

This led to what I termed Nvidia’s Risky Business: Nvidia increasingly used its cash flow and credit rating to backstop and fund the companies who were buying its chips. Bears called this circular financing; bulls called it a necessary bridge to a future where AI revenue paid down these companies’ debt and drove massive upside. What is undoubtedly true is that this was the sort of risky business that is uniquely possible for a multi-trillion dollar company that is completely controlled by one man, who has made an entire career of pushing the limits and making risky bets — and seeing them pay off.

It’s also a series of bets that are unlikely to continue. The neoclouds should be very nervous about losing their patron, along with their creditors and equity holders. The other problem is that the revenue necessary to make all of this build-out work is something on the order of a trillion dollars industry-wide, and it needs to materialize sooner rather than later; if it falls short, it’s the hyperscalers who will prioritize their own compute first, and they will likely be seen as a safe haven for everyone committing to spending. In that world, Nvidia’s neocloud hedge — absent Huang’s willingness to shore the ecosystem up — is liable to turn into a millstone, with their assets flooding the market even as the supply chain ramp-up brings ever more supply to market.

AI as Normal Technology and the U.S. Semiconductor Industry, 1947~2047

Perhaps because he had been preaching the gospel of accelerated computing for so long, Huang was the leading figure pushing back against the doomer narrative surrounding AI. Yes, AI was a massive business opportunity, but it was still normal technology; the safety issues presented were engineering challenges to be solved. What required consideration was not just the next five years, but the next fifty. It’s a view that I am, in full disclosure, generally aligned with.

Many others are not. On one hand there are the aforementioned doomers, certain that fast takeoff is imminent — or has already started — as AI increasingly builds better AI in a recursive loop. The end state is an AI that is massively more capable than humans, and uncontrollable by them; the only hope is to ensure that AI is aligned with humanity, by which adherents to this viewpoint mean aligned with them and their view of the world. This contingent is, broadly speaking, represented by Anthropic. And, in this view, actively working to enable and accelerate uncontrollable open weights models is a threat to humanity.

On the other hand there are the China hawks, who view AI as a national security issue, and the key to U.S. military dominance in a world where China owns the means of production of most militarily relevant hardware. In this world giving China access to chips is effectively treason against the United States.

For both of these groups, Huang was public enemy number one, because of his determination to do what was best for Nvidia’s business, which was to sell chips to China. This made sense for Nvidia for multiple reasons:

  • The first and most obvious reason is that it is good for a company to be able to sell to everyone, including the second largest market in the world (China has traditionally made up about a quarter of Nvidia’s sales, long before AI was even a thing).
  • The second is that China is a large enough market, with sufficiently motivated and capable developers, that it can actually create a meaningful CUDA alternative; furthermore, such an alternative would, in the long run, not be constrained to China, but rather compete with Nvidia all over the world.
  • The third is that China’s AI ecosystem, unconstrained as it is by such niceties as terms of service, distills frontier lab models and releases them as open weights models; those models, meanwhile, are tuned to run on Nvidia chips. These models give Nvidia leverage versus the frontier labs all over the world, including in the West.
  • The fourth is that China is uniquely positioned to create a fundamentally different approach to systems design using optical interconnects to scale out training clusters. This is much more inefficient in terms of power usage than Nvidia’s more elegant designs, but China is also much more capable of manufacturing excess amounts of power to make it work.
  • The fifth is that, in the very long run, China can create an entire alternative supply chain for semiconductors broadly, rendering Nvidia’s mastery of the Western-aligned supply chain much less important.

This last point is worth dwelling on. The chief objection that China hawks in particular make to the idea that it is a good idea to sell China chips in order to prevent them from surpassing the U.S. is that China is already heavily invested in building their own ecosystem. This is certainly true, but I think it underplays the complexity of chips and what is necessary to actually compete with the West.

Specifically, the Chinese government can only control the supply side, by spending money and making top-down imperatives; building an ecosystem, however, whether that be for AI specifically, or semiconductors broadly, requires demand as well. Progress in models and systems and chips depends on a feedback loop between the user and the developer, or the customer and the manufacturer. The demand side, however, is much more short-term oriented than the Chinese government might prefer. The model companies’ concern is the other model companies: that means if they are distilling, we must distill too. If they are using Nvidia chips, then we must too. This matters up and down the stack, just as it has always mattered in technology, which really is different in this regard from almost every other industry.

A useful analogy is to consider the Internet. Why is it that country after country can profess a desire to have an indigenous alternative to the American tech giants, yet miserably fail in every attempt to generate it? It’s because the tech giants are only a click away! In this regard, China’s Great Firewall was one of the most brilliant geostrategic moves ever: by virtue of cutting off access to the American tech companies, China created the demand that pulled China’s own tech giants into existence. You need demand, not just desire.

This is why China itself is currently banning the import of Nvidia’s two-generations-behind H20 chips, after the Trump administration foolishly banned their import, only to reverse themselves while bragging about the reason to do so — i.e. keep China addicted to Nvidia. China is replaying the Great Firewall playbook: force its internal demand to use its much worse alternatives, because that is the only way those alternatives become better. And, in the long run, those alternatives, and the entire ecosystem that supports them, will flood the world.

Huang was, to be perfectly clear, talking his book when it came to his insistence on selling chips to China, or, in the case of the current controversy, allegedly turning a blind eye towards nominally legal buyers who were intent on violating the chip ban; that doesn’t mean, however, that he was wrong about the long-term effects, at least if AI is a normal technology (and I haven’t gotten to the risks this imposes on the Taiwan Strait). What is clear now, however, is that the doomers and the hawks have won: AI, at least in terms of policy, will be treated as anything but normal, and in the fullness of time, it is the U.S. chip ecosystem that will pay the ultimate price.

Tech Company Independence, 1968–2026

The birth date for the last obituary was the invention of the transistor; the birth date for this one is the founding of Intel. Robert Noyce and co-founders had spent the last decade at Fairchild Semiconductor, but were constrained by their parent company’s fundamental conservatism and chafed at their lack of upside. Arthur Rock effectively created the venture capital industry in Silicon Valley through his financing of Intel; Noyce created the concept of the commercial-market-led technology company that made it up in volume. At that time the largest single purchaser of chips was the U.S. government; Noyce realized that the fastest way to progress was to make chips for everyone, including the government, and on his terms, not theirs.

From that point on, tech as an industry operated with the assumption that the world was its customer, and that their own executives defined the route to progress. Government was free to buy their products, but not to define them, and if they wanted the best products, then they best not restrict who they could sell them to either. That’s how important volume was, and, over time, it became clear how powerful and essential ecosystems were.

Other industries operate differently; I thought this article in the Financial Times was striking, and not just because of the headline: Bessent says Nvidia needs ‘shake-up’ with external CEO:

Bessent said that it is important “to examine whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions” and whether its top executives knew they were being skirted. “Was it a low-level fail? Was it in the middle, or was it up in the C-suite? And who knew? These shell companies were obvious, they were being investigated, and did Nvidia use them as a workaround to sell chips to the Chinese?” he said. “Were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?” The Treasury secretary added that Nvidia needs to provide answers within a matter of days: “I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel”. He added that “we will see if Nvidia intentionally ignored the warning signs of these shell companies, many of them in Singapore”.

Bessent has pointed the spotlight on Howard Lutnick’s commerce department for failing to ban exports of Nvidia’s chips to Megaspeed, the Singaporean company linked to the alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Huang. US authorities have been investigating whether Megaspeed, which builds AI data centres in Asia, has been involved in smuggling high-end Nvidia chips, which are powering the AI boom, into China. Bessent has blamed the commerce department more than once this week for failing to ban exports of Nvidia’s chips to Megaspeed. Commerce delayed efforts to add Megaspeed to Washington’s blacklist of companies the US considers a risk to national security. “Many other departments were pushing for this, and commerce had the pen,” Bessent repeated on Sunday. “We have all the rules we need. We just need them enforced.”

Lutnick is under mounting pressure from within the administration and from Congress, which has demanded that he explain how he allowed chips to be exported to a company linked to an alleged Chinese spy. US lawmakers are also accelerating efforts to crack down on advanced AI chips reaching China. If Nvidia “were a bank and they hadn’t complied like this, the [Treasury’s Office of the Comptroller of the Currency] would be in there right now, and a lot of the executives would be removed”, Bessent said.

Scott Bessent is the Treasury Secretary, which is to say that he operates an apparatus that is arguably just as, if not more, powerful than the U.S. military. Treasury controls the flow of money around the world, and its soldiers are the banks; if Treasury has sanctioned an entity, then it is up to banks to ensure those sanctions are enforced. They need to know their customers, and they need to analyze every dollar flowing through their systems; if they do not, they are breaking the law. Ignorance is not a defense.

Ignorance, on the other hand, has been tech’s defense basically forever. Yes, there are bad people in the world, which means that if the whole world is using your products, they will be used to do bad things. That was considered an acceptable trade-off, however, because most people are good and the benefits that come from scale — and an avoidance of the friction that comes from trying to track the activities of billions of people — were worth the risk.

This was certainly what Huang believed, and, to his detriment, he aggressively belittled anyone who dared disagree (the extent to which Huang is despised in Washington D.C., as evidenced by the giddiness and bloodlust online last week, is extraordinary). In Huang’s view, as long as the Commerce Department said that it was ok to sell to Megaspeed, then it was ok to sell to Megaspeed — and to sleep with one of its executives.

Bessent views the matter entirely differently: he thinks that Nvidia should operate like a bank. It’s not just their job to abide by the letter of the law, but the spirit of it. It’s not the government’s job to enforce the chip ban, but the company’s. An attestation from a Singaporean customer that chips aren’t going to China isn’t worth anything; actually putting boots on the ground and ensuring compliance is the only way Nvidia cannot be in violation of the U.S. government’s dictates.

Again, for tech, this is extraordinary, even if it is normal in banking. Extraordinary enough, in fact, that Huang is being labeled by many — not just in Washington, but also in the finance world — as a traitor. Huang, in my estimation, is just a businessman who cares about nothing else other than Nvidia; that worked out great when he made GPUs for gaming that no one in government cared about or understood. That’s just a normal technology; when AI was deemed to be anything but normal, however, business as usual wasn’t just over: it was a crime, and it cost Huang his job — and maybe more.

It’s worth pointing out that while this episode was shocking, I should not, in retrospect, have been surprised. Earlier this year, when Anthropic faced off against the U.S. government, I wrote in Anthropic and Alignment:

At the same time, what is the standard by which it should be decided what is allowed and not allowed if not laws, which are passed by an elected Congress? Anthropic’s position is that Amodei — who I am using as a stand-in for Anthropic’s management and its board — ought to decide what its models are used for, despite the fact that Amodei is not elected and not accountable to the public.

And, on the second point, who decides when and in what way American military capabilities are used? That is the responsibility of the Department of War, which ultimately answers to the President, who also is elected. Once again, however, Anthropic’s position is that an unaccountable Amodei can unilaterally restrict what its models are used for.

My point in that Article was that if AI is as exceptional as claimed, then the government will demand a say in how it is used, whether or not private company executives agree; moreover, that was a good thing, or at least a least-bad thing. The same analysis applies to Nvidia and Huang: Huang may have fundamentally disagreed with the chip ban, but at the end of the day, it was his duty to accept that it was the law of the land. To the extent he did not do so is ultimately his responsibility.

American Exceptionalism, 1776–2026

Perhaps the most tragic aspect of the Huang affair is the extent to which he was the personification of The American Dream. Huang was sent to America as a nine year old who didn’t speak a lick of English, and somehow ended up at a boarding school in rural Kentucky for misbehaving youth, where he would trade help on homework for protection from bullies. From there he went to a state school in Oregon, became an engineer, before famously ending up at a Denny’s diner where he and his co-founders decided to start Nvidia. Then, over the following 33 years, he took risk after risk, created innovation after innovation, until he became a hero not just in the United States, but across the world.

And then, you might say, he flew too close to the sun. Certainly he did so in his private life: it’s not just the affairs, which may be par for the course for rich and powerful men; rather, it’s notable just how reckless the affairs were. The ones that were revealed last week were with a customer and potential Chinese spy, and two of his own employees; both are fireable offenses. Meanwhile, the way in which Huang treated his opponents — including actively seeking to get people fired who he felt stood in the way of getting his way — bore the marks of a man who has constructed a life, and a company, where no one can or will stand up to him. That is a recipe for disaster, and here we are.

At the same time, it really does bum me out that what ultimately doomed Huang was a set of rules that really are a big departure from the status quo — and, in my opinion, misguided. Huang’s actions — or lack of actions, in terms of enforcing compliance with the chip ban — are treated as if they are an obvious crime, when in fact this is a dramatic shift in expectations from a short time ago (although there is certainly a callback to previous controversies around selling advanced computing to adversaries). Huang should have adjusted and accepted the new reality, make no mistake; I’m sympathetic to the fact he couldn’t, and recognize the failure in not having structures in place that could have warned him about the dangerous road he was embarking on, even as I realize Huang’s willingness to navigate dangerous roads is precisely why he was an American success story.

Beyond Huang, however, there is the question of how we compete with China, and I am disappointed, although not surprised, that we are pursuing the route of bans and forced compliance, instead of innovation and openness. Make no mistake, I am no China dove, and I have been very early to the argument that we erred greatly in willingly exporting entire industries to the communist state. That, however, makes it even more imperative that we sprint in the opposite direction of China, towards more freedom in a bet on inventing new industries, not more control and a focus on gatekeeping what we have. I get the logic, particularly in the case of AI, which is extraordinary; I lament the implications of what it says about our belief in ourselves and our ability to stay ahead.

Presented by

As AI models improve, you might expect the market will consolidate around a handful of providers. But user data tells a different story.

Among OpenRouter customers spending at least $100 a month, the median number of AI model families in use has doubled over the past year, from three to six.

Even as AI models become more capable, businesses are using more models, not fewer. This makes sense when you consider that intelligence isn’t one-dimensional. A model that’s exceptional at writing code may not be the fastest at answering customer questions, or the most economical at processing millions of documents.

The question is shifting from “which AI model should we build on?” to “which model should handle each task?” The answer, increasingly, is ‘it depends.’ Which is great for flexibility, less great for simplicity.

OpenRouter, which recently joined Stripe, allows businesses to access and govern hundreds of models with the flexibility to optimize for cost, performance, and reliability as the market evolves.

issues.title: 🔮 What Anthropic is really listing
issues.summary: Tithes, not tokens
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
Azeem’s sketchbook is an experimental format we’re trialing for paying members, where we share raw research notes, early frameworks, and unfinished ideas. They are the earliest indication of what I’m thinking through.

It’s Anthropic’s big week. It will become the first real AI company in the West to list on a public market.

Anthropic has an extraordinary market opportunity. The battle hangs on the sustainability of its business model – whether falling token costs or competition from open-weight models won’t simply erode its margins. These forces, no doubt, exist. The bear case claims the company is merely a peddler of progressively devalued tokens. This misses the point.

Anthropic is building an ever-improving system that produces machine intelligence. That machine intelligence is valuable because of the nature of modern economies. Most value in our economies now comes from intangibles, scientific knowledge, patents, software, brand, and data. If Anthropic’s machine intelligence can create intangibles like these – breakthrough science, information, or software – then it should be able to create extraordinary value.

Over the past fifty years, value in the S&P 500 has shifted from tangibles, things you can count in warehouses or can stub your toe on. Most value now resides in that ethereal flim-flam of the intangible: brand, customer lists, patents, and software.

Put another way, Anthropic’s machine intelligence lets it compete for 92% of the value of the S&P 500 before it needs to deploy a single robot.

That is the big macro-level survey that paints the opportunity. But I’ve been digging deeper. My conclusion is that AI companies in general, and Anthropic, are in a unique position. Look at the chart below. Each time Anthropic announced a new product feature that encroached on a given sector, the stock prices of firms in that sector responded as you’d expect.

AI companies might be able to extract a permanent tithe on the economy. Anthropic, as the leading player, is best positioned to do that.

The following are my sketches. They’ll give you a sense of the direction that I think merits further exploration.

Capturing the intangible

Anthropic has three approaches to capturing value in an intangible economy:

  1. It can ask companies to pay to defend their assets. As I wrote in The Internet’s Wuhan moment, AI has laid bare the software’s non-existent security model. Anthropic’s Mythos is the world’s most powerful security-oriented AI.

issues.title: 🔮 The $22 billion question about AI self-improvement #610
issues.summary: Plus: Cheap solar, who pays for Claude & DNA immunotherapy++
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
It’s simply the best, data-rich source for the money on how AI is reshaping the economy. — Matt G., a paying member

Subscribe now

My AI agent bought an iPhone for me this week. For an Uber, I’d still reach for the app.

That’s where we start today – I look at which jobs are worth handing over to AI, and why more Brits are paying for Claude. We’ll also look at what cheaper renewable power still needs and whether AI self-improvement owes more to intelligence or a massive research budget.

If you’re a member of Exponential View, join me in the subscriber chat:

Claude Britannia

Brits are spending more and more on AI. One in twenty adults in the UK pays for AI, spending more than $1.3 billion a year. Five percent is early days, but it is a fast ramp – it was 1% two years ago, and 2.5% a year ago. London is the hotspot; the professional skew is predictable, with those involved in tech, finance, education, and PR. And we are increasingly falling for Claude. Its share has quadrupled in a year.1 Was the trigger the improved harness on Claude Cowork?

Separately, made his first purchase using his Instinct agent, sweaters for winter. My Instinct agent secured my iPhone Duo for me on Tuesday. ’s agent booked a squash court for a showdown with . We’re playing around with them and finding them quite useful.

But in general, agent-based shopping is still early. Uber says four rides out of 320 million during Halloween week were booked by agents. I’m not sure I’d use an agent to book an Uber yet; hitting the app is easier. But getting an iPhone Duo, which involved checking Apple’s website every few minutes from 7 am, is a perfect job for them. So is finding finicky, complicated products like surge-protected power extensions, medicine pouches, or, in Will’s case, woolly jumpers.

Subscribe now

Fair-weather friends

The technology is doing its bit. Adding wind to solar and batteries cuts the median cost from $105 to $86 per MWh. North of Milan and Montreal (yes, they are on the same latitude), it falls from $164 to $99. Based on hourly modeling over ten years, and reckon that sun and wind mostly cover for each other – except for a difficult combined lull for about a week every four.

Ember also finds that 83% of the 750GW of fossil plants being planned sit where reliable renewables (with a bit of gas backup) cost under $100/MWh (which is roughly implied with oil at $60 a barrel).

My take is that technology costs will keep falling, and those that haven’t yet benefited from reductions (like panel installations) will start to yield as robotics improve. But redesigning the grid into a largely renewable-based one also requires more than better technology. It’ll need both a better cost of capital (gas plants still find capital cheaper than solar) and financial instruments that match energy prices to the volatility renewable-based energy brings.

issues.title: 🔮 What does it cost to make a worker?
issues.summary: Some early sketches of the economics of manufactured intelligence
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
Azeem’s sketchbook is an experimental format we’re trialing for paying members, where we share raw research notes, early frameworks, and unfinished ideas that haven’t been fully polished. They are the earliest indication of what I’m thinking through.

Here is another peek into my sketchbook. I’m trying to understand the economic trade-off between getting work done by an AI or a human. One way of doing this is to look at tasks in the economy and see how much it costs a human to do them compared to a machine.

Another way is to view the worker as an entity the economy needs, and to consider the minimum cost of creating one. (Of course, humans are much more than that, but I’m limiting the frame purely to economics here.) Those costs include the parenting, educating, and feeding from bairn to adult. We can then compare that to the cost of bringing in a machine capable of doing the same types of work using AI.

AI is manufactured intelligence. That is not the same intelligence that we humans have, but it’s clearly something that looks like intelligence.

While it is being manufactured, it’s highly replicable and follows the classic learning curve I described in my first book. And in my forthcoming second book, I extend these ideas.

Economically useful human intelligence is created very differently. It takes much longer than making a chip, and you don’t know the outcome for a long time.

issues.title: 🔥 Jensen Huang and the future of the AI boom
issues.summary: Good news for some, not so good news for others
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
Jensen Huang has resigned.

The company is in an awkward position, having refused to put a succession policy in place. Colette Kress, the CFO, will step in until it finds a replacement.

Company scandal aside, and there has been a lot, it’ll have a big impact on the AI boom.

Nvidia has been, without doubt, the linchpin of that boom. In the five years to 2026, the firm sold nearly 14 million flagship AI chips. They account for 85% of the market. The company has provided financial guarantees to the constellation of upstart AI infrastructure companies, the so-called neoclouds, so they can get their business moving. It has been a substantial venture capital backer of AI companies, with nearly $10 billion across Europe in the last year – the biggest investor there.

The numbers don’t do justice to how important Jensen himself has been. This isn’t like Apple without Steve Jobs. When Steve Jobs relinquished the CEO role in 2011, shortly before he passed away, he left a well-briefed successor and a management team known to customers and the market alike. And if Nvidia has been the linchpin of the AI boom, Jensen has been the linchpin of Nvidia.

I thought of him as the person with the best visibility into what was going on in AI, simply because everything ran on his chips. He advocated open-source models, including, uncomfortably now, Chinese ones. And pushed for a more accommodating approach to China.

I’ve seen him in London a couple of times. Once, he arrived on stage from down the street with then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer in tow. He brings energy and hands out billions of dollars. Calling out a startup’s name, followed by “I’m backing you with $500m” or whatever the number was. He returned a printout of our State of the AI Economy report, his signature across the front in gold marker, telling me it would be worth more now. Maybe even more after today.

The linchpin seems to be made less of solid steel and more of a well-worn leather. Will the ecosystem that depends on it stay on the road?

The current wave of AI investments, in model makers and infrastructure, is predicated on massive customer demand, not rampant oversupply. The industry’s common refrain over the past two years has been consistent: we are short on capacity. Not tomorrow, but today. That is why the spot prices for AI chips stay high even as they age. It’s why Anthropic has lined up $900bn of computing supply over the next 15 to 20 years – to make sure they don’t run short.

We’ve estimated that in the last 12 months, total revenues in the AI sector (outside of China) came to $188bn, growing faster than 4.2x a year. About 75% of that ends up at the infrastructure layer: the companies that own and operate the chips that do the calculations that make ChatGPT run for you.

The vast majority of revenue comes from chips made by Nvidia.

And the lack of capacity is what has created opportunities for new infrastructure companies, the so-called neoclouds. These young pups don’t have the track record of Microsoft or Google, so they have had to lean on Nvidia, their main supplier, for various kinds of guarantees. These guarantees range from the reasonably above-board to things that smell circular. While the numbers are large, for some companies (like Anthropic or XAI), Nvidia’s contribution is not a do-or-die proportion. But the man behind it all is leaving the building.

Demand stays

The post Can Network Science Transform Health and Nutrition? first appeared on Quanta Magazine
issues.author: Steven Strogatz and Janna Levin
issues.content_html:
Nothing really exists in isolation. Almost every part of our lives exists in a network. Consciousness arises from what neurons do together, life from what genes and proteins do together, society from what we do together.
