issues.title: Anthropic’s IPO nets Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley $113 million apiece in fees, eclipsing their SpaceX paydays
issues.summary: The blockbuster public debut delivered one of Wall Street’s largest underwriting paydays in history.
issues.author: Morgan Chittum
issues.content_html:
Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO on Thursday delivered one of Wall Street’s largest underwriting paydays in history, with the banks behind the listing raking in at least $550 million in fees, eclipsing the $500 million that was earned from Elon Musk–led SpaceX’s debut in June.

Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, the lead underwriters on the deal, each garnered fees of $113 million, according to Anthropic’s prospectus and confirmed by a source familiar with the matter. That’s because they both took on underwriting commitments of 20.5% of the $81.3 billion IPO. It’s also more than the roughly $100 million Goldman and Morgan Stanley each raked in from fees on the SpaceX deal over the summer.

JPMorgan and Citigroup each agreed to underwrite 10% of the Claude maker’s offering, putting their estimated fees at roughly $55 million apiece if allocated in proportion to their commitments. Bank of America, which committed to underwriting 3%, would receive an estimated $16.5 million in fees.

The last IPO to generate more than Anthropic’s in underwriting commissions was Visa’s 2008 debut, which delivered a $550.2 million fee pool. Anthropic could surpass that figure if underwriters exercise the offering’s over-allotment option, which allows banks to sell up to 15% more shares than initially planned.

Anthropic shares, trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, surged 17% in their Thursday debut, giving the company a fully diluted market capitalization of $1.27 trillion at the close. The $81.3 billion offering was the largest IPO in history by deal size.

Anthropic’s listing generated roughly 30 to 40 times the commissions of a typical IPO owing to its massive size, according to Matt Kennedy, senior IPO market strategist at Renaissance Capital. “By deal count, 2026 wasn’t the blowout year many were hoping for,” Kennedy said in a statement to Fortune. “So, mega IPOs like Anthropic have done a lot of the heavy lifting to make this a standout year for investment banks.”

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

issues.title: ‘The whole internet screams at once’: Downdetector logged 6.4 million U.S. outage reports in a week as Microsoft, the FAA, Chase, and Apple went down
issues.summary: Downdetector’s research chief sees “a bit of a coincidence” and a falling trend. Sen. Mark Warner blames a rush to patch software.
issues.author: Catherina Gioino
issues.content_html:
Microsoft’s email, the FAA, Chase, and Apple all went down within a week. Downdetector, the site people check when an app or a website stops working, logged 6.4 million U.S. reports in the seven days ending on Tuesday, four times a typical week’s number, and 14 million worldwide, three times its usual level. The company that runs it thinks the timing is mostly coincidence.

That puts the outage tracker at odds with the explanation taking hold in Washington, where Sen. Mark Warner has blamed organizations racing to patch software flaws that AI tools now find faster than companies can fix them. Downdetector’s data shows big outages getting rarer, and it can’t see what caused any of them. For companies watching their own update queues, the question is whether this week is a blip or the start of something.

Microsoft’s Outlook and Teams went down last week on Nov. 12 and 13, taking out email in more than 70 countries for almost 24 hours. With nearly 3.9 million U.S. reports and 7.8 million worldwide, it was Downdetector’s largest outage since Amazon Web Services went down in October 2025. Then on Friday, the FAA grounded every flight in the country in response to what it called unstable legacy equipment. Its initial investigation points to two sites, including a radio site in El Dorado, Ark., where its network contractor, L3Harris, had been installing a new router.

And on Monday, a software bug at Chase meant Chase and Wells Fargo customers couldn’t get to their money. Chase drew about 90,000 U.S. reports, roughly 165 times normal and more than twice any other U.S. bank outage this year. And on Tuesday, Apple Pay, iCloud, the App Store, and Apple Support drew about 81,000 reports as a result of what Apple said was a faulty internal update. Downdetector flagged 67 U.S. services that day, as opposed to the 16 it would get on a typical day, the broadest results of any day so far this year.

“You always wait for a bus, and then they come all at once,” Mark Giles, director of Ookla Research (Downdetector’s parent company), told Fortune. “I think this looks like a bit of a coincidence. There’s nothing really linking the outages.”

Downdetector, which collects user complaints about apps and websites, is the closest thing to a public scoreboard for these failures. Companies disclose their own outages, if at all, one at a time, and no U.S. agency publishes a running count. That’s part of what drives visitors to the site.

“We’re more connected than ever,” Giles said. “There’s these foundational points of the internet, which when something happens there, then the whole internet screams at once.”

And despite the four outages in a week, they’re becoming a rarer occurrence. Once the pandemic years are set aside, outages in Downdetector’s U.S. and U.K. data have fallen since about 2022. He said on average, Downdetector sees one large outage—which it defines as more than 50,000 U.S. reports for one company in a day—a little more than once a week. In the past year, only Christmas week and one week in June had more than this week’s four. Over the past 30 days the count is typical, because October was quiet, and Downdetector calls this week a cluster so far.

“This is a big blip, but it’s kind of on par for the course for what we’re seeing in terms of those longer-term trends,” he said. “Most of the time they’re fairly self-contained and remedied quite quickly. It’s the ones where you can’t withdraw money or you can’t access your emails that really get the headlines.”

Giles described a cycle he has seen in banking over the past three to four years. A company rolls out something new and spends less on making its systems resilient, and outages creep up. Then customers complain, the company invests, and outages fall. “I’m not saying that’s the case for Chase here,” he said. “A lot of these are just one-offs, maybe software problems or updates.”

The site can also overstate an outage, because it counts complaints rather than confirmed failures. Monday’s bank problems were a Chase outage, Giles said, but customers at other banks whose payments to Chase users failed reported their own banks as down. “We tend to overrepresent in some cases the actual outage,” he said. Outage news also brings more people to the site, which pushes up reports for other services.

Washington blames the patch rush

Updates are now at the center of the explanation in Washington. Sen. Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, told the Financial Times there was no sign of a cyberattack and that the outages most likely came from organizations racing to patch software. Part of it is new technology: AI tools are now finding flaws faster than companies can safely fix them, and Warner said the pressure to fix them right away is straining systems that were never designed for that speed.

On Wednesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the New York Times’ DealBook Summit that the company had already pushed at least three critical patches that day, the FT reported. Citigroup CEO Jane Fraser, whose bank reported no outages, said the volume of patches moving through the world at once is “five-, 10-fold what we’ve ever seen before.” Still, neither Microsoft nor JPMorgan Chasetied their respective outages to patching AI-found flaws.

It proves trickier for companies to stay up to speed with this new tech when there are also nefarious actors using AI. Companies are rushing because attackers have the same tools: Giles said the patch rush “has to be an increasing concern for security and IT teams,” and it “speaks to a concern that hackers with swarms of AI agents are better able to find and exploit these.”

However, none of that shows up on Downdetector’s charts. “[It’s] not something that Downdetector can pick up on, though, as a root cause,” Giles said.

Currently, Downdetector flags a service only when its reports stand out from its own normal level. It plans to build AI tools over the next year to tie related spikes together and show which company actually failed.

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

issues.title: Britain and the Pentagon told people to get ready in October. Now Costco is selling out of generators, and billionaires have ‘apocalypse insurance’
issues.summary: A string of tech outages has Costco members stocking up on rice, water, and generators. The buying started weeks before the outages did.
issues.author: Nick Lichtenberg
issues.content_html:
Costco shoppers are “pantry-loading” again. As of Sunday night, 21 of the 26 high-ticket generators on Costco’s website were sold out, according to Mizuho Securities analyst David Bellinger. One of the sold-out models, a Kohler, runs about $7,000.

The last time Costco members bought like this was March 2020, when then-CFO Richard Galanti told investors the buying was “off the charts” across the U.S. On March 12 of that year, U.S. toilet paper sales were up 734% from the same day a year earlier.

This time the buying picked up after a run of tech failures that has kept people out of their email, grounded flights, and left bank customers unable to move money, and households are now spending to get ready for the next one. Bellinger told clients that consumer anxiety after the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stop for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up on social media is behind the buying. He raised his Costco price target to $1,150 from $1,100 and said Walmart and Sam’s Club could see similar “pantry-loading lifts.”

What’s selling

Costco CFO Gary Millerchip told Bloomberg that stronger sales of rice, canned goods, water, paper products, generators, and batteries came toward the end of October. Mizuho says Home Depot and Lowe’s could sell more generators, too.

Smaller sellers are seeing the same thing. Survival Frog, which sells emergency food, radios, and other survival gear, saw sales jump 450% between Oct. 27 and Nov. 16 compared with prior weeks, founder and CEO Byron Walker told Axios. Most of the recent buyers were new customers, and food, led by canned meats, is the top seller, followed by radios, solar generators, battery packs, and water filters. Competitors saw similar trends, Walker said.

“You can’t turn on the news without hearing about a new cyberattack or a tech meltdown,” he said.

Costco’s reported sales don’t show the spike yet. U.S. comparable sales excluding gas rose 8.1% in the four weeks ended Nov. 1, according to Costco, the same pace as the first nine weeks of its fiscal year. Mizuho estimates U.S. growth sped up to 11% to 12% in the last week of October and into early November, and holiday shopping may be part of that.

The Federal Reserve’s cash data covers only the week before the bank outages. Currency in circulation averaged about $2.5 trillion in the week ended Nov. 11, roughly 3% more than a year earlier, according to the Fed’s weekly H.4.1 release. The next reading, covering the week of the Chase outage, comes out Thursday afternoon.

The buying started before the outages

The stockpiling began more than two weeks before Microsoft 365 went down on Nov. 12 and the FAA’s nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13, which halted departures for more than four hours, the longest in 25 years. In late October, governments sent the warnings. On Oct. 21, CISA said critical PHP vulnerabilities required immediate patching; PHP runs nearly 70% of websites. The next day, the U.K. launched its “Be Ready” campaign, urging families to stockpile three days of water, shelf-stable food, and cash. Within days came reports that the Pentagon wants every major base in the lower 48 states able to run on its own for at least 90 days. All of it landed during what was dubbed “Black October,” a month of cyberattacks on hundreds of companies and institutions.

Walker credits his sales boom to exactly those warnings: the U.K. and EU urging households to keep three days of supplies, and the Pentagon’s 90-day plan for bases, which fed rumors online of a 90-day U.S. “blackout.”

The ultrawealthy got there first. Reid Hoffman told The New Yorker in 2017 that he believed more than half of Silicon Valley’s billionaires had invested in “apocalypse insurance.” For everyone else, apparently, there’s Costco.

A few years ago, the Costco hedge was gold. The warehouse club’s one-ounce bars sold out within hours after their 2023 launch, and Costco capped how many bars each member could buy. That trade has cooled. U.S. Mint sales of gold bullion coins fell 34% in the first 10 months of 2026 from a year earlier, to 185,500 ounces, and October’s 11,000 ounces were down 58% from October 2025. North America was the only region to see outflows from gold ETFs in October, $512 million, according to the World Gold Council. Gold fell 6.3% for the month and fell to about $3,693 an ounce on Thursday, its lowest since September 2025. Costco members who bought bars in September are down about $700 apiece, by 24/7 Wall St.’s math.

What’s actually breaking

Officials keep saying the outages aren’t connected to one another. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday there’s “zero evidence” linking them. “The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA,” he said. Vice President JD Vance told Fox News’ Laura Ingraham that friends have asked him whether they should be “preparing to build a bunker” or stock up on food and water. “And my answer to that is no,” he said. “We do not see some crisis coming down.”

Part of the problem is the cleanup from October. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told Fox Business that patching after last month’s PHP alert left some systems, including at the NSA, that would “not come back up.” Microsoft blamed a “latent defect” in a network fix deployed over the summer. The FAA is switching off its new routers and leaning on 25-year-old equipment, and the White House is starting to admit AI is part of the story.

In the AxiosBehind the Curtain column, Jim VandeHei and Mike Allen wrote that government officials and AI experts expect the disruption to last for months, under a catchphrase gaining currency: “Software Beirut.” They told readers to keep more cash on hand in case their bank is down for a day or two, the same advice Britain gave in October.

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

issues.title: Anthropic stock pops 30% to $2 trillion market cap in mega IPO
issues.summary: Its Wall Street debut instantly puts the five-year-old AI company in the elite club of trillion-dollar public companies.
issues.author: Beatrice Nolan
issues.content_html:
Anthropic’s stock surged more than 30% in its first minutes as a public company, a roaring debut that crowned the AI company—at least briefly—with a stunning, $2 trillion market cap.

Shares of Anthropic opened at $111.50 per share on Thursday, up 34% from the $83 IPO price. The stock pop began to moderate as the trading day continued, and Anthropic finished its first day as a public company up 17%, at $97.17 per share.

The strong demand for Anthropic shares came as the broader market was under pressure, with the Nasdaq down 550 points and the Dow Jones industrial average down 1101 points at the close of market.

At its $97 closing price, Anthropic’s market cap was just shy of $1.8 trillion—an astounding Wall Street debut that instantly puts the five-year-old AI company in the elite club of trillion-dollar public companies, alongside giants such as Alphabet, Apple, and Amazon. (Some calculations use a lower share count that excludes potential dilution from restricted stock, convertible notes, and other items, giving Anthropic a roughly $1.3 trillion market cap).

“This moment is bigger than any one company, or any one country. It will take all of us, working together, to ensure this technology goes well for us and the many generations to come,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in a statement posted on X on Thursday.

Anthropic priced the offering Wednesday night at $83 a share, above its marketed range of $70 to $78, giving the company a $1.5 trillion valuation. Demand was strong enough that it raised the deal to 980 million shares from 825 million.

There had been endless speculation about whether Anthropic would top SpaceX as the largest IPO of all time. At a $1.5 trillion IPO valuation, Anthropic would be the second most valuable IPO of all time, behind SpaceX’s $1.77 trillion IPO in June. Measured by capital raised however, Anthropic’s $79 billion ($81.4 billion, if stock sold by insiders is included) topped the $75 billion raised by SpaceX.

Seven strategic partners, including Google and Nvidia, have also agreed to buy $26 billion of nonvoting Anthropic stock at the IPO price. And the deal’s underwriters also have a “greenshoe” option to purchase an additional 147 million shares of Anthropic stock. If exercised, that would bring the total proceeds of Anthropic’s IPO to $118 billion.

The offering will provide Anthropic with a vital infusion of capital as it seeks to stay ahead in the AI race and to invest in the computing infrastructure to train its models. It will also make instant billionaires out of numerous Anthropic employees and early investors, particularly the seven cofounders who created Anthropic. At least 400 early hires will be worth $100 million or more, according to CNBC.

“Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” Amodei said in his statement Thursday. “We will not bend to either business or political pressure,” Amodei said, invoking the company’s stated commitment to develop AI technology with safeguards.

Anticipation for the IPOs of Anthropic and its archrival, OpenAI, has been building ever since OpenAI ignited the generative AI boom in late 2022 with the launch of ChatGPT. With OpenAI holding off on its IPO until at least 2027, Anthropic becomes the first pure-play maker of frontier AI models to go public (SpaceX also makes rockets, and Google and Meta both have massive businesses in search and social media).

But the Anthropic IPO also comes at a tenuous time for the AI industry. It’s been barely a week since the sector lost one of its most powerful figures. Nvidia cofounder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO last Thursday, following reports that he had engaged in two extramarital affairs: one with a customer suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese intelligence asset, and one with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. His exit added fresh pressure to a listing that was already seen as a stress test of investors’ appetite for AI.

Analysts and investors told Fortune they didn’t expect the Nvidia shock to derail the offering or touch Anthropic’s core business. The bigger risk, they said, may come later. Seaport Research Partners analyst Jay Goldberg warned that turmoil at Nvidia could bring Anthropic “much tougher questions” once it starts reporting quarterly results as a public company. Georgetown associate professor Jason Schloetzer predicted closer scrutiny of Anthropic’s ties to Nvidia and to customers associated with the chipmaker.

Soaring revenue—and expectations

Anthropic’s revenue has soared thanks to strong demand from business customers, a market in which Anthropic has been especially successful. In the nine months ending Sept. 30, Anthropic generated $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. The company posted a $104 billion net loss in its most recent nine-month period, though the bulk of the red ink is because of the way it accounted for its convertible notes.

But the high share price straight out of the gates will put immense pressure on Anthropic as it seeks to justify its valuation to investors and to prove that AI tools can deliver the massive payoff Wall Street expects.

Anthropic CEO Amodei, once the VP of research at OpenAI, left to cofound Anthropic at the end of 2020, along with sister Daniela and several other OpenAI employees, when they became disillusioned with OpenAI’s approach to AI safety. Still, the company’s IPO prospectus is replete with warnings of the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence including “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

The IPO also comes amid growing public backlash to AI data centers, underscored by the results of the U.S. midterm elections. High-profile incidents of rogue AI agents, from OpenAI as well as Anthropic, have added to the unease over the technology.

Anthropic has sought to allay some of these concerns by touting its structure as a public benefit corporation, which requires the company to balance shareholder interests with its corporate mission of “the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.” The structure also ensures that Amodei and the other six cofounders maintain majority voting control via multiple classes of shares with different voting rights.

The stakes of Thursday’s IPO reach well beyond one company. Anthropic has more than 400 backers, and nearly every major venture firm owns a piece of it, so the IPO is effectively a liquidity event for the AI boom itself. A strong debut and a stable stretch of trading afterward would suggest the boom has more runway. A stumble would be read as a sign the bubble is near its peak. At least one investor argued that Huang’s departure could even help Anthropic: CEO Dario Amodei had clashed with Huang over chip exports to China and over AI regulation.

Several Wall Street research firms, including Wolfe Research, Citizens, and Melius Research initiated coverage of Anthropic with buy ratings.

There was tremendous demand for Anthropic’s shares, according to news reports. Bloomberg News cited Anthropic’s underwriters as saying the shares were as much as seven times oversubscribed and that only about half of the institutional orders for shares were filled. The company had reserved about 20% of its shares for retail investors, and those investors had reported that they had begun to receive their allocations through brokerage platforms such as E*Trade, Charles Schwab, SoFi, and Fidelity.


This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

Today is a profoundly sad day. Russia’s aggressive action is heartbreaking for the death, suffering, and economic turmoil it will cause in Ukraine and, indirectly at least, beyond. Here at Rick Steves’ Europe, we hope that a diplomatic solution can be found and peace will return to that fragile and long-suffering part of our world.

Our mission at RSE is to help Americans better know and understand our neighbors through travel. But when we bring travelers to another country, we also bring their dollars — dollars that would support Putin’s aggression. Therefore, as of today, we have canceled all 2022 tours that include a stop in Russia.

Of course, we will keep a close eye on unfolding events and monitor any travel impacts through the rest of Europe. But it is important to keep geographic realities in mind and remember that a war in Ukraine is as far from our European vacation dreams as a war in Guatemala would be from Texas or Florida. For 40 years now, we have lived, worked, and traveled through many periods of tragic warfare in lands far from where we lead our tours (and some closer). And at this time, we see no reason to change the rest of our travel and touring plans.

The tragic reality unfolding in Ukraine only reminds me how important it is for Americans to keep on traveling and to do so in a way that makes us better and more engaged citizens of our world. I’m flying to Europe next month for a 40-day trip through a dozen great cities from London to Athens — and I’m proud that thousands of my fellow travelers will experience the European trip of their dreams while having rich learning experiences far from home on a 2022 Rick Steves tour.

In the meantime, let’s be thankful for our blessings, support our nation’s leaders as they do their best to navigate this crisis, and keep the troubled corners of our world (Ukraine, Russia, Afghanistan, and more) in our thoughts and prayers.

—Rick

issues.title: The Tour du Mont Blanc: Some Tips I Learned Along the Way
issues.summary: At 66, I felt a bit like the father of the hiking community when I hiked around Mont Blanc earlier this fall. But the Tour du Mont Blanc is doable for any reasonably fit hiker, and there were plenty of people on the trail who were older than me. For total novices like Shelley … Continue reading "The Tour du Mont Blanc: Some Tips I Learned Along the Way"
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
At 66, I felt a bit like the father of the hiking community when I hiked around Mont Blanc earlier this fall. But the Tour du Mont Blanc is doable for any reasonably fit hiker, and there were plenty of people on the trail who were older than me.

For total novices like Shelley and me, it’s wise to be proactive about health and safety. Here are some tips I learned along the way:

Good boots, liner socks, slippery powder, and moleskin for tender skin are essential. We kind of became gear geeks — investing in good day bags (Osprey), woolen clothes (socks, underwear, shirts), and great hiking shoes. I was never so thankful for a wool cap in Europe.

I was skeptical about a lot of “good ideas,” but two things I eventually appreciated were a daily baggie of trail mix and my metal water bottle. (I complained about its steep $40 price tag…but soon came to recognize it was a great value).

I must say, if the weather turned bad and it rained hard, I think much of the trail would become no fun at all. In fact, it would be dangerous. Hiking poles are essential, and even in perfect weather, I would have been worried about a stumble without my own trusty set.

Eat a solid breakfast. The one day we had breakfast with no protein, climbing was tougher.

Put on sunscreen, even if the weather’s bad.

After learning my lesson on other long hikes, I decided to be religious about stretching on the Tour du Mont Blanc from the start. I had a routine of six stretches and spent time throughout the day making sure I didn’t tighten up. Very important!

Don’t be a hero. If skin is getting hot, wrap it up. I did the entire TMB hike without a blister — and then just got one on purpose in the last two hours.

Good gear, smart and proactive ways to stay healthy, stretching, and taking it easy… it all worked just great.

issues.title: Taking it Easy on the Tour du Mont Blanc
issues.summary: While the Tour du Mont Blanc is demanding, it’s not a particularly difficult hike. It’s just long, with lots of altitude gain and loss, and always scenic. On my recent trek around the mountain with three friends, it seemed each of us had a weak spot: knees, toes, or lungs. For some, the challenge was … Continue reading "Taking it Easy on the Tour du Mont Blanc"
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
While the Tour du Mont Blanc is demanding, it’s not a particularly difficult hike. It’s just long, with lots of altitude gain and loss, and always scenic. On my recent trek around the mountain with three friends, it seemed each of us had a weak spot: knees, toes, or lungs. For some, the challenge was the uphill part, and for others (with weak knees), it was going downhill. We just took it easy, with lots of little breaks.

For long climbs, steady, smaller steps are best. The trail could be really rocky, and I can’t imagine doing it without hiking poles. The trail signs were great, and apps made staying on the trail easy: Just follow the blue dot. And I got good use out of a top-quality printed map. (I’d spend time the night before reading up on the hike and familiarizing myself with the trail on the map.)

While the weather forecast looked threatening, we hiked six days (in September, during the last week of the season) and, thankfully, had only one hour of rain. Still, each day we’d pack rain gear, and we’d add on and take off layers as we gained and lost altitude. After four days, we had it sorted out, and it occurred to us rank beginners, “We’re getting good at this.”

As we were hiking in a big circle around a big clump of mountains and sleeping in charming towns each night, every day seemed to be up and over a daunting mountain pass. A nightly treat was a stroll under a milky blanket of stars.

issues.summary: Hiking Europe’s Tour du Mont Blanc was a totally different slice of European culture for me: Coming upon a remote farmhouse-turned-thriving-cafe serving wonderful lunches…flowers and cows (with classic bells) scenically sprinkled throughout…and an esprit de corps where everyone is like family. As nearly everyone hikes in the same direction (counter-clockwise), you become friends … Continue reading
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
Hiking Europe’s Tour du Mont Blanc was a totally different slice of European culture for me: Coming upon a remote farmhouse-turned-thriving-cafe serving wonderful lunches…flowers and cows (with classic bells) scenically sprinkled throughout…and an esprit de corps where everyone is like family.

As nearly everyone hikes in the same direction (counter-clockwise), you become friends with fellow hikers. It seemed like half the people on the trail were from the US, and I met lots of Seattleites.

And in the interest of hiking light, lunches were very simple — just a sandwich from the hotel, maybe a carrot, a piece of fruit, and water. But upon reaching the mid-day summit, lunch was a marmot’s banquet. (Speaking of marmots, we saw no wildlife except a couple of mice that had been squished under hiking boots on the trail.)

issues.author: Beth Mole
issues.content_html:
In the wake of the Make America Healthy Again movement's midterm wipeout, a top leader suggested the heavy losses came down to being outspent by wealthier, more powerful rivals. But a Stat report on MAHA's own spending in the run-up to the election raises questions about whether the group's priority was ever winning elections in the first place.

The dive into the financial documents reveals that the MAHA PAC, led by Tony Lyons, spent more on allies, boosters, meals, luxuries, and its affiliated nonprofit than it did on political candidates.

The findings are in stark contrast to an announcement from Lyons in the spring that he was heading a $100 million fundraiser to boost MAHA's clout in the midterms. In reality, MAHA PAC took in $3.2 million. During the election cycle, the PAC spent more than $10.5 million, with over $7 million coming from money it had collected previously.

issues.title: Man hired by Russia spied on Silicon Valley tech and defense company, feds say
issues.summary: 25-year-old accused of stalking employees at coffee shop and in an "aggressive" car pursuit.
issues.author: Dan Goodin
issues.content_html:
A Russian national has been indicted on suspicions he was a Russian spy who stalked and surveilled employees of a Silicon Valley company that was assisting Ukraine in its ongoing war with its eastern neighbor.

Igor D’iu, 25, allegedly photographed the employees and their computer screens as they worked at a coffee shop located near the company’s Palo Alto office, federal prosecutors said Wednesday. He also kept a list of home addresses of employees and a senior executive. At one point, prosecutors said, D’iu trailed an employee as she traveled home from Palo Alto to San Francisco. An affidavit filed in the case referred to the employee as FEMP1, short for female employee, and said the event left her “in a state of emotional distress.”

Evasive and irregular turns

“FEMP1 made evasive and irregular turns, took back roads, and turned into a grocery store parking lot where D’IU continued aggressively following her vehicle,” an FBI special agent wrote. “D’IU followed FEMP1 through U-turns, illegal left turns, and ran a red light to stay with FEMP1 for nearly thirty miles. FEMP1 called 911 while driving and was instructed to drive directly to San Francisco Police Department (“SFPD”) Mission Station. Near SFPD Mission Station, FEMP1 flagged an SFPD patrol vehicle and reported the incident. D’IU left once FEMP1 made contact with the patrol vehicle.”

issues.title: Traumatized teens sue school, cops after Doritos bag triggers AI gun alert
issues.summary: Lawsuit: Over 99% of school system’s AI gun alerts were false positives.
issues.author: Ashley Belanger
issues.content_html:
In October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down and waiting for their rides home. It was then, in the lull of a moment any teen with after-school activities knows well, that the school’s AI gun detection system suddenly flagged one teen holding a bag of chips as a potential gunman.

Within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat. They recognized the Doritos bag and canceled the alert, which notified not only other school officials but also the Baltimore County Police Department that no response was needed.

The false alert could have ended there—before a traumatizing campus clash with police—but it didn’t.

issues.title: Think It, Say It: A Two-Step Guide To Writing
issues.summary: Everyone has the ability to write, especially when called into service, whether to pen a novel or an important press release.
issues.author: Andrew Welsh-Huggins
issues.content_html:
Today’s guest post is by author Andrew Welsh-Huggins.

Good writing advice can come in the most unexpected ways, as I learned recently at an event where I was the one who was supposed to be doling out ideas.

The forum was a “meet the author” event at a bookstore in our neighborhood on the West Side of Columbus, Ohio, during which I talked about my writing journey, followed by Q&A and a book signing.

After my presentation, rather than ask a question, an audience member related his own experience writing many years ago. A supervisor had asked him to draft a press release, striking terror in this non-writer’s heart.

“How do I do that?” he asked.

The supervisor responded: “Well, think about what you want to say, then say it.”

The story elicited a chuckle from audience members. But the more I thought about it, the more I realized how sound the advice was, and how succinctly it encapsulated a writing philosophy to live by.

Here are three things the remark brought to mind:

First off, unbeknownst to the person relating this anecdote, he waded perfectly into the plotter vs. pantser debate. As someone who has tried both pure pantsing and extensive plotting, and now straddles the line between the two approaches, I value the idea of thinking about what I’m going to write before I pen a single word. In my case, the “thinking” that comes before beginning a new book involves an outline that covers around 75% of what I expect to happen, leaving me plenty of wiggle room as unexpected characters and plot twists emerge during the “say it” portion of writing.

While not an outliner, crime novelist Karin Slaughter, in a 2023 interview, captured what I consider an ideal way to think about plotting and writing:

Before I start a book, I think about it a lot, and I get some idea of the story. Then I sit down with my editor, and we talk it through. And she’s like, ‘Okay, this sounds good’ or ‘Well, you’ve killed everybody in the first chapter.’ And I’ll be like, ‘Oh, maybe I should kill someone in the fifth chapter.’ That kind of thing. We don’t outline. It’s more like this happens, this happens, this happens. And that’s a good scaffolding for me to follow.

Secondly, the “first this, then that” structure of the audience member’s advice is a reminder that, having conceived of an idea, it’s important to get the work done. As crime writer Susan Isaacs has noted, “Writing may be an art. It is certainly a craft. But also it’s a job. You have to put in regular hours and go to work whether you feel like it or not.” Similarly, you can’t just think about what you want to say. At some point, you also have to say it however you best work: pen on paper, fingers on keyboard, dictation app primed and ready to go.

Finally, the audience member provided a valuable lesson in how we define writers. One of my least favorite words is the adjective-turned-noun “creative,” as in, “Of course he’s a good writer—he’s a ‘creative’.” A creative, the implication being, as opposed to the rest of us mere mortals. I couldn’t disagree more. Everyone is a creative in some form or fashion, whether they’re a gifted artist, baker, or car mechanic. And within the context of this essay, everyone has the ability to write, especially when called into service, whether to pen a novel or an important press release. As novelist Phoenicia Rogerson has said:

It’s quite common, I think, to have this idea of what a real writer is, and to go chasing after that, rather than letting yourself be who you are. If you write, you’re a real writer, and there’s no superiority in writing one genre over another.

“Think about what you want to say, then say it.”

I couldn’t have put it better myself.

Less than 40 cm (16 inches) under the surface, the … Read the full post → "Celtic silver coin ho
issues.author: livius drusus
issues.content_html:
A hoard of more than 200 Celtic silver coins has been discovered during construction of an electrical substation in Szombathely, Hungary. The new substation is being built on a site where archaeological remains have been found in the past, triggering a professional excavation before construction began. Less than 40 cm (16 inches) under the surface, the team from the National Archaeological Institute of the Hungarian National Museum Public Collection Center uncovered a few silver coins that had been scattered by agricultural work. Metal detectors then located the core of the hoard.

They were cached in a pit, some loose, some inside a small earthenware container. The coins are all Velem-type tetradrachms dating from the late 2nd century B.C. to the beginning of the 1st century B.C. On the obverse of the coins is a Celticized head in profile facing right bearing a pearl diadem and necklace. On the reverse is a stylized horse and rider wearing a crested helmet. They were probably minted in the Velem-Szentvid area, less than 10 miles from the find site.

Worth four drachmae a piece (hence “tetradrachms”), the denomination was widely used as trade coin and for state expenses throughout the Greco-Roman world. Their high silver content and large value made them unsuitable as a daily currency for individuals to spend, but perfect for them to store their wealth. The number of tetradrachms found in hoards attest to this usage.

The coin hoard is not the only significant find made in the two years since excavations began. Archaeologists have found material remains and thousands of artifacts covering almost 7,000 years of history. The oldest object is a polished stone axe used to fell trees and work wood. Another stand-out piece is a peacock-eye glass bead from the Early Iron Age (7th-6th century B.C.). From the remains of a Roman building, archaeologists recovered a fragment of a brick with a dog pawprint. It’s a flat tile, perhaps from a pilae stack that raised the floor over a hypocaust heating system.

A selection of the finds from the excavation will be exhibited at the Savaria Museum in Szombathely.

issues.author: livius drusus
issues.content_html:
A rare medieval copper scepter head has been discovered in Kapan, southeast Armenia. Similar to a modified mace, the scepter is decorated with swirl patterns on the top and eight flattened blades. It was a symbol of royal power from a time when Armenia had vassal kingdoms under the central monarch. It dates to the 10th or 11th century.

The Kapan area was part of the territories of the princely Siunia dynasty. There was a small settlement at the site of what would become Kapan by the 5th century, and a fortress was built nearby in the 4th century. Kapan rose to major prominence in the 10th century when it became the capital of the self-style Kingdom of Kapan. It was a vassal of the Bagratid dynasty rulers of Greater Armenia, and survived a little more than 100 years, from 987 to 1170.

According to Stepanos Orbelian, a medieval Armenian historian, bishop, and a prominent member of the noble Orbelian dynasty, the capital of the Kingdom of Syunik was destroyed in 1126 under the command of Amir Harun as a result of Seljuk invasions, but the kingdom, thanks to the already impregnable fortress of Baghaberd, survived until 1170, being the last independent Armenian kingdom of Greater Armenia.

The first systematic archaeological investigations at the site of Old Kapan an environs began only in 2024. They found evidence of powerful fortifications, double-layered walls and a larger defensive tower near the entrance to the fortress.

Last year’s excavation uncovered the remains of foundations and column bases from a three-aisled basilica dating to the 4th or 5th century. Near the church, archaeologists found a stone oil press four feet in diameter. This year the team uncovered a furnace of polished stone that likely heated the water of a public bath at the site.

The scepter has been transferred to the Kapan Geological Museum for conservation and display.

The leg was found in a … Read the full post → "Huge leg came from monumental bronze emp
issues.author: livius drusus
issues.content_html:
A larger-than-life-sized gilded bronze leg discovered in 1820 has been newly identified as a fragment of a monumental statue of Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius erected in the Scottish Borders. Since its discovery, the leg was believed to have come from England, likely the urban center of Eboracum, modern-day York.

The leg was found in a bog in Milsington near Hawick. It was exceptional for its great size and condition, with much of its original gilding still intact. It is a lower leg below the knee wearing with straps crossed the top of the foot, wrapping around the ankle and tied in front knot. It dates to 140 A.D.

Scholars initially thought it came from northern England because its high quality and rich gilding suggested close proximity to expensive craftspeople and materials, but more recent studies of Roman statue fragments has found that in fact, frontier forts on the Scottish border did erect bronze statues of the emperor, even equestrian ones.

In addition, the cut line where the leg was removed was handled very gently. There are no cut marks on the top. It was taken down as cast. Had the statue been dismembered by angry locals after the Romans withdrew from southern Scotland in 160-180 A.D., it would have been hacked off, not carefully removed, and chopped up for scrap.

Once curators had established that the statue was likely to have been erected in Scotland, they looked to answer the question of who it depicted. Just one emperor paid particular heed to his Scottish victories – Antoninus Pius. His conquest of southern Scotland was the only foreign adventure that he commemorated with the title Imperator, a battle-honour meaning ‘commander’ which marked an emperor’s victory.

Dr Fraser Hunter, Principal Curator of Prehistoric and Roman Archaeology at National Museums Scotland said:

“This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome’s second attempt at conquering Scotland. This was a big deal for the Emperor, something which was worth celebrating. It offers us a tantalising glimpse into the kind of grand monuments which once stood in southern Scotland and shows the importance Pius placed on his victories in Scotland. But it begs the question … where is the rest of the statue?”

Mounted to a model of an equestrian statue like the iconic Marcus Aurelius in the Capitoline Museums in Rome, the leg is now on display in Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire, alongside a wealth of other priceless Roman-era artifacts, including the incredible Mithraic altar with the cutouts of the sun god Sol so it glowed when lit from behind found at Inveresk. The exhibition opened Saturday and runs through April 18th, 2027.

issues.title: In Search of the Deep Life
issues.summary: Early in the coronavirus pandemic, as I sat at home channeling my anxiety into publishing daily essays on this newsletter (a streak I kept up ... Read more The post In Search of the Deep Life appeared first on Cal Newport .
issues.author: Cal Newport
issues.content_html:
Early in the coronavirus pandemic, as I sat at home channeling my anxiety into publishing daily essays on this newsletter (a streak I kept up for six weeks), I had a revelation: none of my advice, ideas, or systems really mattered if you didn’t build them on the foundation of a meaningful life.

Who cares about losing yourself to social media or letting work devolve into email whack-a-mole if the world outside of your phone and inbox isn’t that compelling?

On March 17th of that infamous spring, I captured these notions in an essay titled ​“The Deep Life: Some Notes.”​ As I explained:

“To me, the deep life is about focusing with energetic intention on things that really matter — in work, at home, and in your soul — and not wasting too much attention on things that don’t.”

In the weeks that followed, I wrote ​several​​more​​essays​ on pursuing the deep life. Later that summer, when I ​launched my podcast​, I dedicated a third of my inaugural episode to this concept. (My original tagline: “a show about work, technology, and the deep life.”)

Two years later, as we returned to normalcy, I convinced my publisher to let me try writing a book on these ideas. I then set out on the long, patient process of elaborating and developing my thoughts into a coherent system.

All of this brings me to the current moment. I’m proud to finally announce that my next book, ​The Deep Life: A Structured Approach​, is now ​available for pre-order​.

The Deep Life brings together and significantly expands on my past thinking on this topic. It presents a step-by-step approach to achieving the intentional-living goal laid out in that original March 2020 post. It’s less an idea book than a classic-style advice guide, offering practical details on how to identify what resonates, refine it into an actionable vision, and then move toward that vision systematically.

My friend ​Oliver Burkeman​, to whom I sent a proof copy of the manuscript, had the following reaction:

“It’s hard to imagine a more timely or inspiring manual for a life of sanity and accomplishment, or a better guide than Cal Newport. This is a profound book, but just as importantly, a profoundly practical one: it shows that depth is something we can do.”

I believe that this book is thekey that unlocks the value in almost everything else I write about. If you’ve followed me this far, then you need to read this one.

With this in mind, here are some of the places where you can pre-order the book right now in advance of its March publication date:

  • ​Amazon​
  • ​Barnes & Noble​
  • ​Bookshop.org​
  • ​Amazon UK​
  • ​Waterstones ​

You can also pre-order ​a signed copy​ from my local bookstore here in Takoma Park.

If you think you’ll eventually read this one, I humbly ask that you consider pre-ordering it, as these early purchases signal to booksellers that the book is worth stocking on their shelves. (And if you do pre-order, hold on to your digital receipt, as I’m working on a pretty cool bonus that I’ll announce soon.)

Most of all, however, I want to extend my thanks for your support over all these years as I’ve explored these fundamental ideas. We only get one life. Why not make it deep?

issues.title: The Good Thing About Hard Things
issues.summary: A new research paper titled “​AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance,”​ which was recently presented at the ​Conference on Language Modeling​, has been ... Read more The post The Good Thing About Hard Things appeared first on Cal Newport .
issues.author: Cal Newport
issues.content_html:
A new research paper titled “​AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance,”​ which was recently presented at the ​Conference on Language Modeling​, has been attracting attention.

It explores an obvious question: do AI tools negatively affect your ability to think? It does so with a simple experimental design: participants were divided into two groups tasked with solving a series of math problems involving fractions. One group had to find answers on their own, while the other used ChatGPT to help.

At first, the ChatGPT group performed better, which is not surprising because LLMs are good at solving math problems. But then the researchers turned off the chatbot. Not only did the AI group’s accuracy fall below the control group, but many participants in the AI group gave up and started skipping questions altogether.

The researchers repeated the same experiment several more times, including one instance where math problems were replaced with an SAT reading comprehension prompt. They kept finding the same drop-offs in accuracy and persistence.

Here’s how ​a press release​ about the paper summarized these results:

“The findings backed up what anecdotes and surveys have increasingly found in recent years: An overreliance on AI for answers erodes our cognitive fitness. When AI produces answers in seconds, we get used to that speed; anything that takes longer feels inefficient.”

Brian Christian, one of the paper’s authors, put it plainly: “You almost couldn’t ask for a clearer story.”

I’ve spent the last decade thinking and writing about how technologies might accidentally degrade our ​cognitive fitness​, and how this might in turn degrade not only our economic productivity, but also the quality of the human experience more generally.

In this sense, these LLM findings aren’t revealing something new.

What is new, however, is the jaw-dropping speed of these impacts. We’re accustomed to slow-moving techno-cognition trends such as the negative effects of ubiquitous smartphone usage, which took years to emerge in the data.

With chatbots, the negative impact is immediate. The high generated by side-stepping mental effort using LLMs is so compelling that, with only a short exposure, hard thinking quickly becomes intolerable.

The good news is that we don’t yet know if these effects are permanent. Presumably, the research participants who struggled immediately after ChatGPT was turned off might do much better on the same type of test if they tried again later in a setting where AI help was clearly not an option.

But we cannot ignore the warnings that these early studies are generating. When it comes to our cognitive fitness, we’re playing with a powerful new force that we don’t yet fully understand.

A key theme of my work in the technology critic space is that a life without serious, sustained, intentional thought is impoverished. Thinking is how we make sense of ourselves and the world, and is how we imagine new horizons and create the key elements of our future. It’s at the heart of philosophy, theology, and human empathy; the ability that separates our species from all other animals.

Silicon Valley is good at creating tools, but terrible at figuring out how we should use them. The latter step is still up to us — but it requires us to care.

The post The Good Thing About Hard Things appeared first on Cal Newport.

issues.title: It’s Time to Investigate the AI Labs
issues.summary: Over the last several months, the two leading frontier AI labs have shown some brazen behavior. It started with a series of​ carefully planned announcements​ ... Read more The post It’s Time to Investigate the AI Labs appeared first on Cal Newport .
issues.author: Cal Newport
issues.content_html:
Over the last several months, the two leading frontier AI labs have shown some brazen behavior.

It started with a series of​ carefully planned announcements​ and reports from OpenAI that try to establish how unnerving and powerful (not to mention ​felonious​) their LLM-powered agent systems have become.

They then handed the baton to Anthropic, whose employees began ​publicly debating​ the exact probability that these technologies would lead to human extinction. They delivered this all with an eerie calmness that conveyed a nihilistic inevitability about their work.

The ground suitably softened, the campaign crescendoed with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodi releasing a letter, titled ​“We Must Pace the Frontier,”​ in which he enumerates all the harms his own company’s research might cause, and then, instead of apologizing and promising to stop, concludes that catastrophe can only be avoided if we “build the technology in the right way,” which involves – surprise, surprise – the government slowing down potential competitors and allowing the labs to take the lead in advancing the relevant tech. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman quickly ​tweeted his support​ for this brave plan.

Internally, these labs have long embraced this style of messianic thinking, casting themselves as humanity’s only hope against the defied powers of superintelligent AI. This summer, in some sense, was their attempt to induct the rest of us into this long-held ideology.

It didn’t work.

Instead of inspiring the masses to stand up and applaud these engineers’ heroic rationalism, it made us instead start to ask, “What the hell is going on over in those labs?”

To that end, last Thursday ​I published an op-ed in TheNew York Times​ calling on Congress to begin a public fact-finding mission to uncover what research projects OpenAI and Anthropic are conducting, how they’re conducting them, and for what purposes.

I suggested three key areas to explore with this questioning:

  1. We must move past vague discussions of “AI” and instead isolate the specific types of systems that are creating problems. The frontier labs want us to think of AI as a singular technology on an inevitable, fixed trajectory. In reality, most of the problems in recent months result from a​ narrow band of incautious experiments​, conducted mainly by the frontier labs. They need to justify why they’re running them.
  2. We must examine the internal safety procedures surrounding these research efforts. ​OpenAI revealed​ a long series of unauthorized hacking attacks by their autonomous agents. Why weren’t these efforts stopped after the first such incident was revealed? Why not pursue criminal liability for them running systems they knew would likely commit crimes?
  3. We have to investigate the role of apocalyptic futurist ideologies in the decisions being made by the frontier labs, both about what research to pursue and how fast to pursue it. I’m increasingly concerned that OpenAI and Anthropic, in particular, are becoming increasingly reckless because they believe collateral damage is justified in a race to redeem humanity. (For more on these beliefs and their connections to the labs, see: ​this​ and ​this​ and ​this​, all published in the Times in just the last several weeks.)

“We need to stop letting a small number of private companies, acting and talking in increasingly erratic ways, dictate how we’re supposed to feel about A.I.,” I concluded. “We’ve heard what they want to say; now it’s Congress’s turn to step in on our behalf to find out what’s really going on.”

issues.title: Superintelligence is a Fairy Tale. But Chasing It Can Still Cause Harm.
issues.summary: Yesterday, multiple Anthropic employees casually announced online that they thought the types of AI they’re building could kill billions of people. Not in some distant ... Read more The post Superintelligence is a Fairy Tale. But Chasing It Can Still Cause Harm. appeared first on Cal Newport .
issues.author: Cal Newport
issues.content_html:
Yesterday, multiple Anthropic employees casually announced online that they thought the types of AI they’re building could kill billions of people. Not in some distant hypothetical future, but in the next few years. Understandably, this created a tsunami of media attention and anxious discussion.

I added to this debate with a ​brief essay​ of my own. I fear, however, that in the Sturm und Drang of that charged news cycle, some of my conclusions might have been hard to follow. So, I thought it would be useful to publish three short follow-up points that summarize my core claims more directly…

Point #1:Anthropic and OpenAI arenotable to create superintelligent AI.

The Anthropic employees who spoke out yesterday believe the force that might wipe out humanity will be “superintelligent” AI systems that are much too capable for us to control. Let me be clear: We have no idea how to create such machines. We don’t even know if they’re possible. And if they are possible, we are many, many key technical innovations away from getting there. (Simply scaling LLMs won’t be nearly enough.)

The LLM labs attempt to sidestep this reality ​by claiming​ their models will figure this all out on their own, programming better versions of themselves that will be far more capable than anything us measly humans can conceive. But this is just a warmed-over version of the recursive self-improvement trope that Silicon Valley futurists have been peddling ​since the 1960s​; a rhetorical crutch that lets you somberly discuss sci-fi scenarios without actually engaging with relevant technical details.

Point #2:But their obsession with superintelligence can still create real harm.

When you believe,​ as many at OpenAI and Anthropic reportedly do​, that humanity’s fate rests on winning a race to create the most powerful technology ever, you tend to care less about the damage you inflict along the way.

This is what happened with the HuggingFace hacking attacks from this summer. The experiments OpenAI ran were reckless. They took a relatively common technology called an LLM-powered agent, which is used with minimal issues by millions of software developers every day, and ​then added​ a bunch of dangerous features, removed restrictions, and released a whole mess of them into poorly fenced digital wilds. Why? They were desperate to make as much progress as quickly as possible on a hacking test that they felt was an important milestone en route to superintelligence.

This is the equivalent of deploying a fleet of experimental self-driving cars onto the interstate, hoping that at least one will avoid crashing long enough to win a navigation challenge.

In other words, this behavior was negligent. But they likely justified it because it served the far grander goal of summoning a digital God. (Clearly, there may be additional motivations at play here as well. Given OpenAI’s interest in an IPO, for example, there might have been pressure to do well on this particular benchmark to establish their model’s power. But the more I talk to sources connected to these companies, the more I’ve come to believe that their commitment to futurist ideas is what really drives a lot of their more irresponsible behavior.)

Ultimately, I think the HuggingFace attack is a good representation of the types of near-future harm we should actually be fearing if the LLM labs continue to operate as they currently are: that is, more cyber mayhem than catastrophic risk.

But just because these impending harms aren’t nearly as scary as the extinction events touted by the true believers, they’re still plenty worrisome. More importantly, they’re entirely avoidable!

Which brings me to my final point…

Point #3:AI progress does not have to be this scary or dangerous

First things first, it’s important to emphasize something that many media figures and commentators seem to be missing: AI is not the same thing as LLMs. Many of the most impressive AI systems that exist today – including those that beat humans at games, win Nobel prizes for studying proteins, and self-drive cars through crowded city streets – have very little to do with LLMs. Slowing down OpenAI and Anthropic doesn’t mean that you’re stalling AI progress in general. You would only be impacting the subset of AI research that focuses on hyper-scaled LLMs as a central component.

But even when we do focus specifically on LLM-based AI research, none of the harms I described above are unavoidable. They’re instead side effects of reckless experiments motivated by the pursuit of superintelligence.

If the LLM labs simply acted more responsibly, focusing on producing useful products instead of summoning an AI messiah, and following common-sense research safety protocols instead of racing haphazardly toward some imagined utopia, we could be enjoying a steadily advancing AI industry promising tools that excite us, all without having to endure regular doses of dread and fear.

But due to their ideological commitments to superintelligence, these labs seem incapable of such reforms.

This last observation is what’s driving me to advocate for intervention. Those Anthropic employees absurdly implying that they’re willing to risk a digital holocaust to realize their futurist vision was my last straw. They’re far too weird for us to expect them to ever act reasonably.

Please don’t take this as a call for abandoning AI research or somehow ceding AI supremacy to China. Our problem is not with AI progress, but instead with the eccentric way this small group of companies is trying to achieve it. Fix that, and AI innovation can continue, free from all the doom and with much less potential for collateral damage.

The post Superintelligence is a Fairy Tale. But Chasing It Can Still Cause Harm. appeared first on Cal Newport.

issues.title: 20VC x SaaStr: Jensen Out at Nvidia, Anthropic’s $1.4 Trillion IPO, and HubSpot Brings Back Brian Halligan
issues.summary: Plus: why LPs will now grade VCs on $20B+ outcomes, why SMBs stopped buying software, and what a two-day Microsoft outage says about how fragile everything has become There was more news this week than in almost any week since Harry, Rory and I started doing this together. Nvidia lost its founder. Anthropic got set... Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
Plus: why LPs will now grade VCs on $20B+ outcomes, why SMBs stopped buying software, and what a two-day Microsoft outage says about how fragile everything has become

There was more news this week than in almost any week since Harry, Rory and I started doing this together. Nvidia lost its founder. Anthropic got set to price the largest IPO ever. HubSpot went back to its founder. Microsoft 365 went down for most of two days. We recorded Monday, before Anthropic priced and before anyone knew whether Jensen would come back. Here are the 11 things that mattered most, followed by the best lines from each of us.

1. Jensen Huang Resigned After 33 Years, and Rory and I Disagree on Whether He Comes Back

What happened: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s president, chief executive and a member of its board, effective immediately, with CFO Colette Kress serving as interim CEO while the company searches for a permanent successor. The trigger: Huang admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy and Megaspeed executive, and after the board opened an investigation, a second alleged affair was reported involving a direct report. Separately, Commerce and Justice are looking at chips sold into Southeast Asian data centers that may have served Chinese customers. A petition to bring him back drew around 200,000 signatures, and by Monday Jensen said he’d return if asked.

Rory’s read: Decisions made in haste are usually wrong. He would have pushed for a leave of absence and an interim CEO to buy time. Four or five of these directors have been on the board for 30 years, and Jensen is the most important business relationship of their lives. For them to vote against him, something serious had to be going on. His gut says no return without a board change.

My read: I think there’s a high chance he comes back. The spy story will fade. The export issue is bigger, possibly 20% of revenue counting China, but if Jensen is guilty, so is the CFO who signed the financials. Colette Kress now has to stand behind the guidance she signed as CFO. Her job, more than his, was to know where every GPU went.

Rory’s twist: If he owned 100% of the stock, Jensen is the person he’d most want running Nvidia. But even if he returns, Rory doesn’t think he gets back the freedom to finance the AI ecosystem. The minute he left, everyone started trashing the circular deals they’d cheered for two years.

2. Anthropic Is the Biggest Winner of the Nvidia Mess

What happened: Jensen’s biggest strategic push heading into 2027 was a credible U.S. open-weight alternative, including a pending acquisition of Hugging Face. Reports say some Anthropic people were pleased with how the week went.

Rory’s read: The S-1 says roughly $10B went into training Anthropic’s last model. Nobody but Nvidia had the money and motive to fund a serious U.S. open-weight effort. If that stalls, and China pressure pushes buyers away from Chinese open models, the winner is the closed-weight U.S. provider with pricing power. Anthropic isn’t a big Nvidia customer. OpenAI is.

My read: Nvidia’s remote data centers near China were legal at the time. They no longer are. But if you’re Anthropic watching your models get distilled a few hundred miles from your biggest competitors, that loophole looked like theft. I don’t know that Dario is gloating. It’s still a real boost.

What the Nvidia board should have done

“One of the things I have learned is decisions in haste are often wrong.

Take a leave of absence. We need to figure this out, get to the bottom of it and slow the whole thing down so you can make a better decision.

When I have made dumb… https://t.co/sNw1Sh7qAZpic.twitter.com/BcJiPIsu25

— Harry Stebbings (@HarryStebbings) November 19, 2026

3. Anthropic Will Hit $100B in Revenue With 1/12th the Employees Google Had at the Same Size

What happened: The 825 million-share offering could raise up to $64.4 billion at a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion, with pricing expected November 18. The IPO was reported six times oversubscribed, and could raise as much as $90.4 billion including a $26 billion private placement. Trading on Nasdaq as ANT was set to start November 19.

My read: The oversubscribed book is the least interesting part. At $100B in revenue, Google had 81,000 employees and Meta had 71,000. Anthropic will get there, likely by Q1 on run-rate, with fewer than 6,000. Yes, $10B goes to compute instead of humans. But that’s 1/12th the headcount, versus the roughly 30% smaller go-to-market teams at AI-native companies like Harvey and Sierra. For jobs, that’s worse than anything we’ve discussed.

Rory’s pushback: This is the extreme case of compute leverage, which is why the people there get paid so much. An old-school consulting firm won’t end up with $5 to $7 of inference per $1 of labor. He thinks it’ll be less grim for jobs than I do.

Harry’s addition: The rumored 40% layoffs at ServiceNow. Unconfirmed, but I think it’s real.

At $100 billion in revenue Anthropic got there with 1/12 the employees that Google had.

“At $100BN in revenue, Google had 81,000 employees. Meta had 71,000. Anthropic will have fewer than 6,000.

The next $100BN company got there with a 12th of the employees of Google and Meta.… https://t.co/sNw1Sh7Yqxpic.twitter.com/MGRWSNjivv

— Harry Stebbings (@HarryStebbings) November 19, 2026

4. LPs Will Now Grade VCs on How Many $20B+ Companies They Own

What happened: Anthropic went from founding to a trillion-dollar listing in about five years. SpaceX took more than two decades. Spark and Menlo led the key early rounds. Sound Ventures turned roughly $435M into about $7B.

Rory’s read: Spark and Menlo will play with house money for years, and everyone else will work just as hard for a tenth or a twentieth of the return. That’s an extreme power law, and it can get in your head. No meaningful venture money got into Anthropic below $5B, and Spark came in from its growth fund while the company was pre-revenue. If only 10 or 20 companies a cycle reach $20B+, the odds of landing one at seed or A go down. That favors the early-plus-growth fund structure.

My read: When I started, one unicorn was enough for LPs to come find you. Now it’s how many $20B+ companies you have, ideally bought below $20B. Carta’s Q3 2026 data shows deal count down 21% and dollars up 2.5x. Fewer rounds, much bigger checks.

Harry’s addition: LPs getting Anthropic distributions will redeploy, and early Anthropic employees are already angel investing in U.K. companies.

5. Every Mega Fund Is Raising Again in Q1 2027

What happened: The mega platforms all raised in Q1 2026. Every one of them is now lining up to raise again starting January 1, roughly 12 months later.

Rory’s read: When you raise money quickly, you usually don’t make as much. The smartest Anthropic checks were written in early 2023 and 2024, when people were scared.

My read: Deployment pace is feeding the markups. Do the best AI companies justify $10B to $20B to $40B in six months? On a spreadsheet, sure. But some of it is the need to deploy justifying itself. If 8x funds compress to 3x or 4x, maybe that’s fine.

6. IC: $200M Into Mercor at $20B, a Pass on Kalshi and Fractile

What happened: Kalshi is in talks to raise fresh capital at a valuation of $65 billion, roughly 62.5% above the $40 billion valuation it locked in only weeks earlier. Mercor, a leader in AI training data, is raising at $20B. Fractile, an inference chip startup competing with Groq and Cerebras, is raising $720M at $7.5B.

My read: A weak lineup after last week’s Zipline, Fal and Revolut. Kalshi at $65B carries too much regulatory and litigation risk. Fractile has no revenue and is the 11,000th inference chip startup. Mercor is a great space because the labs don’t want this work, but I can’t predict the future of the dirty work. I’d pick it because we have to put money to work.

Harry’s read: Bull on all three. Kalshi leads a monster U.S. sports betting market, and states will get too addicted to the revenue to ban it. Mercor could see $10B of spend from the labs. Fractile has a reported $250M order from Anthropic, and chips are specializing.

Rory’s read: At this stage, every company is good. The only question is value relative to TAM. Cerebras is public at roughly $1B of revenue this year, valued in the high $20Bs. Would he buy Fractile over that? He doesn’t know. Mercor has five or ten customers, but each may spend a billion on training data. For Kalshi at around $5B in revenue, the question is the sober TAM: how many bored 25-year-old guys bet on sports?

The decision: $200M into Mercor at $20B.

7. Without Jensen, the Liquidation Preference Got Weaker

What happened: Nvidia’s run of acqui-hires and backstops, including talks around Reflection and the pending Hugging Face deal, is now in doubt. Poolside sold because it couldn’t raise the capital it needed.

My read: For two years, a lot of AI deals carried an unspoken safety net: Nvidia or a friend would buy the team or backstop the round. I don’t think the CFO-turned-CEO is going to buy all these kids for $15B or $17B. If Salesforce also sits out 2027 digesting this year’s deals, it’s a very different year from the “you can’t lose with a liq pref” year of 2026. Will Thinking Machines survive? I don’t know.

Rory’s read: Washington is split, with Commerce and Lutnick in the sell-to-China camp and Rubio in the don’t-sell camp. You’re dealing with a government that’s mad at itself, which could mean two years of regulators kicking back any acquisition. He hopes Hugging Face got a good breakup fee.

Harry’s read: Nearly perfect timing on Hugging Face, assuming it closes.

8. HubSpot Went From 10,000 Net New Customers a Quarter to Guiding Below 5,000

What happened: Co-founder Brian Halligan returned as CEO, replacing Yamini Rangan in an abrupt leadership reset as the company races to reposition around AI agents. Its shares have halved this year, and Adobe’s Karen Burgess will become finance chief. Halligan called it a refounding, with HubSpot as a “customer relationship harness.”

My read: HubSpot added about 10,000 net new customers a quarter like clockwork, even through the 2024 downturn. Then 6,000, then 5,000, and now guiding below that. Monday.com went from roughly 1,200 net new 10-plus-seat customers to under 200. Net new logos were always my lighthouse metric, and price increases can mask the decline for years. Founder energy will help. The question is whether it’s enough, fast enough. And Intercom doesn’t prove what VCs say it does. Eoghan came back and went all-in on agents, and it worked, but it got to roughly $100M of agentic revenue and we never saw the next act.

Rory’s read: No B2B company from the pre-AI era has reaccelerated above 30%. At a billion in revenue, you’re playing to push growth back to 25%, while a Sierra growing 4x gets all the sizzle. Scale backed HubSpot’s Series C in 2010, and he isn’t sure a 100-person HubSpot customer has an opinion on “harnesses.” But when boards’ backs are against the wall, they bring the founder back, and in each recent case it was right.

Harry’s read: He asked Daniel Dines why he’d go back to UiPath. Man loves to struggle, and founders who’ve already made their money come back with an aggression outside CEOs can’t match.

9. SMBs Stopped Buying Software, but They Buy an $800 Receptionist Agent the Same Day

What happened: Net new customer counts at HubSpot and Monday.com have fallen sharply over three quarters, and Ramp data shows newer CRMs like Attio picking up only a small amount of that spend.

My read: This isn’t vibe coding. Your average SMB isn’t building its own CRM. They’re just not buying, running Google Sheets plus ChatGPT another six months rather than spend $40K on HubSpot. Meanwhile, three of my portfolio companies selling $500 to $1,000 a month front-office agents close prospects the same day. The SMB’s P0 is “my receptionist quits every Wednesday,” not a Kanban board.

Rory’s read: The truth is in the middle. Every associate at his firm has built a Claude front end on Salesforce, and nobody logs into Salesforce anymore. Granted, they went to HBS and work in San Francisco.

Harry’s read: Monday’s users are not vibe coding their own CRM.

10. Microsoft 365 Was Down for Two Days, and Fireworks Got Called Out by Its Own Customers

What happened: Microsoft says its Microsoft 365 services are fully operational again after a global outage that ran from November 12 to November 14, 2026. An issue linked to an earlier network-capacity upgrade surfaced after a more recent network change. The FAA also had a nationwide ground stop tied to a contractor’s router problem. Notion, Cursor and Harvey all publicly named Fireworks after a breach, and an Optimizely compromise hit sites including CNN, the BBC and Zoom.

Harry’s read: Air traffic control, Microsoft, the NSA’s internal comms. He’s never seen systems this fragile. The FAA outage was straight out of Die Hard 2.

Rory’s read: These were old-school IT failures, not AI attacks. When DocuSign got big, he brought in a board member with a cyber background who told the team: you’re going to get hacked, here’s what you spend. Mission-critical companies need that seriousness now.

My read: It’s DDoS 2.0. Microsoft’s bug sat in production for four months until load hit a new level. Now anyone can spin up 10,000 agents and probe every network with traffic, load and hacking at once. We want one-person billion-dollar startups, and those products will have close to zero security. I’m not sure you should trust any web analytics plugin, or any new payments startup besides Stripe or Adyen.

Harry’s addition: Fireworks has a world-class engineering team. If it still happened to them, everyone should be worried.

11. OpenAI Bought Adessia, and Horizontal Agents Are Already Locking In

What happened: OpenAI acquired Adessia, a travel-focused personal agent founded by Sonder founder Francis Davidson. Harry’s question: are vertical personal assistants over?

My read: I’m all-in on Muse, Meta’s horizontal agent. It runs our outbound, content editing, clips and attendee analysis, and reranks every inbound venture deal each night. Mine and Amelia’s coordinate with each other without telling us. With 20 or 30 workflows running, a shallow moat has gotten wide. And this is how SMB software gets displaced: you get a $30K HubSpot quote, realize Muse can do more of it than you thought, and push the purchase out.

Harry’s read: He has about 50 automations on Instinct. Switching would be a real pain.

Rory’s read: Power users will gravitate to whoever can give them the most functionality at a tenth of the cost, and that’s Meta. If most users don’t need that much compute, Instinct has a chance. Still scary when a company with 4 to 5 billion users ships something more powerful than yours. It didn’t work for Threads, though.

On the workforce: Harry’s biggest challenge is getting teams to ask “could an agent do this?” first. My view: our agents now do all our collections, replacing a contractor who billed $3,000 to $4,000 a month. You won’t fire people. They’ll leave, and you won’t backfill. We went from 20 people to 3 humans and 21 agents. Rory’s counter: someone then spends 6 to 10 hours a day managing agents.

On SpaceX, briefly: Rory called Starship one of the year’s top five achievements. But launch is under 10% of SpaceX’s market cap, and most of the TAM is compute. You buy SpaceX based on whether Anthropic is buying more compute a year from now.

Quotable Moments

Rory O’Driscoll

  • “If I owned 100% of the stock of this company, the person on the planet I would most want to run this company is Jensen.”
  • “You’re not just dealing with a government that might be mad at you. You’re dealing with a government that might be mad at itself.”
  • “You buy SpaceX the stock entirely on the basis of what you think Anthropic will be paying you one year from now for that compute.”

Jason Lemkin

  • “At $100 billion in revenue, Google had 81,000 employees. Meta had 71,000. Anthropic will have less than 6,000.”
  • “I think the liquidation preference has been weakened by the Nvidia drama.”
  • “You know what my P0 is? My receptionist quits every Wednesday. That’s what people want to buy. Not Kanban crap.”

Harry Stebbings

  • “Every single fund is queuing up out the door for Jan 1. We have to get the bag.”
  • “Man loves to struggle.”
  • “Right now the clips that you make, we can’t do with AI. In a year we will be able to. You need to get better or you will be replaced.”

issues.title: The Top 10 Metrics From Anthropic’s IPO for B2B Execs: $33 Billion in Nine Months, 900% NRR, and 12x More $100K Customers in a Year
